questions.title: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q95 — Quantifiers and a wrapping function
questions.text: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q95 — Quantifiers and a wrapping function Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 21 · question 95 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. In a model with domain { 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } , f ( n ) = n + 1 ( mod 5 ) and R ( x , y ) means x < y . Evaluate (a) ∀ x ∃ y R ( x , y ) and ( b ) ∀ x ∀ y ( R ( x , y ) ⇒ R ( f ( x ) , f ( y ) ) ) . 1. Only (a) is true. 2. Only (b) is true. 3. Both are true. 4. Neither is true. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. Statement (a) fails at x = 4 : there is no larger domain element. A universal statement is false after one counterexample. Statement (b) is an implication, so a counterexample must make its antecedent true. Take x = 3 , y = 4 . Then 3 < 4 , but f ( 3 ) = 4 and f ( 4 ) = 0 , so the consequent 4 < 0 is false. Both statements are false. Testing only adjacent pairs that do not cross the wrap would miss the decisive boundary. Options 1 and 2 incorrectly assert one universal formula; option 3 asserts both. Transfer rule. Test extremal domain values and discontinuities of the interpretation before attempting a complete table.

questions.title: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q97 — Assignments in a finite model
questions.text: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q97 — Assignments in a finite model Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 21 · question 97 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. The domain is { 0 , 1 , 2 } ; c = 0 ; f ( 0 ) = 1 , f ( 1 ) = 2 , f ( 2 ) = 0 ; R = { ( 0 , 1 ) , ( 1 , 2 ) , ( 2 , 0 ) } . For ϕ ( x ) = ∀ y ( R ( x , y ) ⇒ R ( f ( y ) , c ) ) , let v 1 ( x ) = 0 and v 2 ( x ) = 2 . Under which assignments is ϕ true? 1. Only v 1 . 2. Only v 2 . 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. For x = 0 , only y = 1 makes the antecedent true. Its consequent is R ( f ( 1 ) , 0 ) = R ( 2 , 0 ) , which is true. The other two implications are vacuously true. For x = 2 , the relevant witness is y = 0 . Its consequent is R ( f ( 0 ) , 0 ) = R ( 1 , 0 ) , which is false. Therefore the universal formula fails. Only v 1 satisfies the formula. Options 2 and 3 overlook the failed consequent for v 2 ; option 4 overlooks vacuous implications and the successful successor for v 1 . Transfer rule. First identify the assignments that satisfy an implication's antecedent, then apply the interpreted function in the consequent.

questions.title: Question 3. MSc CS 1405, Q99 — Canonical CNF from true rows
questions.text: Question 3. MSc CS 1405, Q99 — Canonical CNF from true rows Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 22 · question 99 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. A formula in A , B , C is true exactly on rows 110 , 100 , 011 , 001 . Does its canonical conjunctive normal form include (a) ¬ A ∨ ¬ B ∨ ¬ C and ( b ) A ∨ B ∨ C ? 1. Only (a). 2. Only ( b ). 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Canonical CNF contains one maxterm for each false row. A maxterm is false at its designated row. Clause (a) is false at 111; that row is absent from the true-row list, so (a) occurs. Clause (b) is false at 000; that row is also false, so (b) occurs. The other false rows are 010 and 101. Their clauses complete the canonical CNF. The function simplifies to A ⊕ C , but the question asks which canonical clauses occur, not which survive minimization. Options 1 and 2 omit a required maxterm; option 4 omits both. Transfer rule. Minterms are indexed by true rows; maxterms by false rows. Canonical and minimized forms answer different questions.

questions.title: Question 4. PhD CS 1405, Q13 — Evaluate a finite relational specification
questions.text: Question 4. PhD CS 1405, Q13 — Evaluate a finite relational specification Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 13 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. The universe is { 01 , 02 , 03 , 04 , 05 , 06 , 07 , 08 , 09 } ; girls are { 03 , 06 , 09 } ; boys are { 02 , 04 , 05 , 08 } ; the love relation is E = { ( 03 , 02 ) , ( 06 , 08 ) , ( 04 , 03 ) , ( 09 , 02 ) } . Evaluate (a) every girl loves exactly one boy; (b) some boy loves some girl. 1. Only (a). 2. Only ( b ). 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Restrict the first coordinate of E to girls. The three girls have respectively the unique targets 02, 08, and 02, all boys. Thus (a) is true. The pair ( 04 , 03 ) witnesses ( b ): 04 is a boy and 03 is a girl. Uniqueness in (a) is per girl, not a requirement that different girls have different targets. Shared target 02 is permitted. The distractors confuse uniqueness with injectivity or read an ordered pair in reverse. Transfer rule. Separate domain restrictions, existence, and uniqueness; a relation is not automatically a one-to-one function.

questions.title: Question 5. PhD CS 1405, Q14 — Translate a nested conditional with an exception
questions.text: Question 5. PhD CS 1405, Q14 — Translate a nested conditional with an exception Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 14 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. B ( x ) means that x is a boy, E ( x , y ) that x likes y , and H ( x , y ) that x dislikes y . Translate: Every boy who likes Maryam dislikes every other boy whom Maryam likes. Use M for Maryam. 1. ∀ x ( ( B ( x ) ∧ E ( x , M ) ) ∧ ∀ y ( ( B ( y ) ∧ E ( M , y ) ) ⇒ H ( x , y ) ) ) 2. ∀ x ( ( B ( x ) ∧ E ( x , M ) ) ∧ ∀ y ( ( B ( y ) ∧ E ( M , y ) ∧ y ≠ x ) ⇒ H ( x , y ) ) ) 3. ∀ x ( ( B ( x ) ∧ E ( x , M ) ) ⇒ ∀ y ( ( B ( y ) ∧ E ( M , y ) ) ⇒ H ( x , y ) ) ) 4. ∀ x ( ( B ( x ) ∧ E ( x , M ) ) ⇒ ∀ y ( ( B ( y ) ∧ E ( M , y ) ∧ y ≠ x ) ⇒ H ( x , y ) ) ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. The subject restriction is conditional: only x values satisfying B ( x ) ∧ E ( x , M ) create an obligation. The target restriction is also conditional, and other requires y ≠ x . The direction of liking is E ( M , y ) , not E ( y , M ) . Option 4 expresses all three requirements. Options 1 and 2 use a conjunction at the outer level and incorrectly assert every object is a boy who likes Maryam. Option 3 requires self-dislike when Maryam likes x , because it omits the exception. A model containing any nonboy immediately refutes the outer conjunction alternatives without affecting the English statement. Transfer rule. Translate restricted universal claims using implications; encode exceptions inside the target restriction.

questions.title: Question 7. PhD CS 1405, Q22 — Canonical product of maxterms
questions.text: Question 7. PhD CS 1405, Q22 — Canonical product of maxterms Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 22 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. What is the canonical product-of-maxterms form of ( p ⇒ r ) ∧ ( p ⇔ q ) , with index order p , q , r ? 1. ∑ m ( 0 , 1 , 7 ) 2. ∏ M ( 0 , 1 , 3 , 4 , 6 ) 3. ∑ m ( 2 , 5 , 7 ) 4. ∏ M ( 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. The equivalence forces p = q . If both are zero, the implication is true regardless of r , giving indices 0 and 1. If both are one, r must be one, giving index 7. All remaining indices 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 are false. The canonical product includes the corresponding maxterms, giving option 4. Option 1 is the equivalent canonical sum, but the question requests a product. Option 2 uses the wrong zero rows; option 3 is both the wrong form and the wrong function. Keep the source variable order: permuting bit significance changes the indices. Transfer rule. Enumerate satisfying rows, then complement their index set when a product-of-maxterms form is requested.

questions.title: Question 8. A formula with conditional and parity constraints
questions.text: Question 8. A formula with conditional and parity constraints Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q99; Phd_CS_1405_Q22. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. How many assignments to p , q , r , s satisfy ( p ⇔ q ) ∧ ( p ⇒ r ) ∧ ( r ⊕ s ) ? 1. 2 2. 3 3. 4 4. 6 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. First force q = p . If p = 0 , the implication permits either value of r ; each determines exactly one s through XOR, giving two assignments. If p = 1 , then r = 1 and s = 0 , giving one more. The total is three. Count cases after propagating equalities. Four treats r as free even when p = 1 ; six fails to enforce all dependent choices; two omits the valid all-one antecedent case. This is a model count, not a count of distinct syntactic formulas.

questions.title: Question 9. The exact CNF index set
questions.text: Question 9. The exact CNF index set Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q99; Phd_CS_1405_Q15. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. The true rows of F ( p , q , r ) have indices 1, 2, 4, and 7, with p the most significant bit. Which canonical product of maxterms represents F ? 1. ∏ M ( 1 , 2 , 4 , 7 ) 2. ∏ M ( 0 , 3 , 5 , 6 ) 3. ∑ m ( 0 , 3 , 5 , 6 ) 4. ∏ M ( 0 , 2 , 4 , 6 ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The full index set is zero through seven. Complement the given true indices to obtain false indices 0, 3, 5, and 6. Canonical CNF contains a maxterm for each of those false rows, so the second option is correct. The first product represents the complemented function. The third is a sum rather than the requested product and also selects the complemented truth set. The final product corresponds to a fixed least-significant-bit condition. As a cross-check, the stated true rows have an odd number of true bits, so this function is three-input parity.

questions.title: Question 10. A cyclic successor and two universal formulas
questions.text: Question 10. A cyclic successor and two universal formulas Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q95; MS_CS_1405_Q97. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. The domain is { 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 } , f ( x ) = x + 1 ( mod 4 ) , and R ( x , y ) means y = f ( x ) . Assess ( I ) ∀ x ∃ y ( R ( x , y ) ∧ R ( y , x ) ) and (II) ∀ x ∃ y ∃ z ( R ( x , y ) ∧ R ( y , z ) ∧ R ( z , f ( x ) ) ) . 1. Only I . 2. Only II. 3. Both. 4. Neither. questions.title: Question 11. Translate exactly one without an accidental injection
questions.text: Question 11. Translate exactly one without an accidental injection Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q13; Phd_CS_1405_Q14. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Every researcher reviews exactly one paper, but several researchers may review the same paper. Which formula states this, with predicates R ( x ) , P ( y ) , V ( x , y ) ? 1. ∀ x ( R ( x ) ⇒ ∃ y ( P ( y ) ∧ V ( x , y ) ∧ ∀ z ( ( P ( z ) ∧ V ( x , z ) ) ⇒ z = y ) ) ) 2. ∀ y ( P ( y ) ⇒ ∃ ! x ( R ( x ) ∧ V ( x , y ) ) ) 3. ∀ x ∃ y ( R ( x ) ∧ P ( y ) ∧ V ( x , y ) ) 4. ∃ y ( P ( y ) ∧ ∀ x ( R ( x ) ⇒ V ( x , y ) ) ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The first formula imposes existence for each researcher and makes every other reviewed paper equal to the chosen paper. It does not compare choices made by different researchers, so shared targets are allowed. The second reverses the source and target roles and requires exactly one researcher per paper. The third asserts that every domain object is a researcher and supplies no uniqueness clause. The fourth requires one common paper for all researchers, which the statement does not require. Here ∃ ! in option two abbreviates existence and uniqueness, rather than a new primitive proof rule.

questions.title: Question 12. An implication under an empty restriction
questions.text: Question 12. An implication under an empty restriction Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q14; Phd_CS_1405_Q16. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A nonempty model has no objects satisfying A ( x ) . Which pair of truth values belongs to ∀ x ( A ( x ) ⇒ B ( x ) ) and ∃ x ( A ( x ) ∧ B ( x ) ) ? 1. True, true. 2. True, false. 3. False, true. 4. False, false. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. For every domain object the implication has a false antecedent, hence is true. Its universal closure is true. The existential conjunction requires an A witness, but none exists, so it is false. The nonempty domain does not ensure that a restricted predicate has a witness. Options one and three invent an A object; options three and four also confuse vacuous truth with failure of universal quantification. This distinction is essential when converting an English subject restriction into a formula.

Which statement must follow? 1. s ⇒ p 2. p ⇒ s 3. q ⇒ p 4. ¬ s ⇒ r Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Rewrite the third premise as q ⇒ s . questions.title: Question 14. Count assignments with precisely two true implications
questions.text: Question 14. Count assignments with precisely two true implications Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q99; Phd_CS_1405_Q22. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Among p ⇒ q , q ⇒ r , and r ⇒ p , exactly two must be true. How many assignments to p , q , r meet this requirement? 1. 2 2. 3 3. 4 4. 6 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. The all-zero and all-one assignments make all three implications true. Each of the other six binary cycles contains exactly one transition from 1 to 0, so exactly one implication is false and two are true. For example, 110 makes the middle implication false and the other two true. Three would count only the rows with a single true variable; four would miscount the mixed rows. The cyclic structure limits the number of false transitions, which is more informative than evaluating each implication independently.

questions.title: Question 15. Negate a uniqueness specification
questions.text: Question 15. Negate a uniqueness specification Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q13; Phd_CS_1405_Q14. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Let S ( x , y ) mean that y is a solution for input x . What is the negation of “every input has exactly one solution”? 1. Every input has no solution. 2. Some input has no solution or at least two distinct solutions. 3. Some input has exactly two solutions. 4. Every input has at least two solutions. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Write the original as ∀ x ∃ y ( S ( x , y ) ∧ ∀ z ( S ( x , z ) ⇒ z = y ) ) . Negating the outer universal supplies an input at which existence or uniqueness fails. Existence fails when no y satisfies S . Uniqueness fails when two distinct solutions both satisfy S . Their disjunction is the complete negation. Exactly two excludes three or infinitely many solutions, while the universal alternatives change the quantifier and are too strong.

This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. There are n + 2 Boolean variables. The constraints are x 1 ⇔ x 2 and x 2 ⇒ x 3 ; all other variables are free. Those expressions discard or alter a condition in the model; the derivation above shows where the discrepancy enters. Recomputing the defining constraints, rather than selecting the numerically nearest option, determines the answer.

questions.title: Question 19. Equalities followed by one implication — applicability and boundary
questions.text: Question 19. Equalities followed by one implication — applicability and boundary Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q95; MS_CS_1405_Q97. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. There are n + 2 Boolean variables. The constraints are x 1 ⇔ x 2 and x 2 ⇒ x 3 ; all other variables are free. Count satisfying assignments. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? 1. The implication leaves all four pair assignments legal. 2. Changing an implication to equivalence never changes the model count. 3. Adding another equality between two previously free variables generally halves the count. 4. An equality always doubles the count. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Check the hypothesis. An equality replaces two independent bits by one bit. In this model there are at least two free variables. Requiring those bits to agree removes one independent binary choice; the constrained three-variable component is unchanged. Connect it to the calculation. Identify x 1 with x 2 . The allowed pair values of ( x 2 , x 3 ) are 00, 01 and 11. The remaining n - 1 variables are independently free, so multiply three allowed pairs by their Boolean choices. Do not multiply by an extra choice for x 1 . The valid statement is: Adding another equality between two previously free variables generally halves the count. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule. Distinguish the mathematical identity from the modeling assumptions that permit this identity to count or measure the requested objects.

questions.title: Question 52. Count two-sided logical specifications
questions.text: Question 52. Count two-sided logical specifications Original integrated challenge · retained after review For four Boolean atoms, G = p ∧ q and H = p ∨ r . How many functions F ( p , q , r , s ) satisfy both G ⇒ F and F ⇒ H on every row? 1. 16 2. 64 3. 256 4. 4096 Correct option: 3. First check compatibility: every row with G = 1 has p = 1 and therefore H = 1 . Among sixteen rows, G is true on four, while H is true on twelve. Thus four outputs are forced1, four forced0, and eight free. The count is 2 8 = 256 . Free rows are the difference of the two true sets, not the full H set. The otherwise unused atom s doubles each relevant row count and cannot be discarded when counting tables.

questions.title: Question 53. Mix row and column constraints
questions.text: Question 53. Mix row and column constraints Original integrated challenge · retained after review On a labeled three-object domain, how many relations satisfy both ∀ x ∃ y R ( x , y ) and ∃ y ∀ x R ( x , y ) ? 1. 169 2. 192 3. 343 4. 512 Correct option: 1. A full column already supplies an outgoing witness in every row, so the second condition implies the first. Count only matrices with at least one full column. Three single-column events each leave six bits free and contribute64; three two-column intersections each leave three bits free and contribute8; the all-column intersection contributes1. Inclusion-exclusion gives 3 ( 64 ) - 3 ( 8 ) + 1 = 169 . Multiplying counts of the two conditions would incorrectly treat them as independent constraints.

questions.title: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q101 — Two tests for a transitive set
questions.text: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q101 — Two tests for a transitive set Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 22 · question 101 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. A set A is transitive when x ∈ y ∈ A implies x ∈ A . Which conditions must hold: (a) ⋃ A ⊆ A ; ( b ) A ⊆ P ( A ) ? 1. Only (a). 2. Only ( b ). 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Every x ∈ ⋃ A lies in some y ∈ A . Transitivity places x in A , proving (a). Fix y ∈ A . Every member of y lies in A , hence y ⊆ A and consequently y ∈ P ( A ) . This proves ( b ). Conversely, either condition implies transitivity: (a) controls every member of a member; (b) says every member of A is a subset of A . Both conditions express the same property. The distractors confuse membership with subset inclusion. Transfer rule. Expand the definitions of union and power set into element statements before comparing them.

questions.text: Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q25 — A subset containing an odd pair sum Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 25 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. How many four-element subsets A of { 1 , 2 , … , 10 } contain two elements x , y such that x + y is odd? 1. 200 2. 205 3. 208 4. 209 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. A sum is odd exactly when one summand is even and the other odd. Thus the set must contain both parities. There are ( 10 4 ) = 210 unrestricted subsets. The failing subsets consist entirely of the five even or entirely of the five odd elements. Subtract 2 ( 5 4 ) = 10 to get 200. The two failure classes are disjoint, so no overlap correction is required. Counting a chosen odd/even pair and then two other elements would overcount sets containing several witness pairs. Transfer rule. Count an existential-witness property by its complement when each valid object may have several witnesses.

200

questions.title: Question 5. Recover exactly-two and outside counts
questions.text: Question 5. Recover exactly-two and outside counts Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q21. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Three subsets of a 60-element universe have sizes 25, 22, and 20. Their pairwise intersections have sizes 10, 9, and 8; the triple intersection has size 4. What are the numbers in exactly two sets and in none? 1. 15 and 16. 2. 27 and 16. 3. 15 and 20. 4. 19 and 16. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The sum of pair intersections is 27, but each triple member contributes three. Exactly-two membership is 27 - 3 · 4 = 15 . Inclusion-exclusion gives union size 25 + 22 + 20 - 10 - 9 - 8 + 4 = 44 , so sixteen elements are outside. These data are feasible: exclusive pair cells have sizes 6, 5, and 4; the single-only cells are 10, 8, and 7. The distractors either retain triple overcounts or subtract the triple correction with the wrong sign.

questions.title: Question 7. Power-set difference is not a power set
questions.text: Question 7. Power-set difference is not a power set Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q101; MS_CS_1405_Q37. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. | A | = 4 , | B | = 3 , and | A ∩ B | = 2 . What is | P ( A ) ∖ P ( B ) | ? 1. 4 2. 8 3. 12 4. 16 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. A set belongs to both power sets exactly when it is a subset of A ∩ B . Hence the intersection of the two power sets has size 2 2 = 4 . There are 2 4 = 16 subsets of A , so the requested difference has size 16 - 4 = 12 . It is not P ( A ∖ B ) : a subset using both shared and exclusive elements is still counted in the requested difference. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. | A | = 11 , | B | = 9 , and | A △ B | = 12 . Find | A ∩ B | and | ( A △ B ) △ B | . 1. 4 and 11. 2. 8 and 11. 3. 4 and 12. 4. 4 and 9. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Use | A △ B | = | A | + | B | - 2 | A ∩ B | , yielding an intersection size of four. Membership in symmetric difference is XOR. The two quantities ask different questions: one is recovered numerically, the other follows from algebraic cancellation.

This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Fix B ⊆ U with | U | = 8 and | B | = 3 . How many A ⊆ U satisfy A ∪ B = U and A ∩ B ≠ ∅ ? 1. 7 2. 31 3. 56 4. 63 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Every one of the five elements outside B must lie in A . questions.title: Question 12. A Cartesian-product identity with a boundary case
questions.text: Question 12. A Cartesian-product identity with a boundary case Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q40. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Which identity holds for every set C , including C = ∅ ? 1. ( A ∖ B ) × C = ( A × C ) ∖ ( B × C ) 2. ( A × C ) ∖ ( B × C ) = ( A ∖ B ) × ( C ∖ C ) 3. A × C = B × C ⇒ A = B 4. ( A ∪ B ) × C = ( A × C ) ∩ ( B × C ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. A pair lies in the left side exactly when its first coordinate lies in A but not B and its second coordinate lies in C . This is precisely membership in the right-side product difference. The second proposed identity always has empty right side. The third fails when C is empty and A ≠ B . The fourth would require union on the right, not intersection. Product cancellation requires a nonempty common factor, whereas the distributive difference identity needs no such assumption.

questions.title: Question 16. Element categories under containment — applicability and boundary
questions.text: Question 16. Element categories under containment — applicability and boundary Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Count ordered pairs of subsets ( A , B ) of an n -element labeled universe satisfying A ⊆ B . Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? 1. Proper containment has exactly the same count as containment. 2. Every contained pair must have an empty smaller set. 3. Proper containment requires subtracting pairs with equal sets. 4. Containment permits all four membership states. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Check the hypothesis. Equal pairs have two choices per element and therefore number 2 n . Subtracting them from the containment count gives 3 n - 2 n . Empty and equal pairs are distinct issues; proper containment excludes all equal pairs, not only the empty pair. Connect it to the calculation. Prescribed symmetric difference — applicability and boundary Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Fix a subset D in an n -element universe. Count ordered pairs with A △ B = D . Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? 1. The number depends on the cardinality of the fixed set. 2. The map taking a set to its symmetric difference with a fixed set is a bijection. 3. Symmetric difference with a fixed set is always idempotent. 4. questions.text: Question 45. Two strict inclusions Original integrated challenge · retained after review For a four-element universe, how many ordered triples satisfy A ⊂ B ⊂ C ? 1. 65 2. 81 3. 110 4. 256 Correct option: 3. For nonstrict chains, each element is in none, only C , in B , C , or in all three: four choices, hence256 triples. The failure A = B removes one membership state and has 3 4 = 81 triples; so does B = C . Their intersection has all three sets equal and 2 4 = 16 triples. questions.title: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q98 — Identify a proof rule
questions.text: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q98 — Identify a proof rule Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 21 · question 98 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. A natural-deduction argument assumes ∀ x P ( x , x ) , derives P ( u , u ) by universal elimination, then ∃ z P ( u , z ) by existential introduction. It next obtains ∀ y ∃ z P ( y , z ) and discharges the initial assumption to conclude ∀ x P ( x , x ) ⇒ ∀ y ∃ z P ( y , z ) . Which rule justifies the next-to-last line? 1. Existential elimination. 2. Universal elimination. 3. Universal introduction. 4. Existential introduction. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The derived formula ∃ z P ( u , z ) applies to a fresh, arbitrary parameter u ; the initial assumption does not depend on a particular value of u . Universal introduction may therefore generalize this parameter to y , producing ∀ y ∃ z P ( y , z ) . Universal elimination specializes a universal premise rather than introducing one. Existential introduction was already used to create the z quantifier. Existential elimination would require an existential premise and a scoped witness subproof. The freshness condition matters: generalizing from a special named element would be invalid. Transfer rule. Read both the direction of the quantifier rule and its side condition; matching only the symbol is insufficient.

questions.title: Question 3. MSc CS 1405, Q101 — Two tests for a transitive set
questions.text: Question 3. MSc CS 1405, Q101 — Two tests for a transitive set Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 22 · question 101 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. A set A is transitive when x ∈ y ∈ A implies x ∈ A . Which conditions must hold: (a) ⋃ A ⊆ A ; ( b ) A ⊆ P ( A ) ? 1. Only (a). 2. Only ( b ). 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Every x ∈ ⋃ A lies in some y ∈ A . Transitivity places x in A , proving (a). Fix y ∈ A . Every member of y lies in A , hence y ⊆ A and consequently y ∈ P ( A ) . This proves ( b ). Conversely, either condition implies transitivity: (a) controls every member of a member; (b) says every member of A is a subset of A . Both conditions express the same property. The distractors confuse membership with subset inclusion. Transfer rule. Expand the definitions of union and power set into element statements before comparing them.

questions.title: Question 4. PhD CS 1405, Q16 — Two categorical arguments
questions.text: Question 4. PhD CS 1405, Q16 — Two categorical arguments Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 16 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Assess (a) Some humans are ignorant; all humans are thinkers; therefore some thinkers are ignorant. (b) No ignorant person is a thinker; all humans are thinkers; therefore no human is ignorant. 1. Only (a) is valid. 2. Only (b) is valid. 3. Both are valid. 4. Neither is valid. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. For (a), retain the witness that is both human and ignorant. The universal second premise makes that same witness a thinker, proving the conclusion. For ( b ), assume a human were ignorant. It would also be a thinker by the second premise, contradicting the disjointness of ignorant people and thinkers. Both conclusions follow. The second argument does not need any human to exist: a universal negative conclusion can hold vacuously. The incorrect options either discard the existential witness in (a) or impose an unnecessary existence premise on ( b ). Transfer rule. Track the same existential witness across premises; do not invent existential import for universal assertions.

questions.text: Question 6. PhD CS 1405, Q19 — Strict order and injectivity Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 19 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Evaluate (a) if ( A , < ) is linearly ordered and f : A → A preserves that strict order, then f is injective; (b) every countable set is well-orderable. 1. Only (a). 2. Only ( b ). 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. If x ≠ y , linearity makes either x < y or y < x . Strict preservation gives a strict inequality between the outputs, so the outputs are different. A finite set can be listed in a finite order. A countably infinite set can inherit the natural-number order from a listing/bijection. Each nonempty subset then has a least-indexed member. Thus both claims hold. Preservation of a weak order would not imply (a): a constant map is weakly monotone. The strict symbol in the source is essential. The other options falsely reject one or both arguments. Transfer rule. Read strictness and comparability assumptions before invoking order-based injectivity.

questions.title: Question 7. A congruence implication and its converse
questions.text: Question 7. A congruence implication and its converse Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q38; MS_CS_1405_Q125. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. For integers n , assess ( I ) 6 ∣ n ⇒ 6 ∣ n 2 and (II) 6 ∣ n 2 ⇒ 6 ∣ n . 1. Only I . 2. Only II. 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. I follows by writing n = 6 k . For II, divisibility of n 2 by two implies n is even, and divisibility by three implies n is divisible by three, since two and three are prime. Their coprimality gives 6 ∣ n . The corresponding converse for a non-squarefree divisor can fail: 4 ∣ 2 2 but 4 ∤ 2 . The correct proof therefore uses the prime structure of six, rather than asserting that squaring preserves every divisibility equivalence.

questions.title: Question 9. Which counterexample refutes a universal claim?
questions.text: Question 9. Which counterexample refutes a universal claim? Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q95; Phd_CS_1405_Q16. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. The claim is “for all positive integers a , b , if a + b is even then a and b are both even.” Which pair is a valid counterexample? 1. (2,4). 2. (1,2). 3. (3,5). 4. (0,2). Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. A counterexample must satisfy the domain, make the antecedent true, and make the consequent false. The pair ( 3 , 5 ) consists of positive integers with even sum eight, but neither is even. The first pair satisfies the conclusion and is not a counterexample. The second has odd sum and therefore does not activate the implication. Zero violates the stated positive domain in the last pair. This three-part check avoids a common mistake: refuting the conclusion where the theorem makes no assertion.

questions.text: Question 10. Two forms of evidence Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q98; Phd_CE_1405_Q3. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A formula P ( n ) has been verified for 1 ≤ n ≤ 10 6 . Which additional statement proves it for all positive integers? 1. It also holds at 10 6 + 1 . 2. For every n ≥ 1 , P ( n ) ⇒ P ( n + 1 ) . 3. A random integer above 10 6 satisfies it. 4. No counterexample was found. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The verified range contains the base case P ( 1 ) . A universal valid successor implication propagates truth from that base through all positive integers, completing induction. One more check still leaves infinitely many untested inputs. A random success and absence of a found counterexample are evidence, not a proof of a universal theorem. The second statement must itself be proved; assuming it merely repeats the missing obligation.

questions.title: Question 11. Witnesses depend on quantifier order
questions.text: Question 11. Witnesses depend on quantifier order Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q14; MS_CS_1405_Q95. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Over the integers, compare ( I ) ∀ x ∃ y ( y > x ) and (II) ∃ y ∀ x ( y > x ) . 1. Both are true. 2. Only I is true. 3. Only II is true. 4. Both are false. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. For I , choose y = x + 1 after the input x is known. It is an integer and larger than x . For II, any proposed fixed witness y is defeated by choosing x = y . The strict inequality then fails. A witness depending on the universal variable cannot be used before that variable has been chosen. The difference is dependency, not the number of symbols or the domain's nonemptiness.

This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. For positive x , y with x + y = 10 , which statement is correct? 1. x y ≥ 25 , equality iff x = y . 2. x y ≤ 25 , equality iff x = y = 5 . 3. x y < 25 for every such pair. 4. x y = 25 for every such pair. questions.title: Question 13. What follows from inconsistency?
questions.text: Question 13. What follows from inconsistency? Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q16; MS_CS_1405_Q98. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. In classical propositional logic, premises include p and ¬ p . Which statement is correct? 1. Only contradictions can be derived. 2. An arbitrary formula q is derivable, and the premise set has no satisfying assignment. 3. Every formula becomes a tautology. 4. A satisfying assignment exists with p both true and false. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. From p infer p ∨ q . Combine it with ¬ p by disjunctive syllogism to obtain q . Semantically, no assignment satisfies both premises, so entailment from this premise set is vacuous. Derivability under inconsistent assumptions does not make q a tautology under no assumptions. Classical assignments give each variable one truth value, not both. Keeping the premises attached to a conclusion distinguishes explosion from a change in the logic's definition of validity.

questions.title: Question 14. A false cancellation in a proof
questions.text: Question 14. A false cancellation in a proof Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q40; Phd_CS_1405_Q19. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A proof starts with x = y ≠ 0 , obtains ( x - y ) ( x + y ) = y ( x - y ) , cancels x - y , and concludes 2 = 1 . Where does it fail? 1. The factorization is false. 2. The assumption x = y ≠ 0 is impossible. 3. It divides by zero. 4. It uses integers instead of reals. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The starting assumption is possible and the displayed identity is true: both sides equal zero when x = y . The cancelled factor x - y is exactly zero. Cancellation in a field is justified only for a nonzero common factor. Since that hypothesis fails, the purported equation x + y = y does not follow. The nonzero condition on x does not make x - y nonzero. Checking the precise divisor, rather than any nearby quantity, exposes the invalid step.

questions.title: Question 47. A universal prime claim
questions.text: Question 47. A universal prime claim Original integrated challenge · retained after review Which n is a counterexample to “ n 2 + n + 41 is prime for every integer n ≥ 0 ”? 1. 0 2. 1 3. 2 4. 40 Correct option: 4. At n = 40 , the value is1600+40+41=1681= 41 2 , a composite. It satisfies the nonnegative-domain premise and falsifies the conclusion. At0,1,2 the values41,43,47 are prime and do not disprove the claim. The argument needs one verified composite, not a characterization of every earlier input. Recognizing that substituting one less than the constant yields its square constructs the counterexample rather than guessing.

questions.title: Question 48. An inequality with domain-sensitive division
questions.text: Question 48. An inequality with domain-sensitive division Original integrated challenge · retained after review For real x > 0 , which statement about x + 1 / x is correct? 1. Its minimum is0. 2. Its minimum is2, attained only at x = 1 . 3. It is always strictly greater than2. 4. It has the same lower bound for all nonzero real x . Correct option: 2. Compute x + 1 / x - 2 = ( x - 1 ) 2 / x . The numerator is nonnegative and the denominator positive, proving the lower bound2. Equality forces x - 1 = 0 , and x = 1 is admissible. Strictness fails at that witness. If negative x were admitted, dividing by x would reverse the sign argument and the expression could be negative without this lower bound. The domain and equality case are both part of the conclusion.

questions.title: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q121 — A weighted binomial sum
questions.text: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q121 — A weighted binomial sum Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 26 · question 121 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Let A = 1 10 ∑ i = 3 7 ( i 3 ) ( 7 i ) . Which interval contains A ? 1. [ 1 , 30 ] 2. ( 30 , 60 ] 3. ( 60 , 90 ] 4. ( 90 , + ∞ ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Count the same choice in two orders: choosing an i -set and then three marked elements equals choosing the marked three first and then i - 3 more elements. Hence ( 7 i ) ( i 3 ) = ( 7 3 ) ( 4 i - 3 ) . 2. Sum over all possible subsets of the remaining four elements: ∑ j = 0 4 ( 4 j ) = 2 4 . 3. Therefore A = 35 · 16 / 10 = 56 , which lies in ( 30 , 60 ] . 4. The other intervals cannot contain 56; omitting the free subset produces 3.5, while forgetting the factor 1 / 10 produces 560. Transfer rule. Products of binomial coefficients often encode a marked-subset double count.

questions.title: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q130 — A prefix-sum recurrence
questions.text: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q130 — A prefix-sum recurrence Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 28 · question 130 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Let c 0 = 1 and c n + 1 = ∑ i = 0 n c i for n ≥ 0 . Its generating function is C ( x ) = ( 1 - x ) / ( 1 - α x ) . What is α ? 1. 2 2. 3 3. 4 4. 5 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The first recurrence value is c 1 = 1 . For n ≥ 1 , subtract the equation for c n from that for c n + 1 to obtain c n + 1 = 2 c n . Therefore c n = 2 n - 1 for n ≥ 1 , proved directly by induction from c 1 = 1 . Sum the formal series: C ( x ) = 1 + x ∑ j ≥ 0 ( 2 x ) j = 1 + x / ( 1 - 2 x ) = ( 1 - x ) / ( 1 - 2 x ) . Thus α = 2 . 4. Values 3, 4, and 5 would already produce the wrong coefficient of x 2 . Applying c n = 2 n at n = 0 would also miss the initial exception. Transfer rule. Subtract consecutive prefix recurrences; state precisely where the simplified recurrence begins.

questions.title: Question 3. PhD CE 1405, Q3 — Leaf weights in a binary tree
questions.text: Question 3. PhD CE 1405, Q3 — Leaf weights in a binary tree Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 3 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. For each leaf x at depth d of a binary tree T , put w ( x ) = 2 - d . If L is the set of all leaves and α = ∑ x ∈ L w ( x ) , which is always correct? 1. α = 1 . 2. α ≤ 1 . 3. α > 1 . 4. α < 1 . Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Assign mass one to the root and half of a node's mass to each possible child. Missing children leave unused mass; a leaf receives exactly 2 - d . Leaf masses are disjoint allocations of the root mass, so their sum is at most one. This can also be proved by structural induction on the two subtrees. Equality occurs in a finite full binary tree, including a single root leaf. A root with just one leaf child has sum one half, so equality is not guaranteed. These examples eliminate the always-equal and always-strict alternatives; the greater-than alternative contradicts conservation of mass. Transfer rule. An upper bound can be universal even when equality depends on fullness of the structure.

questions.text: Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q28 — Parity far from the given recurrence values Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 28 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Let a n = 3 a n - 1 + 5 a n - 2 + 4 , with a 16 = 1403 and a 17 = 2025 . How many of a 100 , a 101 , … , a 113 are even? 1. 4 2. 5 3. 7 4. 10 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Reduce modulo two: a n ≡ a n - 1 + a n - 2 . questions.title: Question 6. A residue-class induction requires multiple bases
questions.text: Question 6. A residue-class induction requires multiple bases Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q130; MS_CS_1405_Q125. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A proposed proof uses P ( n ) ⇒ P ( n + 4 ) for all n ≥ 3 . Which minimal consecutive base set proves P ( n ) for every n ≥ 3 ? 1. 3 only. 2. 3,4. 3. 3,4,5. 4. 3,4,5,6. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. A step of four never changes the residue class modulo four. The four bases 3 through 6 represent all four classes among integers at least three. For each target, repeatedly subtract four until reaching exactly one of those bases. Fewer bases leave at least one progression unreachable. This is a dependency argument, not a requirement to test arbitrary extra values; the number of bases comes from the step's residue classes.

questions.title: Question 7. A divisibility induction with a factored step
questions.text: Question 7. A divisibility induction with a factored step Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q125; MS_CS_1405_Q38. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Which statement is correct for every integer n ≥ 0 ? 1. 8 ∣ 5 2 n - 1 2. 8 ∣ 5 n - 1 3. 16 ∣ 5 2 n - 1 4. 3 ∣ 5 2 n + 1 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. For the first statement, the base n = 0 is zero. In the step, 5 2 ( n + 1 ) - 1 = 25 ( 5 2 n - 1 ) + 24 . Both terms are divisible by eight if the hypothesis holds. The second fails at n = 1 , since four is not divisible by eight. The third fails there too, since 24 is not divisible by sixteen. The fourth fails at n = 0 , where the value is two. Factoring the successor expression connects it directly to the induction hypothesis.

questions.text: Question 8. The exact prefix-doubling exception Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q130. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. u 0 = 2 and u n + 1 = ∑ i = 0 n u i . What is u 8 ? 1. 128 2. 256 3. 512 4. 1024 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Compute u 1 = 2 . For n ≥ 1 , subtract consecutive prefix equations to obtain u n + 1 = 2 u n . Induction then gives u n = 2 n for n ≥ 1 , so u 8 = 256 . The formula is not intended at zero, where u 0 = 2 rather than one. Using the initial value as if doubling began immediately gives 512; failing to count one doubling gives 128. A simplified recurrence often starts later than the original one.

questions.title: Question 9. An inequality starts later than expected
questions.text: Question 9. An inequality starts later than expected Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q2; MS_CS_1405_Q130. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. What is the smallest positive N such that 2 n > n 2 holds for every integer n ≥ N ? 1. 3 2. 4 3. 5 4. 6 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The claim fails at three and is equality at four. At five it holds: 32 is greater than 25. For n ≥ 5 , 2 n 2 - ( n + 1 ) 2 = n 2 - 2 n - 1 > 0 . Hence 2 n > n 2 implies 2 n + 1 > 2 n 2 > ( n + 1 ) 2 . Induction proves the entire tail from five, and failure at four establishes minimality. Merely observing rapid exponential growth does not identify the earliest universal threshold.

questions.title: Question 10. A full branching-tree formula
questions.text: Question 10. A full branching-tree formula Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q3. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A finite rooted tree has exactly three children at every internal node. If it has 17 internal nodes, how many leaves does it have? 1. 34 2. 35 3. 36 4. 51 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Let I and L count internal nodes and leaves. Counting edges by parents gives 3 I ; counting edges in a finite tree gives I + L - 1 . Equating yields L = 2 I + 1 = 35 . Alternatively, replacing a leaf by an internal node with three leaves increases I by one and L by two, preserving the formula from the one-leaf base tree. The finite and full-branching assumptions are essential; arbitrary missing children would change the identity.

questions.text: Question 25. Strong induction on a tree constructor — exact instance 1 Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q121; MS_CS_1405_Q130. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A full binary tree has n internal nodes. Find its total node count. Calculate the requested quantity for n = 5 . 1. 31 2. 11 3. 6 4. 10 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Step 1 — model and conditions. questions.title: Question 45. Weighted binomial sum
questions.text: Question 45. Weighted binomial sum Original integrated challenge · retained after review What is ∑ j = 0 6 j 2 ( 6 j ) ? 1. 192 2. 480 3. 672 4. 768 Correct option: 3. Write j 2 = j ( j - 1 ) + j . A subset with one distinguished member is counted by n 2 n - 1 ; one with two ordered distinct distinguished members is n ( n - 1 ) 2 n - 2 . For n = 6 , these counts are192 and480. Their sum is672. The endpoint j = 0 contributes zero; the two-member part cannot count the repeated-member case, which is why the additional one-member count is necessary. Pascal induction provides another proof of the two identities.

questions.title: Question 1. PhD CE 1405, Q3 — Leaf weights in a binary tree
questions.text: Question 1. PhD CE 1405, Q3 — Leaf weights in a binary tree Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 3 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. For each leaf x at depth d of a binary tree T , put w ( x ) = 2 - d . If L is the set of all leaves and α = ∑ x ∈ L w ( x ) , which is always correct? 1. α = 1 . 2. α ≤ 1 . 3. α > 1 . 4. α < 1 . Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Assign mass one to the root and half of a node's mass to each possible child. Missing children leave unused mass; a leaf receives exactly 2 - d . Leaf masses are disjoint allocations of the root mass, so their sum is at most one. This can also be proved by structural induction on the two subtrees. Equality occurs in a finite full binary tree, including a single root leaf. A root with just one leaf child has sum one half, so equality is not guaranteed. These examples eliminate the always-equal and always-strict alternatives; the greater-than alternative contradicts conservation of mass. Transfer rule. An upper bound can be universal even when equality depends on fullness of the structure.

questions.title: Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q16 — Exact merge comparisons
questions.text: Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q16 — Exact merge comparisons Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 4 · question 16 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Merge sort repeatedly divides an eight-element array into equal halves and merges by comparing the two current front elements until one side is exhausted. For A = [ 12 , 7 , 5 , 9 , 3 , 8 , 2 , 6 ] , how many element comparisons are performed? 1. 14 2. 16 3. 10 4. 12 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Four size-two merges cost one comparison each: subtotal four. Merging [ 7 , 12 ] with [ 5 , 9 ] costs three comparisons. Merging [ 3 , 8 ] with [ 2 , 6 ] also costs three. The subtotal is ten. The final merge of [ 5 , 7 , 9 , 12 ] with [ 2 , 3 , 6 , 8 ] compares front pairs until the right list empties: emitted comparison results are 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, and 8. Six comparisons bring the total to sixteen. Ten omits the final merge; twelve undercounts intermediate comparisons; fourteen is not the trace count. Remaining elements copied after exhaustion incur no key comparison. Transfer rule. A worst-case merge bound is not automatically the exact cost of a supplied input.

questions.title: Question 3. PhD CS 1404, Q72 — Expected running-minimum updates
questions.text: Question 3. PhD CS 1404, Q72 — Expected running-minimum updates Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 72 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. An array contains n distinct values in a uniformly random permutation. Set min to positive infinity, scan from index 1 to n , and replace it whenever the next value is smaller. If Y counts replacements, which expression is closest to its mean for large n ? 1. 1 2. ln n 3. n 4. n ln n Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Let I i indicate that position i contains the smallest of the first i values. Uniform permutation symmetry gives P ( I i = 1 ) = 1 / i . Linearity of expectation requires no independence between these indicators: E [ Y ] = ∑ i = 1 n 1 / i = H n . Integral bounds give ln ( n + 1 ) ≤ H n ≤ 1 + ln n , so ln n is the listed large- n approximation. The exact mean is H n , not exactly ln n . One counts only the first update; n assumes every position is a record; n ln n multiplies counts that should be summed. Transfer rule. Distinguish the number of loop tests (always n ) from the number of successful updates (random).

questions.title: Question 4. MSc CE 1405, Q56 — Sequentially merging equal sorted lists
questions.text: Question 4. MSc CE 1405, Q56 — Sequentially merging equal sorted lists Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 12 · question 56 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. There are k sorted lists, each containing n / k elements. Merge lists 1 and 2, then merge the result with list 3, and continue in this way. What is the worst-case running-time bound of this algorithm? 1. O ( k log n ) 2. O ( n ) 3. O ( n log k ) 4. O ( n k ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. At stage j , merge an accumulated list of j n / k elements with the next list of n / k elements. In the standard linear-time merge model, the worst-case work is proportional to ( j + 1 ) n / k . Sum the stage costs for j = 1 , … , k - 1 : ( n / k ) ( 2 + 3 + … + k ) = ( n / k ) ( k ( k + 1 ) / 2 - 1 ) . For 2 ≤ k ≤ n , this is Θ ( n k ) , so option 4 is the stated bound. 3. A balanced merge tree instead processes all n elements at each of Θ ( log k ) levels and takes Θ ( n log k ) . A heap can achieve the same asymptotic bound, but neither is the sequential algorithm in the question. 4. The worst case includes inputs whose keys remain interleaved at successive merges; one cannot price every stage at the size of the incoming list alone. If k is fixed independently of n , the expression becomes linear in n , but the listed options treat both parameters as variable. Transfer rule. Write the accumulated problem size at each iteration before summing costs. A correct bound for a different merge strategy is a distractor, not an answer.

questions.title: Question 5. Numeric value versus encoded length
questions.text: Question 5. Numeric value versus encoded length Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q20; Phd_CE_1405_Q1. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A positive integer N is encoded in exactly b binary bits. An algorithm performs N unit-cost iterations. Which tight worst-case bound in b is correct? 1. Θ ( b ) 2. Θ ( b 2 ) 3. Θ ( 2 b ) 4. Θ ( 2 2 b ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. A b -bit positive integer ranges from 2 b - 1 through 2 b - 1 . Thus N iterations can number nearly 2 b , and every such input already requires at least 2 b - 1 iterations. The tight order in encoded length is exponential. Linear time in the numeric parameter does not imply polynomial time in its encoding. Squaring the exponential would require an extra nested value-dependent loop that is not present.

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q113; Phd_CE_1405_Q16. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

A dense real r×c matrix is read entry by entry and multiplied by a vector using the usual row dot products. What is the count of multiplications and additions, respectively?

1.

rc and r(c-1)

2.

rc and c(r-1)

3.

r+c and rc

4.

r2 and c2

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

Each of the r rows requires c multiplications and c-1 additions to combine its products, under the stated usual dot-product implementation. Multiply those counts by r.

The second alternative adds down columns rather than along each row. The other counts replace the rectangular input with unrelated one-parameter shapes. For c=1, the addition count is zero, a useful boundary check. Counting an initial addition into a zero accumulator would be a different exact-cost convention.

questions.title: Question 10. Actual comparison count versus a worst-case maximum
questions.text: Question 10. Actual comparison count versus a worst-case maximum Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q16. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Two ascending lists have lengths three and five. Ordinary merging stops comparing when either list empties. What pair gives the minimum and maximum number of comparisons? 1. 3 and 8. 2. 3 and 7. 3. 5 and 7. 4. 1 and 7. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The earliest exhaustion is the three-element list, requiring three comparisons if all its values precede the other list's first value. No fewer comparisons can exhaust either list. The maximum is 3 + 5 - 1 = 7 , attained when neither list is exhausted until one element remains overall. Copying the remainder uses no key comparison. The exact number for a supplied input may fall anywhere between these limits; the universal worst case is not its automatic trace count.

questions.text: Question 11. Recursive work and stack depth are different Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q16; Phd_CE_1405_Q1. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A routine processes two equal half-sized children sequentially, uses constant local storage per call, and spends linear work combining. What are its total work and auxiliary recursion-stack space? 1. Θ ( n log n ) and Θ ( log n ) 2. Θ ( n log n ) and Θ ( n ) 3. Θ ( n ) and Θ ( log n ) 4. Θ ( log n ) and Θ ( n ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. questions.title: Question 12. A weighted leaf bound with an equality test
questions.text: Question 12. A weighted leaf bound with an equality test Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q3. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A binary tree has leaves at depths 1, 2, 3, and 3. What is the sum of 2 - d , and can these depths belong to a finite full tree? 1. 1 and yes. 2. 1 and no. 3. 7/8 and yes. 4. 9/8 and no. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The weight sum is 1 / 2 + 1 / 4 + 1 / 8 + 1 / 8 = 1 . Construct the tree by taking one root child as a leaf, extending the other to a depth-two leaf and a final branch with two depth-three leaves. Every internal node has two children, so the construction is full. Equality of the weight bound is consistent with this full tree; the explicit construction verifies that the proposed depths are realizable, rather than relying solely on an inequality.

questions.title: Question 45. Growing arithmetic objects
questions.text: Question 45. Growing arithmetic objects Original integrated challenge · retained after review Begin with integer x = 2 and square it six times exactly. How many bits are needed for the final positive integer? 1. 6 2. 32 3. 64 4. 65 Correct option: 4. After k squarings, x = 2 2 k . At k = 6 , the final value is 2 64 , whose unsigned representation needs65 bits because the top bit is position64. Six source-level multiplications do not imply six constant-time word operations on a64-bit machine; the final value already exceeds its unsigned maximum. This separates operation count, operand growth and representability.

questions.title: Question 46. Capacity measured in input bits
questions.text: Question 46. Capacity measured in input bits Original integrated challenge · retained after review A table allocates 100 W fixed-size cells for a binary-encoded20-bit positive capacity W . What largest cell count is possible? 1. 2000 2. 1048575 3. 104857500 4. 104857600 Correct option: 3. The greatest20-bit value is 2 20 - 1 = 1048575 . Multiplying by100 gives104857500 cells. The20-bit encoding length does not mean the capacity is20. Using 2 20 instead would choose a value needing21 bits. Allocation is pseudo-polynomial in numeric W and can be exponential in its length even before the cells are initialized.

PhD CE 1405, Q1 — Unequal recursive splits Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 1 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Fixed positive constants α , β satisfy α + β = 1 . For T ( n ) = T ( α n ) + T ( β n ) + n with constant small-input base cost, which listed bound is correct? 1. O ( α β n ) 2. O ( n log n ) 3. O ( β n α log n ) 4. O ( α n + β log n ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The Akra–Bazzi exponent satisfies α p + β p = 1 . Here p = 1 . Its integral is ∫ 1 n u / u 2 d u = log n , giving T ( n ) = Θ ( n log n ) . Integer rounding of subproblem sizes is absorbed under the usual bounded-perturbation convention. Constants α , β are fixed; options 1 and 4 are linear bounds and are too small. Since 0 < α < 1 , option 3 grows as n α log n = o ( n log n ) and is also too small. The equal-split Master theorem does not directly apply to unequal branches; equal sizes cannot be invented. Transfer rule. Solve for the branching exponent before comparing candidate bounds; coefficients and exponents play different roles.

questions.title: Question 45. Oscillation across growth classes
questions.text: Question 45. Oscillation across growth classes Original integrated challenge · retained after review For positive integer n , let f ( n ) = n 2 + sin ( ln n ) and g ( n ) = n 2 . Which statement holds? 1. f ∈ Θ ( g ) 2. f ∈ O ( g ) but not Ω ( g ) 3. f ∈ Ω ( g ) but not O ( g ) 4. Neither big-oh nor big-omega relation holds. Correct option: 4. The ratio is n sin ( ln n ) . Near logarithmic phases π / 2 + 2 k π , it grows like n and is unbounded. Near 3 π / 2 + 2 k π , it behaves like 1 / n and tends to zero. Integer indices can be chosen by rounding the corresponding exponentials; their logarithmic error tends to zero. Thus no uniform upper constant or positive lower constant works. A ratio lacking a limit does not always cause incomparability, but these two subsequences do.

questions.title: Question 46. A floor inside an exponent
questions.text: Question 46. A floor inside an exponent Original integrated challenge · retained after review For n ≥ 1 , what is the relation between f ( n ) = 2 ⌊ log 2 n ⌋ and n ? 1. f ∈ Θ ( n ) , but f / n need not converge. 2. f ∈ o ( n ) 3. f ∈ ω ( n ) 4. f / n → 1 Correct option: 1. If 2 k ≤ n < 2 k + 1 , then f = 2 k , so n / 2 < f ≤ n . These constant bounds establish tight linear growth. At powers of two the ratio is1, while near the top of each interval it tends to1/2 . Hence there is no limit1 or any single ratio limit. Rounding the logarithm changes a bounded factor without creating a strict growth relation.

questions.title: Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q16 — Exact merge comparisons
questions.text: Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q16 — Exact merge comparisons Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 4 · question 16 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Merge sort repeatedly divides an eight-element array into equal halves and merges by comparing the two current front elements until one side is exhausted. For A = [ 12 , 7 , 5 , 9 , 3 , 8 , 2 , 6 ] , how many element comparisons are performed? 1. 14 2. 16 3. 10 4. 12 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Four size-two merges cost one comparison each: subtotal four. Merging [ 7 , 12 ] with [ 5 , 9 ] costs three comparisons. Merging [ 3 , 8 ] with [ 2 , 6 ] also costs three. The subtotal is ten. The final merge of [ 5 , 7 , 9 , 12 ] with [ 2 , 3 , 6 , 8 ] compares front pairs until the right list empties: emitted comparison results are 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, and 8. Six comparisons bring the total to sixteen. Ten omits the final merge; twelve undercounts intermediate comparisons; fourteen is not the trace count. Remaining elements copied after exhaustion incur no key comparison. Transfer rule. A worst-case merge bound is not automatically the exact cost of a supplied input.

questions.title: Question 3. PhD CS 1404, Q72 — Expected running-minimum updates
questions.text: Question 3. PhD CS 1404, Q72 — Expected running-minimum updates Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 72 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. An array contains n distinct values in a uniformly random permutation. Set min to positive infinity, scan from index 1 to n , and replace it whenever the next value is smaller. If Y counts replacements, which expression is closest to its mean for large n ? 1. 1 2. ln n 3. n 4. n ln n Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Let I i indicate that position i contains the smallest of the first i values. Uniform permutation symmetry gives P ( I i = 1 ) = 1 / i . Linearity of expectation requires no independence between these indicators: E [ Y ] = ∑ i = 1 n 1 / i = H n . Integral bounds give ln ( n + 1 ) ≤ H n ≤ 1 + ln n , so ln n is the listed large- n approximation. The exact mean is H n , not exactly ln n . One counts only the first update; n assumes every position is a record; n ln n multiplies counts that should be summed. Transfer rule. Distinguish the number of loop tests (always n ) from the number of successful updates (random).

questions.title: Question 4. MSc CE 1405, Q56 — Sequentially merging equal sorted lists
questions.text: Question 4. MSc CE 1405, Q56 — Sequentially merging equal sorted lists Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 12 · question 56 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. There are k sorted lists, each containing n / k elements. Merge lists 1 and 2, then merge the result with list 3, and continue in this way. What is the worst-case running-time bound of this algorithm? 1. O ( k log n ) 2. O ( n ) 3. O ( n log k ) 4. O ( n k ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. At stage j , merge an accumulated list of j n / k elements with the next list of n / k elements. In the standard linear-time merge model, the worst-case work is proportional to ( j + 1 ) n / k . Sum the stage costs for j = 1 , … , k - 1 : ( n / k ) ( 2 + 3 + … + k ) = ( n / k ) ( k ( k + 1 ) / 2 - 1 ) . For 2 ≤ k ≤ n , this is Θ ( n k ) , so option 4 is the stated bound. 3. A balanced merge tree instead processes all n elements at each of Θ ( log k ) levels and takes Θ ( n log k ) . A heap can achieve the same asymptotic bound, but neither is the sequential algorithm in the question. 4. The worst case includes inputs whose keys remain interleaved at successive merges; one cannot price every stage at the size of the incoming list alone. If k is fixed independently of n , the expression becomes linear in n , but the listed options treat both parameters as variable. Transfer rule. Write the accumulated problem size at each iteration before summing costs. A correct bound for a different merge strategy is a distractor, not an answer.

questions.text: Question 7. Geometric outer loop with growing work Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q20; MS_CS_1405_Q130. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Let n = 32 . Start i = 1 and double it while i ≤ n ; for each such i , execute a body i times. What are the outer-iteration and body counts? 1. 5 and 31. 2. 6 and 63. 3. 6 and 32. 4. 32 and 63. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The outer states are 1,2,4,8,16,32, giving six iterations. The body count is their sum, 2 6 - 1 = 63 . The endpoint is included, explaining why neither count stops at sixteen. A logarithmic outer loop does not imply logarithmic whole-program work when the inner work grows geometrically. The exact total is linear in n on these power-of-two inputs.

This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Initialize i = 2 . While i ≤ 65536 , execute one body and replace i by i 2 . How many bodies execute? 1. 4 2. 5 3. 8 4. 16 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The states satisfying the guard are 2,4,16,256,65536. The next square exceeds the bound, so there are five bodies. The sequence is i k = 2 2 k , explaining the double-logarithmic general count. Replacing squaring by doubling would give a different loop. An exclusive guard would omit the last state and give four; the stated inclusive endpoint must be retained.

How many bodies execute? 1. 16 2. 20 3. 28 4. 36 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The kept j values have the same parity as i . questions.title: Question 10. Guard tests and body executions
questions.text: Question 10. Guard tests and body executions Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q20; Phd_CE_1405_Q16. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A nested loop has i = 1 , … , 5 and an inner C -style for(j=1;j<=i;j++) . Count inner-loop body executions and inner guard evaluations across the run. 1. 15 and 20. 2. 15 and 15. 3. 20 and 25. 4. 10 and 15. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The body count is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 . Each invocation of the inner loop evaluates its guard once more than its body count, including the final failed test. There are five inner invocations, so guard evaluations total 15 + 5 = 20 . Initialization and updates would add different costs if requested, but are not guard evaluations. Exact operation accounting requires naming the operation, not just giving a runtime class.

questions.title: Question 11. Input order changes successful branches
questions.text: Question 11. Input order changes successful branches Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q72. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A scan updates its running minimum whenever the next value is smaller. For array [ 8 , 3 , 7 , 2 , 6 , 1 , 5 , 4 ] , how many updates occur, and how many comparisons with the current minimum occur? 1. 4 and 8. 2. 4 and 4. 3. 8 and 8. 4. 3 and 7. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. With an initial infinite minimum, the new record values are 8,3,2,1, so four assignments update it. Every one of the eight array elements is still compared with the current minimum. Record updates are input-dependent, while the scan length is fixed. Initializing the minimum to the first array element and starting at the second would give three later updates and seven comparisons for a different implementation. The initialization convention is part of the count.

questions.title: Question 12. A nonconstant body changes the exponent
questions.text: Question 12. A nonconstant body changes the exponent Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q20; Phd_CE_1405_Q16. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. An outer loop takes i = 1 , … , n , an inner loop takes j = 1 , … , i , and the body performs exactly j unit operations. What is the tight total order? 1. Θ ( n ) 2. Θ ( n 2 ) 3. Θ ( n 3 ) 4. Θ ( n 2 log n ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. For a fixed i , body work sums to ∑ j = 1 i j = i ( i + 1 ) / 2 . Summing across i gives n ( n + 1 ) ( n + 2 ) / 6 . The cubic leading term proves the tight class. Counting only inner iterations would give a quadratic expression and implicitly treat each body as constant cost, contrary to the statement. Exact finite sums support both the numerical and asymptotic conclusions.

Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? 1. An exact count and an asymptotic bound are the same statement. 2. Changing the inner bound changes the iteration region even when the nesting depth stays the same. 3. Two nested loops always execute the body exactly the input size squared times. 4. A maximum inner length is the length of every row. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Check the hypothesis. The shape of the admissible index set controls work. The valid statement is: Changing the inner bound changes the iteration region even when the nesting depth stays the same. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule. questions.title: Question 45. Three-factor integer region
questions.text: Question 45. Three-factor integer region Original integrated challenge · retained after review Count body executions over all positive integer triples ( i , j , k ) satisfying i j k ≤ n . What is the tight order? 1. Θ ( n log n ) 2. Θ ( n log 2 n ) 3. Θ ( n 2 ) 4. Θ ( n 3 ) Correct option: 2. The exact count is ∑ i = 1 n ∑ j = 1 ⌊ n / i ⌋ ⌊ n / ( i j ) ⌋ . Dropping floors and enlarging the inner range gives upper bound n H n 2 = O ( n log 2 n ) . For a lower bound, restrict i , j to at most n 1 / 3 . Their product is at most n 2 / 3 , so for sufficiently large n the floor is at least n / ( 2 i j ) . Summing this restricted square yields a constant times n H ⌊ n 1 / 3 ⌋ 2 , matching the upper order. The feasible product region is not a cube of side n .

questions.text: Question 46. A branch-defined triangular region Original integrated challenge · retained after review For i = 1 , … , n , start j = 1 and execute the body while j ≤ n and i + j ≤ n , incrementing j each time. What is the exact count? 1. n ( n + 1 ) / 2 2. n ( n - 1 ) / 2 3. n 2 4. n - 1 Correct option: 2. For a fixed i , admissible j values are1 through n - i , giving n - i visits including zero visits at i = n . Sum these counts to obtain ( n - 1 ) + … + 1 + 0 = n ( n - 1 ) / 2 . The inclusive sum constraint still excludes the diagonal case i = j = n , and independent-loop multiplication ignores the stopping condition. Evaluating the region directly resolves both tight order and exact endpoints.

questions.title: Question 1. PhD CS 1405, Q21 — Minimum count outside three sets
questions.text: Question 1. PhD CS 1405, Q21 — Minimum count outside three sets Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 21 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Thirty-two offices each have a computer. Fifteen have a laser printer, ten have a scanner, eight have a modem, and two have all three. What is the minimum number with none of these three devices? 1. 1 2. 2 3. 3 4. 4 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The membership total is 15 + 10 + 8 = 33 . The two triple members contribute six memberships but only two union elements, so they force four duplicated memberships. Consequently the union has at most 33 - 4 = 29 members. Additional pair-only overlaps would make it smaller. The upper bound is attainable: use two triple offices, thirteen printer-only offices, eight scanner-only offices, and six modem-only offices. This uses 29 offices and has no pair-only overlaps. Exactly three of the 32 offices are outside this maximal union. questions.text: Question 5. PhD CS 1404, Q72 — Expected running-minimum updates Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 72 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. An array contains n distinct values in a uniformly random permutation. Set min to positive infinity, scan from index 1 to n , and replace it whenever the next value is smaller. If Y counts replacements, which expression is closest to its mean for large n ? 1. 1 2. ln n 3. n 4. n ln n Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Let I i indicate that position i contains the smallest of the first i values. Uniform permutation symmetry gives P ( I i = 1 ) = 1 / i . Linearity of expectation requires no independence between these indicators: E [ Y ] = ∑ i = 1 n 1 / i = H n . Integral bounds give ln ( n + 1 ) ≤ H n ≤ 1 + ln n , so ln n is the listed large- n approximation. The exact mean is H n , not exactly ln n . One counts only the first update; n assumes every position is a record; n ln n multiplies counts that should be summed. Transfer rule. Distinguish the number of loop tests (always n ) from the number of successful updates (random).

Find P ( A ∪ B ) . Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? 1. Cardinality ratios require equally likely elementary outcomes. 2. Counting outcomes gives probabilities under every sample distribution. 3. An overlap is counted once by adding both events without a correction. 4. A union must be contained in its intersection. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Check the hypothesis. Under nonuniform probabilities, sum the actual masses of the included outcomes. Inclusion-exclusion remains valid for probabilities, but raw cardinalities alone no longer determine them. The equal-likelihood premise justifies converting this specific count into a probability. Connect it to the calculation. Add both event cardinalities and subtract their shared outcome once. Divide the resulting union size by the equally likely sample-space size. The intersection is nonempty, so a disjoint-event addition rule would double-count it. The valid statement is: Cardinality ratios require equally likely elementary outcomes. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule.
