questions.title: Question 2. MSc CE 1404, Q80 — Two cascaded multiplexers
questions.text: Question 2. MSc CE 1404, Q80 — Two cascaded multiplexers Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 19 · question 80 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Two 2:1 multiplexers use select values zero and one to choose inputs I 0 and I 1 . The first has ( I 0 , I 1 ) = ( 1 , 0 ) and select b . Its output feeds I 0 of the second, whose I 1 = 0 and select is a . Which function is implemented? Exact two-multiplexer source topology 0 1 0 1 1 0 0 MUX MUX b a F MSc CE 1404, Q80: the first select is b , the second is a . Digits inside each block identify the select value, while digits on wires are constant data inputs. 1. XNOR 2. XOR 3. NAND 4. NOR Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. The first multiplexer produces b ¯ : it is one when its select is zero and zero when the select is one. The second produces the first output only when a = 0 , so its output is a ¯ b ¯ = a + b ¯ . This is NOR. NAND differs at inputs 01 and 10; XOR differs at 00 and the mixed inputs; XNOR is also one at 11, which the second multiplexer forces to zero. questions.title: Question 3. MSc CE 1404, Q81 — A ring-oscillator frequency
questions.text: Question 3. MSc CE 1404, Q81 — A ring-oscillator frequency Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 19 · question 81 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. A ring oscillator contains five inverters in a loop. Each inverter has propagation delay 5 ns. What is its oscillation frequency in megahertz? 1. 5 2. 10 3. 20 4. 40 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. A transition traverses all five inverters in 25 ns and changes polarity because the loop has an odd number of inversions. A complete cycle requires both a rising and a falling traversal, so the period is 2 · 5 · 5 = 50 ns. Frequency is 1 / ( 50 × 10 - 9 ) = 20 × 10 6 Hz, or 20 MHz. Forty megahertz counts only half the period; the other choices confuse the number of stages and their delay. 4. This is the usual equal-delay digital model of the source diagram, not an analog startup or jitter prediction. Transfer rule. Convert time units and distinguish a single polarity traversal from a full oscillation.

questions.title: Question 4. MSc CE 1404, Q91 — Transistor scaling and an Elmore-delay limit
questions.text: Question 4. MSc CE 1404, Q91 — Transistor scaling and an Elmore-delay limit Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 22 · question 91 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. All transistor widths in a three-input NAND are doubled. Under the Elmore model, how does its maximum low-to-high propagation delay change? The load C L is due to next-stage input gates whose dimensions remain fixed. 1. It may be greater or smaller than half the initial delay, depending on original dimensions. 2. It decreases, but remains greater than half the initial delay. 3. It decreases to less than half the initial delay. 4. It does not change. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Doubling widths halves the on-resistances but doubles this gate's width-dependent internal capacitances. The externally specified load remains fixed. An Elmore term from an internal capacitance therefore retains its value: ( R / 2 ) ( 2 C ) = R C . A term due to the fixed load halves. With positive internal and load contributions, write the original delay as D i n t + D L and the new delay as D i n t + D L / 2 . Its ratio is strictly between one half and one. Treating every capacitance as fixed would predict exactly half; treating every capacitance as scaled would predict unchanged delay. Both ignore the question's split between internal and external capacitance. Transfer rule. Scale resistance and capacitance contributions separately before estimating delay.

Question 4. MSc CE 1404, Q91 — Transistor scaling and an Elmore-delay limit

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 22 · question 91. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

All transistor widths in a three-input NAND are doubled. Under the Elmore model, how does its maximum low-to-high propagation delay change? The load CL is due to next-stage input gates whose dimensions remain fixed.

1.

It may be greater or smaller than half the initial delay, depending on original dimensions.

2.

It decreases, but remains greater than half the initial delay.

3.

It decreases to less than half the initial delay.

4.

It does not change.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Doubling widths halves the on-resistances but doubles this gate's width-dependent internal capacitances. The externally specified load remains fixed.
  2. An Elmore term from an internal capacitance therefore retains its value: (R/2)(2C)=RC. A term due to the fixed load halves.
  3. With positive internal and load contributions, write the original delay as Dint+DL and the new delay as Dint+DL/2. Its ratio is strictly between one half and one.
  4. Treating every capacitance as fixed would predict exactly half; treating every capacitance as scaled would predict unchanged delay. Both ignore the question's split between internal and external capacitance.

Transfer rule. Scale resistance and capacitance contributions separately before estimating delay.

questions.title: Question 5. Recognize both outputs of a shared NAND network
questions.text: Question 5. Recognize both outputs of a shared NAND network Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q23. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Let t = NAND ( x , y ) , u = NAND ( x , t ) , v = NAND ( y , t ) . Outputs are D = NAND ( u , v ) and B = NAND ( v , v ) . For ( x , y ) = ( 0 , 1 ) , what are ( D , B ) and the circuit function? 1. (1,1), half subtractor. 2. (1,0), half adder. 3. (0,1), equality comparator. 4. (0,0), half subtractor. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Substitution gives t = 1 , u = 1 , v = 0 , so D = 1 and B = 1 . Algebraically D = x ⊕ y and B = x ¯ y . These are difference and borrow for subtracting y from x . The first three XOR-producing gates do not establish a half-adder carry; the second output must also be derived. A borrow occurs at 0 minus 1, precisely the supplied input.

questions.title: Question 6. A four-gate NOR network
questions.text: Question 6. A four-gate NOR network Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CE_1405_Q77. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Complements are available. Implement majority of x , y , z by NOR gates using its POS ( x + y ) ( x + z ) ( y + z ) . What fan-in combination realizes it directly? 1. Three two-input NORs and one three-input NOR. 2. One three-input NOR only. 3. Three NANDs only. 4. Two two-input NORs only. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Each two-input NOR computes the complement of one pairwise sum. A final three-input NOR computes the complement of their OR; by De Morgan this is the product of the three original sums. The total is four gates with the stated fan-ins. One NOR would instead compute the complement of the total input OR. A direct NAND-only or two-gate construction does not realize the specified two-level POS mapping. This asks for a construction rather than an unsupported minimum over all possible circuit libraries.

questions.title: Question 7. A static-one hazard interval
questions.text: Question 7. A static-one hazard interval Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CE_1405_Q78; Phd_CE_1405_Q23. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. F = a b + a ¯ c with b = c = 1 . When a rises, the falling old product reaches the final OR input at 2 ns and the rising new product arrives at 7 ns. The OR has a 1 ns transport delay. What low interval appears at its output? 1. 2–7 ns. 2. 3–8 ns. 3. 1–6 ns. 4. No interval. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. At the OR inputs, both products are zero from two through seven nanoseconds. Transport delay shifts both transitions by one nanosecond without suppressing the pulse, giving a low output from three to eight nanoseconds. The Boolean endpoint values are both one; the glitch comes from path timing. An inertial model might reject a sufficiently narrow pulse, but the question explicitly uses transport. Adding a continuously high consensus path b c would eliminate the static-one hazard.

questions.title: Question 8. Latest arrival at a reconvergent output
questions.text: Question 8. Latest arrival at a reconvergent output Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q23; MS_CE_1405_Q78. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Two paths feed an AND. One takes 3 ns; the other contains gates taking 2 ns and 4 ns. A final AND takes 1 ns. Inputs transition at time zero and the output requires both paths. What worst-case arrival bound follows? 1. 4 ns 2. 6 ns 3. 7 ns 4. 10 ns Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The path arrivals are three and six nanoseconds. The AND's required output cannot settle before the slower needed input and its own delay, giving max ( 3 , 6 ) + 1 = 7 ns. Summing all gates in the circuit gives ten but counts parallel paths sequentially. Four uses only the fast path; six omits the final gate. This latest-arrival calculation assumes the stated transition sensitizes the paths and does not itself claim hazard freedom.

questions.text: Question 9. A tied-input gate is an inverter Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q23. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A = NAND ( x , y ) and F = NAND ( A , A ) . Which function and output at ( x , y ) = ( 1 , 0 ) are correct? 1. x y and 0. 2. x ∨ y and 1. 3. x y ¯ and 1. 4. x ⊕ y and 1. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Tied NAND inputs invert: A A ¯ = A ¯ . Substituting the first NAND yields F = x y , so the output at 1,0 is zero. This two-stage double inversion restores AND, not OR. An OR from NAND would first invert each individual input and then NAND those complemented inputs. Track the net actually inverted rather than counting two gates and guessing an operator.

questions.title: Question 13. A fixed-fan-in reduction tree — exact instance 1
questions.text: Question 13. A fixed-fan-in reduction tree — exact instance 1 Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q23; MS_CE_1404_Q80. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A binary-input AND tree combines 2 n independent input signals, without sharing or simplification. Count gates. Calculate the requested quantity for n = 5 . 1. 5 2. 4 3. 31 4. 32 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Step 1 — model and conditions. Each binary gate reduces the number of separate partial signals by one. Reducing all inputs to one output therefore needs one fewer gate than inputs. A balanced tree attains this count and has a different depth measure. Step 2 — compute. The general expression is 2 n - 1 . Substituting n = 5 gives 31 . Keep the exact value until all constraints have been applied. Step 3 — audit the alternatives. The other listed values are 32 , 5 , 4 . They are obtained from the three competing expressions 2 n , n , n - 1 , respectively. Those expressions discard or alter a condition in the model; the derivation above shows where the discrepancy enters. Recomputing the defining constraints, rather than selecting the numerically nearest option, determines the answer.

Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? 1. A redundant term in steady-state logic can be necessary under a delay-aware implementation model. 2. questions.title: Question 45. A quantified static hazard window
questions.text: Question 45. A quantified static hazard window Original integrated challenge · retained after review F = a b ∨ ¬ a c has b = c = 1 and a falls at0ns. The a b output falls at2ns and ¬ a c rises at5ns. An OR with equal1ns transport delay follows them. What is its low-pulse width? 1. 1ns 2. 2ns 3. 3ns 4. 4ns Correct option: 3. The OR inputs are both zero from2ns to5ns, a three-nanosecond interval. Equal transport delay shifts the falling output event to3ns and the rising event to6ns without changing pulse width. A steady-state truth table predicts output1 before and after but misses the transient. An inertial model rejecting pulses shorter than4ns could suppress it, which is a different stated timing model.

questions.title: Question 46. Noise-margin bottleneck
questions.text: Question 46. Noise-margin bottleneck Original integrated challenge · retained after review A driver guarantees V O L ≤ 0.2 V and V O H ≥ 2.4 V . A receiver accepts lows through0.7V and highs from2.0V. What is the smaller guaranteed noise margin? 1. 0.2V 2. 0.4V 3. 0.5V 4. 0.7V Correct option: 2. Low margin is 0.7 - 0.2 = 0.5 V and high margin is 2.4 - 2.0 = 0.4 V . The smaller is0.4V. The driver output bounds and receiver thresholds have different roles; subtracting two driver levels would not give either noise margin. Both margins are positive, so the idealized voltage-level compatibility check passes.

questions.title: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q38 — A difference-defined equivalence
questions.text: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q38 — A difference-defined equivalence Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 9 · question 38 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. For real x , y , define x ∼ y exactly when x - y ∈ A . Which choice of A makes this an equivalence relation? 1. The integers divisible by 2 or by 3. 2. { m / n : n ∈ ℕ , m ∈ ℤ , m ≤ n } , with positive denominators. 3. The integers that are not prime. 4. { m / 2 n : n ∈ ℕ , m ∈ ℤ } Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. Reflexivity requires 0 ∈ A . Symmetry requires closure under negation. Transitivity requires closure under addition, because ( x - y ) + ( y - z ) = x - z . Conversely, these three conditions imply all three equivalence properties. Thus A must be an additive subgroup of the reals. Dyadic rationals meet these conditions. Put two fractions over 2 max ( r , s ) to show their sum remains dyadic; negative numerators give closure under negation. Option 1 fails addition: 2 and 3 are permitted, but 5 is not. Option 2 contains - 2 but not its opposite 2. Option 3 contains 1, but 1 + 1 = 2 is prime and excluded. Transfer rule. Translate a relation property into an algebraic closure condition before testing a large family.

questions.text: Question 2. PhD CS 1405, Q13 — Evaluate a finite relational specification Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 13 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. The universe is { 01 , 02 , 03 , 04 , 05 , 06 , 07 , 08 , 09 } ; girls are { 03 , 06 , 09 } ; boys are { 02 , 04 , 05 , 08 } ; the love relation is E = { ( 03 , 02 ) , ( 06 , 08 ) , ( 04 , 03 ) , ( 09 , 02 ) } . Evaluate (a) every girl loves exactly one boy; (b) some boy loves some girl. 1. Only (a). 2. Only ( b ). 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Restrict the first coordinate of E to girls. The three girls have respectively the unique targets 02, 08, and 02, all boys. Thus (a) is true. The pair ( 04 , 03 ) witnesses ( b ): 04 is a boy and 03 is a girl. Uniqueness in (a) is per girl, not a requirement that different girls have different targets. Shared target 02 is permitted. The distractors confuse uniqueness with injectivity or read an ordered pair in reverse. Transfer rule. Separate domain restrictions, existence, and uniqueness; a relation is not automatically a one-to-one function.

PhD CS 1405, Q23 — A closure operation on equivalences Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 23 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. If R 1 and R 2 are equivalence relations on A , which relation below is guaranteed to be an equivalence? 1. R 1 - 1 ∩ R 2 - 1 2. R 1 ∪ R 2 3. R 1 - 1 ∪ R 2 - 1 4. R 1 ∪ R 2 - 1 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Symmetry implies R i - 1 = R i . Thus option 1 is the intersection of two equivalences. Each diagonal pair belongs to both relations. Reversal and composable pairs remain in both, so the intersection is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Every other option is the same union. On { 1 , 2 , 3 } take partitions { { 1 , 2 } , { 3 } } and { { 1 } , { 2 , 3 } } . The union has 1 R 2 and 2 R 3 but not 1 R 3 . That missing pair violates transitivity, ruling out all three union options at once. Transfer rule. Simplify inverse relations using symmetry before testing a set operation.

questions.title: Question 4. A relation defined by a modular difference
questions.text: Question 4. A relation defined by a modular difference Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q38; Phd_CS_1405_Q23. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. On ℤ , x R y iff x - y ( mod 6 ) lies in { 0 , 2 , 4 } . How many equivalence classes are there? 1. 2 2. 3 3. 6 4. It is not an equivalence. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The permitted residues are the multiples of two modulo six. A difference is permitted exactly when it is even. The relation therefore identifies integers of the same parity. Zero belongs to the permitted set, negatives preserve it, and sums preserve it, proving equivalence. There are exactly two classes, even and odd. Counting the three allowed differences as three classes confuses a subgroup's size with its index.

questions.title: Question 5. Transitive closure is not union
questions.text: Question 5. Transitive closure is not union Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q23. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. R 1 has classes { 1 , 2 } , { 3 } , { 4 } and R 2 has classes { 1 } , { 2 , 3 } , { 4 } . How many ordered pairs are in the smallest equivalence containing R 1 ∪ R 2 ? 1. 8 2. 10 3. 12 4. 16 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The edges joining 1 to 2 and 2 to 3 force all of 1,2,3 into one class by transitivity. Element four remains alone. The generated relation therefore has 3 2 + 1 2 = 10 ordered pairs. The original union has only eight, missing both 1-to-3 directions. Sixteen would join the isolated fourth element without justification. Equivalence closure merges connected blocks, not all blocks.

questions.title: Question 9. Minimal does not mean least
questions.text: Question 9. Minimal does not mean least Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q19; MS_CS_1405_Q38. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Order divisors of 12 by divisibility. Within the induced subposet { 2 , 3 , 4 , 6 } , which statement is correct? 1. 2 is least. 2. There are two minimal elements and no least element. 3. 6 is greatest. 4. There are four minimal elements. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Elements 2 and 3 have no smaller elements in this induced set, so both are minimal. Neither divides the other, so no element is below all elements and there is no least element. The maximal elements are 4 and 6; neither divides the other, so six is not greatest. Four is not minimal because two lies below it, and six is not minimal because two and three lie below it. Ambient elements such as one cannot be used when the question restricts to an induced subposet.

questions.title: Question 10. A difference condition that fails one property
questions.text: Question 10. A difference condition that fails one property Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q38. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. On ℝ , define x R y iff x - y ∈ { 0 , 1 , - 1 } . Which classification is correct? 1. Reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. 2. Reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive. 3. Symmetric and transitive, but not reflexive. 4. Only reflexive. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Zero difference proves reflexivity, and the allowed set is closed under negation, proving symmetry. It is not closed under addition: 1 and 1 are allowed, but 2 is not. Concretely, 2 R 1 and 1 R 0 hold while 2 R 0 does not. Thus transitivity fails. The first alternative assumes symmetry and reflexivity imply equivalence; the others discard properties directly established by the permitted differences.

questions.title: Question 11. A quotient map and relation inclusion
questions.text: Question 11. A quotient map and relation inclusion Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q40; Phd_CS_1405_Q23. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. R , S are equivalences on finite A , with R ⊆ S . What can be asserted about the numbers of classes? 1. | A / R | ≤ | A / S | 2. | A / R | ≥ | A / S | 3. They are always equal. 4. They are unrelated. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Each R class lies within exactly one S class. Sending an R class to that containing S class defines a surjective map of quotient sets. Finite surjectivity implies at least as many source classes as target classes. Strict inequality occurs when equality classes are merged into one block; equality occurs when R = S . Adding related pairs coarsens a partition rather than creating more blocks.

A relation built from equal classes — applicability and boundary Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q38; Phd_CS_1405_Q13. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A set of n 2 elements is partitioned into n classes of size n . Count ordered pairs in the induced equivalence relation. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? 1. The relation size equals the number of classes. 2. For unequal classes, sum the squares of their sizes. 3. Every equivalence relation has all classes equally large. 4. Only unordered distinct pairs belong to an equivalence relation. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Check the hypothesis. Reflexivity includes diagonals and symmetry includes both orientations. An equivalence class contributes its full Cartesian square even when its size differs from the others. Equal class sizes are a premise of this calculation, not a property of equivalence relations. Connect it to the calculation. Each class contributes every ordered pair of its members, including diagonal pairs. Its contribution is n 2 , and the disjoint classes contribute independently to the relation size. Sum the class contributions rather than counting unordered edges. The valid statement is: For unequal classes, sum the squares of their sizes. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule. Distinguish the mathematical identity from the modeling assumptions that permit this identity to count or measure the requested objects.

questions.title: Question 39. Reachability in a directed chain — applicability and boundary
questions.text: Question 39. Reachability in a directed chain — applicability and boundary Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q38; Phd_CS_1405_Q13. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A directed path on n vertices has edges only from each vertex to the next. Count pairs in its transitive closure without adding identity pairs. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method? 1. Reachability in a directed path is symmetric. 2. Adding shortcut edges creates backward reachability. 3. Reflexive-transitive closure additionally includes zero-length paths. 4. Transitive closure always contains identity pairs by definition. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Check the hypothesis. A positive-length transitive closure and a reflexive-transitive closure use different path-length conventions. Zero-length paths contribute exactly the diagonal. A directed cycle, unlike this acyclic path, can create diagonal reachability even under the positive-length convention. Connect it to the calculation. Reachability holds from any earlier vertex to any later vertex. It does not hold backward or to itself because this path has no cycle and only positive-length paths are included. Count all distinct ordered forward pairs. The valid statement is: Reflexive-transitive closure additionally includes zero-length paths. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule. Distinguish the mathematical identity from the modeling assumptions that permit this identity to count or measure the requested objects.

questions.title: Question 44. Divisor-poset cover count
questions.text: Question 44. Divisor-poset cover count Original integrated challenge · retained after review The divisor lattice of 72 = 2 3 3 2 is represented by a Hasse diagram. How many vertices and cover edges does it have? 1. (12,17) 2. (12,24) 3. (6,17) 4. (12,29) Correct option: 1. Vertices correspond to exponent pairs 0 ≤ i ≤ 3 , 0 ≤ j ≤ 2 , giving4 times3 = 12. Covers increment exactly one exponent by1. There are3 horizontal increments in each of three rows, giving9, and2 vertical increments in each of four columns, giving8. Total17. Counting all comparable pairs would include transitive edges omitted from a Hasse diagram.

questions.title: Question 45. Height of a product order
questions.text: Question 45. Height of a product order Original integrated challenge · retained after review In the same divisor lattice, what is the longest-chain length measured in vertices? 1. 3 2. 4 3. 5 4. 6 Correct option: 4. The exponent rank i + j starts at0 and ends at5. Every strict cover raises it by1, so a chain can have at most six vertices. The chain1,2,4,8,24,72 attains that bound. Width instead concerns incomparable sets and is not this serial depth. Measuring edges would give5 rather than the requested vertex count.

questions.title: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q40 — Cardinality and a specified function
questions.text: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q40 — Cardinality and a specified function Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 9 · question 40 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. For f : A → B , consider: (a) if f is injective then | A | ≤ | B | ; (b) if f is surjective then | A | ≥ | B | ; (c) if f is bijective then | A | = | B | ; (d) if | A | = | B | then f is bijective. Which are correct? Use the usual set-theoretic choice convention for infinite sets. 1. Only (a) and ( c ). 2. Only (b) and ( d ). 3. Only (c) and ( d ). 4. Only (a), ( b ), and ( c ). Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. An injection witnesses the inequality in (a). A surjection permits a section under the stated convention, giving the inequality in ( b ). A bijection is the definition of equal cardinality, so (c) is true. Equal cardinality guarantees existence of some bijection, not bijectivity of every specified map. On A = B = { 0 , 1 } the constant map f ( x ) = 0 is neither injective nor onto. Hence (d) is false, and option 4 lists exactly the three true statements. Each other option either omits a true implication or includes ( d ). Transfer rule. Distinguish a statement about existence of a map from a statement about the map already named in the question.

questions.title: Question 5. PhD CS 1405, Q19 — Strict order and injectivity
questions.text: Question 5. PhD CS 1405, Q19 — Strict order and injectivity Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 19 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Evaluate (a) if ( A , < ) is linearly ordered and f : A → A preserves that strict order, then f is injective; (b) every countable set is well-orderable. 1. Only (a). 2. Only ( b ). 3. Both. 4. Neither. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. If x ≠ y , linearity makes either x < y or y < x . Strict preservation gives a strict inequality between the outputs, so the outputs are different. A finite set can be listed in a finite order. Transfer rule. Read strictness and comparability assumptions before invoking order-based injectivity.

questions.title: Question 10. Which composition implication survives?
questions.text: Question 10. Which composition implication survives? Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q40; Phd_CS_1405_Q19. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. f : A → B and g : B → C are arbitrary maps. Which implication is always correct? 1. If g ∘ f is injective, g is injective. 2. If g ∘ f is surjective, f is surjective. 3. If g ∘ f is bijective, f is injective and g is surjective. 4. If f is surjective, g ∘ f is injective. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Injectivity of the composite implies injectivity of f : equal f outputs would produce equal composite outputs. Surjectivity of the composite implies surjectivity of g : every target is reached through some intermediate f output. Hence the third claim holds. The composite tests g only on f ( A ) , so g may fail injectivity elsewhere. Likewise, f may miss elements that g does not need to cover C . Surjectivity of f alone gives no injectivity guarantee for either stage.

questions.title: Question 12. Preimages and images behave differently
questions.text: Question 12. Preimages and images behave differently Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q40; MS_CS_1405_Q37. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. For any f : A → B and subsets X , Y ⊆ A , which statement always holds? 1. f ( X ∩ Y ) = f ( X ) ∩ f ( Y ) 2. f ( X ∖ Y ) = f ( X ) ∖ f ( Y ) 3. f ( X ∪ Y ) = f ( X ) ∪ f ( Y ) 4. f ( X ) = f ( Y ) ⇒ X = Y Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. An output is in the image of a union exactly when some preimage lies in at least one input set, proving preservation of union. For all other alternatives, use a constant map on two distinct inputs and take the two distinct singleton subsets. Their image intersection is nonempty although their input intersection is empty; their image difference is empty although the image of their input difference is not; and their equal images do not force equal inputs. Extra injectivity would fix these failures, but was not assumed.

questions.title: Question 47. Count split inverse pairs
questions.text: Question 47. Count split inverse pairs Original integrated challenge · retained after review A has two labeled elements and B has three. How many ordered function pairs f : A → B , g : B → A satisfy g ∘ f = id A ? 1. 6 2. 8 3. 12 4. 18 Correct option: 3. The identity composite forces f injective, giving3 times2 = 6 choices. questions.title: Question 1. PhD CE 1405, Q3 — Leaf weights in a binary tree
questions.text: Question 1. PhD CE 1405, Q3 — Leaf weights in a binary tree Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 3 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. For each leaf x at depth d of a binary tree T , put w ( x ) = 2 - d . If L is the set of all leaves and α = ∑ x ∈ L w ( x ) , which is always correct? 1. α = 1 . 2. α ≤ 1 . 3. α > 1 . 4. α < 1 . Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Assign mass one to the root and half of a node's mass to each possible child. Missing children leave unused mass; a leaf receives exactly 2 - d . Leaf masses are disjoint allocations of the root mass, so their sum is at most one. This can also be proved by structural induction on the two subtrees. Equality occurs in a finite full binary tree, including a single root leaf. A root with just one leaf child has sum one half, so equality is not guaranteed. These examples eliminate the always-equal and always-strict alternatives; the greater-than alternative contradicts conservation of mass. Transfer rule. An upper bound can be universal even when equality depends on fullness of the structure.

questions.title: Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q9 — A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation
questions.text: Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q9 — A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 3 · question 9 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. For an array of distinct values, SplitSort chooses its median m , recursively processes R = { x : x > m } and L = { x : x < m } , and returns concatenate(SplitSort(R), [m], SplitSort(L)) ; arrays of length at most one are returned unchanged. What is the output order? 1. Descending up to the median, then ascending. 2. Approximately random. 3. Ascending. 4. Descending. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. The base cases of zero or one value are descending. Assume recursive outputs are descending. Every value in the first block is greater than m , and every value in the final block is less than m . Concatenating the descending greater block, m , and the descending smaller block therefore produces a descending whole array. Strong induction establishes the claim for every length. Median selection controls balance, not ascending direction. Option 1 misreads one recursive block; option 2 ignores determinism; option 3 would require left–median–right concatenation. Transfer rule. Prove a recursion's semantic invariant separately from its running-time recurrence.

questions.text: Question 3. MSc CS 1393, Q167 — Recursive reverse-stride copying Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 34 · question 167 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Copy every other element of an N -element array a , starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0) . Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure. 1. if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1); 2. if(n<i)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1); 3. if(n<i)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+1); 4. if(n<0)return; b[i++]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+2); Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. After t calls, the intended state is n = N - 1 - 2 t and i = t . Thus the next recursive call must decrease the source index by two and increase the destination by one. Option 1 preserves this state and stops precisely when the source index becomes negative. It writes ⌈ N / 2 ⌉ elements. Option 2 leaves b[0] unwritten and stops too early through an unrelated comparison. Option 3 uses stride one. Option 4 also uses source stride one and has incompatible destination updates. The source lists pseudocode resembling C without parameter type declarations; it is not a strictly compilable C17 function. We assess its specified indexing algorithm, not missing declarations. Transfer rule. Express the intended source and destination indices as functions of recursion depth.

questions.text: Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q28 — Parity far from the given recurrence values Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 28 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Let a n = 3 a n - 1 + 5 a n - 2 + 4 , with a 16 = 1403 and a 17 = 2025 . How many of a 100 , a 101 , … , a 113 are even? 1. 4 2. 5 3. 7 4. 10 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Reduce modulo two: a n ≡ a n - 1 + a n - 2 . The two given values are both odd. The parity states from indices 16 onward are odd, odd, even, repeating every three. This can be checked by advancing the pair state and then proved by induction. Hence even values occur exactly at indices divisible by three. In 100 through 113 these are 102,105,108,111, giving four. There is no need to construct the enormous later terms. Counting a half split or forgetting the inclusive range gives the wrong number. Transfer rule. Project a recurrence into the requested residue system and track its finite pair-state cycle.

questions.title: Question 5. A modular move obstruction
questions.text: Question 5. A modular move obstruction Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q125; Phd_CE_1405_Q3. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A state is ( x , y ) ∈ ℤ 2 . Allowed moves add either ( 2 , 1 ) or ( - 1 , 2 ) , or subtract either vector. Starting at ( 0 , 0 ) , which target is impossible? 1. (5,0). 2. (0,5). 3. (2,1). 4. (1,0). Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. The residue x - 2 y ( mod 5 ) is unchanged: the two move increments are zero and negative five. The initial residue is zero, while ( 1 , 0 ) has residue one, proving impossibility. The other targets are explicitly reachable: twice ( 2 , 1 ) minus ( - 1 , 2 ) gives ( 5 , 0 ) ; once ( 2 , 1 ) plus twice ( - 1 , 2 ) gives ( 0 , 5 ) ; the third is a permitted move. An invariant proves impossibility, but reachability of the other choices needs a construction.

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

A state is (x,y)∈ℤ2. Allowed moves add either (2,1) or (-1,2), or subtract either vector. Starting at (0,0), which target is impossible?

(5,0).

2.

(0,5).

(2,1).

(1,0).

questions.text: Question 6. An invariant that is true but insufficient Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1393_Q167; Phd_CE_1405_Q9. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A sum loop processes a 0 , … , a n - 1 with initialization s = 0 , k = 0 and update s+=a[k]; k++ . Which invariant directly proves that the final sum is correct? 1. s ≥ 0 2. s = ∑ i = 0 k - 1 a i and 0 ≤ k ≤ n 3. s = ∑ i = 0 n - 1 a i at every iteration 4. k < n Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. At initialization the empty prefix sum is zero. The update adds the next element and advances the boundary by one, preserving the prefix equation and bounds. At exit, k = n , so the prefix is the entire array. Nonnegativity is not even valid for arbitrary signed data and would not identify the sum. The third equation is generally false before completion; the final strict inequality fails at exit. A useful invariant connects progress state to the desired postcondition.

questions.title: Question 7. Binary powering: exact multiplication count
questions.text: Question 7. Binary powering: exact multiplication count Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q20; MS_CS_1393_Q167. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Binary exponentiation starts with r = 1 , b = a , e = 13 . Each iteration multiplies r by b if e is odd, then squares b unconditionally and replaces e by ⌊ e / 2 ⌋ . Count all multiplications, including the final square. 1. 6 2. 7 3. 8 4. 13 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The exponent states are 13, 6, 3, and 1, so four iterations square the base. The odd states 13, 3, and 1 each multiply the accumulator, adding three. Seven multiplications are performed. The preserved identity is r b e = a 13 ; odd iterations move one factor to the accumulator before halving. Omitting the final unused square would give six for a different implementation. Counts depend on the exact code, not just the logarithmic complexity.

questions.title: Question 8. A lexicographic termination bound
questions.text: Question 8. A lexicographic termination bound Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1393_Q167; Phd_CS_1405_Q20. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. For integer state ( i , j ) with 0 ≤ i ≤ m and 0 ≤ j ≤ n , a loop decreases j by one when j > 0 ; when j = 0 and i > 0 , it decreases i and sets j = n . Which integer ranking decreases by one at every step? 1. i + j 2. i ( n + 1 ) + j 3. i j 4. i - j Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Within a row, decrementing j decreases i ( n + 1 ) + j by one. At a row boundary, the new value is ( i - 1 ) ( n + 1 ) + n = i ( n + 1 ) - 1 , again one less. The ranking is nonnegative and zero only at ( 0 , 0 ) , so it proves termination and an exact number of steps equal to its initial value. The simple sum can increase on reset; the product is zero along whole boundaries; i - j increases when j decreases.

questions.title: Question 9. Parity in a coefficient problem
questions.text: Question 9. Parity in a coefficient problem Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q125. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A polynomial is built by multiplying ten factors, each contributing either x 3 or x - 1 . Which exponent cannot occur? 1. -10 2. -2 3. 6 4. 8 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. If j factors contribute x 3 , the exponent is 3 j - ( 10 - j ) = 4 j - 10 . Thus every exponent is congruent to two modulo four and 0 ≤ j ≤ 10 . The first three values correspond to j = 0 , 2 , 4 . Eight would require j = 18 / 4 , not an integer. Both congruence and range are required; a congruent exponent outside the achievable interval would also be impossible.

questions.title: Question 10. A conservation law for a full tree
questions.text: Question 10. A conservation law for a full tree Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q3. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A finite full binary tree has 19 leaves. What pair gives its number of internal nodes and total edges? 1. 18 and 36. 2. 19 and 38. 3. 18 and 37. 4. 20 and 38. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. For a full binary tree, L = I + 1 . Hence I = 18 and the total node count is 37. A finite tree has one fewer edge than nodes, giving 36. Equivalently, each of the eighteen internal nodes supplies two child edges. This double check verifies both coordinates. The distractors confuse leaves with internal nodes or count edges as all nodes. Fullness is necessary for the internal-node formula.

questions.title: Question 11. Safety without inductiveness
questions.text: Question 11. Safety without inductiveness Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q3; MS_CS_1393_Q167. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A program starts at x = 0 and repeatedly adds two, never using other moves. Which statement is true of property x ≠ 1 ? 1. It is false at initialization. 2. It is inductive over all states satisfying it. 3. It is true on all reachable states, but not inductive over all states satisfying it. 4. It proves termination. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Every reachable value is a nonnegative even integer, so no reachable value is one. However the property also permits state x = - 1 , whose next state is one. Therefore the property alone is not closed under the transition over its full state set. The stronger invariant “ x is even and nonnegative” excludes the spurious predecessor. Safety can be true without the proposed assertion being inductive. The program can run forever, so a safety condition does not prove termination.

questions.title: Question 12. A recursive permutation preserves a sum but changes order
questions.text: Question 12. A recursive permutation preserves a sum but changes order Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q9; Phd_CE_1405_Q16. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A recursive routine splits distinct values around a pivot and returns greater-block, pivot, smaller-block. Which specification is sufficient to prove descending sorting? 1. The output sum equals the input sum. 2. The output length equals input length. 3. The output is a permutation, each child is descending, and both cross-block inequalities hold. 4. The pivot occurs somewhere in the output. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Permutation preservation ensures no value is lost or duplicated. Child sortedness handles within-block neighbors, and cross-block inequalities place all greater values before the pivot and all smaller values after it. Together they prove the complete ordering and preservation contract. Length and sum alone allow many incorrect multisets; retaining a pivot says nothing about the remaining order. A recursive proof must retain enough information about each child to justify the combine step.

questions.text: Question 46. A modular linear invariant Original integrated challenge · retained after review States are pairs modulo5. The only move adds ( 1 , 2 ) to a pair. Starting ( 0 , 0 ) , which target is unreachable? 1. (1,2) 2. (2,4) 3. (3,4) 4. (4,3) Correct option: 3. The quantity 2 x - y modulo5 is invariant because a move changes it by 2 - 2 = 0 . questions.text: Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q38 — A difference-defined equivalence Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 9 · question 38 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. For real x , y , define x ∼ y exactly when x - y ∈ A . Which choice of A makes this an equivalence relation? 1. The integers divisible by 2 or by 3. 2. { m / n : n ∈ ℕ , m ∈ ℤ , m ≤ n } , with positive denominators. 3. The integers that are not prime. 4. { m / 2 n : n ∈ ℕ , m ∈ ℤ } Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. Reflexivity requires 0 ∈ A . questions.text: Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q125 — An impossible coefficient Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 27 · question 125 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Let A be the coefficient of x 14 in ( x 2 + 1 / x ) 14 . Which interval contains A / 5 ? 1. [ 9 , + ∞ ) 2. [ 3 , 6 ) 3. [ 6 , 9 ) 4. [ 0 , 3 ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. Choosing j factors of x 2 and 14 - j factors of x - 1 yields exponent 2 j - ( 14 - j ) = 3 j - 14 . The desired exponent would require 3 j - 14 = 14 , so j = 28 / 3 , not an integer. No binomial term has that exponent. Therefore A = 0 and A / 5 = 0 lies in option 4. Every exponent is congruent to 1 modulo 3, while 14 is congruent to 2. The other intervals exclude zero. A binomial coefficient cannot be evaluated at a noninteger selection index to manufacture a term. Transfer rule. questions.title: Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q25 — A subset containing an odd pair sum
questions.text: Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q25 — A subset containing an odd pair sum Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 25 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. How many four-element subsets A of { 1 , 2 , … , 10 } contain two elements x , y such that x + y is odd? 1. 200 2. 205 3. 208 4. 209 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. A sum is odd exactly when one summand is even and the other odd. Thus the set must contain both parities. There are ( 10 4 ) = 210 unrestricted subsets. The failing subsets consist entirely of the five even or entirely of the five odd elements. Subtract 2 ( 5 4 ) = 10 to get 200. The two failure classes are disjoint, so no overlap correction is required. Counting a chosen odd/even pair and then two other elements would overcount sets containing several witness pairs. Transfer rule. Count an existential-witness property by its complement when each valid object may have several witnesses.

questions.title: Question 5. PhD CS 1404, Q28 — Parity far from the given recurrence values
questions.text: Question 5. PhD CS 1404, Q28 — Parity far from the given recurrence values Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 28 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Let a n = 3 a n - 1 + 5 a n - 2 + 4 , with a 16 = 1403 and a 17 = 2025 . How many of a 100 , a 101 , … , a 113 are even? 1. 4 2. 5 3. 7 4. 10 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Reduce modulo two: a n ≡ a n - 1 + a n - 2 . The two given values are both odd. The parity states from indices 16 onward are odd, odd, even, repeating every three. This can be checked by advancing the pair state and then proved by induction. Hence even values occur exactly at indices divisible by three. In 100 through 113 these are 102,105,108,111, giving four. There is no need to construct the enormous later terms. Counting a half split or forgetting the inclusive range gives the wrong number. Transfer rule. Project a recurrence into the requested residue system and track its finite pair-state cycle.

questions.title: Question 7. Compatible noncoprime remainders
questions.text: Question 7. Compatible noncoprime remainders Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q38; MS_CS_1405_Q125. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Solve x ≡ 5 ( mod 8 ) and x ≡ 1 ( mod 6 ) . What is the least positive solution and period? 1. 13 and 24. 2. 5 and 48. 3. 13 and 48. 4. No solution. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Compatibility requires the residues to agree modulo gcd ( 8 , 6 ) = 2 ; both are odd, so they do. Set x = 5 + 8 k . Reduction modulo six gives 2 k ≡ 2 ( mod 6 ) , hence k ≡ 1 ( mod 3 ) . Thus x = 13 + 24 t . The period is the lcm, twenty-four, not the product forty-eight. The first residue five fails the second congruence. Compatibility precedes inversion because the original moduli are not coprime.

questions.title: Question 8. Exponent reduction with a nonunit
questions.text: Question 8. Exponent reduction with a nonunit Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q38; MS_CS_1405_Q125. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Find 6 100 ( mod 15 ) . 1. 1 2. 6 3. 0 4. 9 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Six is idempotent modulo fifteen: 6 2 = 36 ≡ 6 . Multiplying by six therefore preserves the same residue for every positive exponent, giving six. Euler's unit theorem cannot be applied because gcd ( 6 , 15 ) = 3 . Reducing the exponent to zero modulo the totient and returning one would be invalid. The same result follows from CRT: the power is zero modulo three and one modulo five, whose combined residue is six.

questions.title: Question 46. Congruence solutions in an interval
questions.text: Question 46. Congruence solutions in an interval Original integrated challenge · retained after review How many integers 0 ≤ x ≤ 100 solve 6 x ≡ 8 ( mod 14 ) ? 1. 7 2. 13 3. 14 4. 15 Correct option: 3. Reduce the congruence to x ≡ 6 ( mod 7 ) . The interval solutions are x = 6 + 7 t with integer t ≥ 0 and t ≤ ⌊ ( 100 - 6 ) / 7 ⌋ = 13 . Thus there are14 values. The two-residues-per14 statement is compatible but does not by itself count a partially filled final interval. Apply floor endpoints after finding the reduced progression.

questions.title: Question 47. Compatible shared-modulus reconstruction
questions.text: Question 47. Compatible shared-modulus reconstruction Original integrated challenge · retained after review What is the least nonnegative x satisfying x ≡ 5 ( mod 12 ) and x ≡ 11 ( mod 18 ) ? 1. 11 2. 17 3. 29 4. 35 Correct option: 3. The gcd6 compatibility test passes because5 and11 have equal residues modulo6. Put x = 5 + 12 t ; then 12 t ≡ 6 ( mod 18 ) . Divide6 to get 2 t ≡ 1 ( mod 3 ) , so t ≡ 2 ( mod 3 ) . Therefore x ≡ 29 ( mod 36 ) and29 is the least nonnegative solution. The lcm36, not product216, is the fundamental period.

MSc CS 1405, Q130 — A prefix-sum recurrence Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 28 · question 130 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Let c 0 = 1 and c n + 1 = ∑ i = 0 n c i for n ≥ 0 . Its generating function is C ( x ) = ( 1 - x ) / ( 1 - α x ) . What is α ? 1. 2 2. 3 3. 4 4. 5 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The first recurrence value is c 1 = 1 . For n ≥ 1 , subtract the equation for c n from that for c n + 1 to obtain c n + 1 = 2 c n . Therefore c n = 2 n - 1 for n ≥ 1 , proved directly by induction from c 1 = 1 . Sum the formal series: C ( x ) = 1 + x ∑ j ≥ 0 ( 2 x ) j = 1 + x / ( 1 - 2 x ) = ( 1 - x ) / ( 1 - 2 x ) . Thus α = 2 . 4. Values 3, 4, and 5 would already produce the wrong coefficient of x 2 . Applying c n = 2 n at n = 0 would also miss the initial exception. Transfer rule. Subtract consecutive prefix recurrences; state precisely where the simplified recurrence begins.

O ( β n α log n ) 4. O ( α n + β log n ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The Akra–Bazzi exponent satisfies α p + β p = 1 . Here p = 1 . questions.title: Question 5. MSc CE 1405, Q59 — An unbalanced pivot selection
questions.text: Question 5. MSc CE 1405, Q59 — An unbalanced pivot selection Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 13 · question 59 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. A quicksort variant sorts the first 2 n + 1 elements by insertion sort and chooses their median as pivot, then proceeds as ordinary quicksort. Which recurrence describes the worst case, suppressing rounding and constant terms? 1. T ( n ) = 2 T ( n - 1 ) + n 2. T ( n ) = 2 T ( n ) + n 3. T ( n ) = 2 T ( n - n ) + n 4. T ( n ) = T ( n - n ) + T ( n ) + n Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. Sorting a sample of size Θ ( n ) by insertion sort costs Θ ( n ) ; partitioning also costs Θ ( n ) . The sample median has at least n sample elements on each side. Thus neither partition can leave fewer than approximately n elements on its smaller side, but the rest of the array can all lie on the larger side. The worst split is therefore approximately n versus n - n , giving option 4. Options 1 and 3 duplicate a large branch and count more elements than the partition contains. Option 2 incorrectly treats the small sample as the whole input. Transfer rule. Derive partition guarantees from the sample, and check that child sizes add to the parent size up to the pivot.

questions.title: Question 7. PhD CS 1404, Q28 — Parity far from the given recurrence values
questions.text: Question 7. PhD CS 1404, Q28 — Parity far from the given recurrence values Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 28 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Let a n = 3 a n - 1 + 5 a n - 2 + 4 , with a 16 = 1403 and a 17 = 2025 . How many of a 100 , a 101 , … , a 113 are even? 1. 4 2. 5 3. 7 4. 10 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Reduce modulo two: a n ≡ a n - 1 + a n - 2 . The two given values are both odd. The parity states from indices 16 onward are odd, odd, even, repeating every three. This can be checked by advancing the pair state and then proved by induction. Hence even values occur exactly at indices divisible by three. In 100 through 113 these are 102,105,108,111, giving four. There is no need to construct the enormous later terms. Counting a half split or forgetting the inclusive range gives the wrong number. Transfer rule. Project a recurrence into the requested residue system and track its finite pair-state cycle.

Θ ( n 2 ) 4. Θ ( n 2 log n ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Naive Fibonacci recursion uses two recursive calls for F ( n ) ; memoization stores each F ( k ) once. Assuming constant-cost integer additions, what are the naive and memoized work classes? 1. Θ ( n 2 ) and Θ ( n ) 2. Θ ( φ n ) and Θ ( n ) 3. Θ ( 2 n ) and Θ ( log n ) 4. Θ ( n ) and Θ ( n ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Naive call counts follow a Fibonacci-type recurrence, giving Θ ( φ n ) with φ = ( 1 + 5 ) / 2 . The bound O ( 2 n ) is true but not the tight naive class. Memoization computes each of n + 1 states once and performs constant work per nonbase state, giving linear work under the stipulated arithmetic model. Bit-cost arithmetic would need a separate analysis because Fibonacci numbers grow in bit length. A call tree and a memoized state DAG count different objects.

questions.title: Question 52. A slowly shrinking argument
questions.text: Question 52. A slowly shrinking argument Original integrated challenge · retained after review For integer n > 1 , T ( n ) = T ( n - ⌈ n ⌉ ) + 1 , with constant base cost for n ≤ 1 . What is its tight order? 1. Θ ( log n ) 2. Θ ( n ) 3. Θ ( n ) 4. Θ ( n log n ) Correct option: 2. Each step removes order n items, and the potential n decreases by a positive constant order: rationalize n - n - ⌈ n ⌉ as the decrement divided by the sum of roots. Away from the fixed small cutoff this difference is bounded above and below by constants. Hence order n steps are necessary and sufficient. The final small states add only a constant. Neither subtract-one unrolling nor equal-fraction master cases model this shrink rule.

questions.text: Question 53. Work with a repeated state Original integrated challenge · retained after review A program recursively calls the identical size- n / 2 subproblem twice, then does n work. If the second call reuses the first result instead of recomputing, what is the resulting work order? 1. Θ ( log n ) 2. Θ ( n ) 3. Θ ( n log n ) 4. Θ ( n 2 ) Correct option: 2. Without reuse the execution tree follows 2 T ( n / 2 ) + n and costs n log n . With one actual child computation per size, the recurrence is T ( n / 2 ) + n and its tolls form n + n / 2 + n / 4 + … = Θ ( n ) . The specification requires identical subproblems and reusable results; equal sizes alone do not prove that the child instances are identical.

PhD CE 1405, Q1 — Unequal recursive splits Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 1 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Fixed positive constants α , β satisfy α + β = 1 . For T ( n ) = T ( α n ) + T ( β n ) + n with constant small-input base cost, which listed bound is correct? 1. O ( α β n ) 2. O ( n log n ) 3. O ( β n α log n ) 4. O ( α n + β log n ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The Akra–Bazzi exponent satisfies α p + β p = 1 . Here p = 1 . with constant small-input base cost, which listed bound is correct?

1.
O(αβn)
2.
O(nlogn)
3.
O(βnαlogn)
4.
O(αn+βlogn)

questions.title: Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q9 — A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation
questions.text: Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q9 — A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 3 · question 9 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. For an array of distinct values, SplitSort chooses its median m , recursively processes R = { x : x > m } and L = { x : x < m } , and returns concatenate(SplitSort(R), [m], SplitSort(L)) ; arrays of length at most one are returned unchanged. What is the output order? 1. Descending up to the median, then ascending. 2. Approximately random. 3. Ascending. 4. Descending. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. The base cases of zero or one value are descending. Assume recursive outputs are descending. Every value in the first block is greater than m , and every value in the final block is less than m . Concatenating the descending greater block, m , and the descending smaller block therefore produces a descending whole array. Strong induction establishes the claim for every length. Median selection controls balance, not ascending direction. Option 1 misreads one recursive block; option 2 ignores determinism; option 3 would require left–median–right concatenation. Transfer rule. Prove a recursion's semantic invariant separately from its running-time recurrence.

questions.title: Question 3. PhD CE 1405, Q16 — Exact merge comparisons
questions.text: Question 3. PhD CE 1405, Q16 — Exact merge comparisons Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 4 · question 16 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. Merge sort repeatedly divides an eight-element array into equal halves and merges by comparing the two current front elements until one side is exhausted. For A = [ 12 , 7 , 5 , 9 , 3 , 8 , 2 , 6 ] , how many element comparisons are performed? 1. 14 2. 16 3. 10 4. 12 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Four size-two merges cost one comparison each: subtotal four. Merging [ 7 , 12 ] with [ 5 , 9 ] costs three comparisons. Merging [ 3 , 8 ] with [ 2 , 6 ] also costs three. The subtotal is ten. The final merge of [ 5 , 7 , 9 , 12 ] with [ 2 , 3 , 6 , 8 ] compares front pairs until the right list empties: emitted comparison results are 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, and 8. Six comparisons bring the total to sixteen. Ten omits the final merge; twelve undercounts intermediate comparisons; fourteen is not the trace count. Remaining elements copied after exhaustion incur no key comparison. Transfer rule. A worst-case merge bound is not automatically the exact cost of a supplied input.

questions.title: Question 4. MSc CE 1405, Q59 — An unbalanced pivot selection
questions.text: Question 4. MSc CE 1405, Q59 — An unbalanced pivot selection Authentic examination · English translation Original booklet · PDF page 13 · question 59 . independently derived; not represented as an official key. A quicksort variant sorts the first 2 n + 1 elements by insertion sort and chooses their median as pivot, then proceeds as ordinary quicksort. Which recurrence describes the worst case, suppressing rounding and constant terms? 1. T ( n ) = 2 T ( n - 1 ) + n 2. T ( n ) = 2 T ( n ) + n 3. T ( n ) = 2 T ( n - n ) + n 4. T ( n ) = T ( n - n ) + T ( n ) + n Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. Sorting a sample of size Θ ( n ) by insertion sort costs Θ ( n ) ; partitioning also costs Θ ( n ) . The sample median has at least n sample elements on each side. Thus neither partition can leave fewer than approximately n elements on its smaller side, but the rest of the array can all lie on the larger side. The worst split is therefore approximately n versus n - n , giving option 4. Options 1 and 3 duplicate a large branch and count more elements than the partition contains. Option 2 incorrectly treats the small sample as the whole input. Transfer rule. Derive partition guarantees from the sample, and check that child sizes add to the parent size up to the pivot.

This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Merge sort splits evenly and compares front elements until one child list is exhausted. questions.text: Question 7. A sufficient summary for maximum subarray Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q9; Phd_CE_1405_Q16. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A segment summary stores total sum, maximum nonempty prefix, maximum nonempty suffix, and maximum nonempty subarray. Left summary is ( - 2 , 3 , 1 , 5 ) and right is ( 4 , 6 , 4 , 6 ) . What is the combined maximum subarray sum? 1. 5 2. 6 3. 7 4. 9 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The optimum is either inside the left child, inside the right child, or crossing the boundary. The crossing value is left suffix plus right prefix, 1 + 6 = 7 . Compare 5,6,7 to obtain seven. The nonempty contract matters for all-negative inputs, where zero cannot be supplied as an automatic candidate.

questions.text: Question 8. Karatsuba reconstruction with exact numbers Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q1; MS_CE_1405_Q58. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Use base ten blocks to multiply 23 by 47. Karatsuba computes z 2 = 2 · 4 , z 0 = 3 · 7 , and z 1 = ( 2 + 3 ) ( 4 + 7 ) - z 2 - z 0 . questions.title: Question 10. Padding for linear convolution
questions.text: Question 10. Padding for linear convolution Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q16; MS_CS_1405_Q125. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. Polynomials have coefficient counts five and four. What is the smallest power-of-two transform length sufficient to recover their complete linear convolution without wraparound? 1. 4 2. 8 3. 16 4. 32 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The product has at most 5 + 4 - 1 = 8 coefficients. A length-eight transform represents all of them without circular aliasing and is already a power of two. Length four would identify distinct output positions modulo four and lose information; sixteen and thirty-two are sufficient but not minimal. Coefficient count is degree plus one, so adding degrees without restoring the final one leads to an endpoint error.

questions.title: Question 11. What a sampling guarantee actually ensures
questions.text: Question 11. What a sampling guarantee actually ensures Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty Pattern reference: MS_CE_1405_Q59. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets. A pivot is the median of nine sampled distinct elements from an array of length n . In the worst case, what lower bound on the numbers strictly below and above it is guaranteed solely by the sample? 1. At least four on each side. 2. At least n / 2 on each side. 3. At least nine on each side. 4. No element on either side is guaranteed. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The sample contains four smaller and four larger elements, so these elements certify the two lower bounds in the whole array. All remaining elements could lie on the same side, so the sample alone does not guarantee a balanced full-array partition. The pivot itself is excluded from both strict sides. Partition-time and sample-sorting cost are separate from the rank guarantee.

questions.title: Question 45. A finite-field Fourier evaluation
questions.text: Question 45. A finite-field Fourier evaluation Original integrated challenge · retained after review Work modulo17 with length-four root ω = 4 . For a = [ 1 , 2 , 0 , 0 ] and forward positive exponents, what is Y ? 1. [3,9,16,10] 2. [3,10,16,9] 3. [1,2,0,0] 4. [3,8,15,9] Correct option: 1. Powers of4 modulo17 are1,4,16,13; the square is - 1 and the fourth power is1, so its order is4. Each evaluation is 1 + 2 ω k , producing3,9,33 modulo17 = 16, and27 modulo17 = 10. Reversing the exponent sign exchanges the second and fourth values. The inverse normalization uses 4 - 1 = 13 modulo17, not real division by4.

questions.title: Question 46. Exact modular recovery range
questions.text: Question 46. Exact modular recovery range Original integrated challenge · retained after review An integer coefficient is known only to lie in [ - 10 , 10 ] , and its residue modulo17 is7. Is its exact value uniquely determined? 1. Yes, it must be7. 2. Yes, it must be-10. 3. No, both7 and-10 fit. 4. No value in the range fits. Correct option: 3. Values7 and 7 - 17 = - 10 share the residue and both lie in the allowed interval. Unique centered recovery needs a modulus greater than the full coefficient-range width20, or additional information excluding one candidate. Exact modular arithmetic prevents rounding error but does not by itself prevent integer aliasing. More CRT moduli can enlarge the combined modulus enough to distinguish the possibilities.

questions.title: Question 1. A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation
questions.text: Question 1. A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation Authentic examination · English translation Phd CE 1405 · Q9 · PDF page 3 . Independently derived solution; not an official key. For an array of distinct values, SplitSort chooses its median m , recursively processes R = { x : x > m } and L = { x : x < m } , and returns concatenate(SplitSort(R), [m], SplitSort(L)) ; arrays of length at most one are returned unchanged. What is the output order? 1. Descending up to the median, then ascending. 2. Approximately random. 3. Ascending. 4. Descending. Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. The base cases of zero or one value are descending. Assume recursive outputs are descending. Every value in the first block is greater than m , and every value in the final block is less than m . Concatenating the descending greater block, m , and the descending smaller block therefore produces a descending whole array. Strong induction establishes the claim for every length. Median selection controls balance, not ascending direction. Option 1 misreads one recursive block; option 2 ignores determinism; option 3 would require left–median–right concatenation. Transfer rule. Prove a recursion's semantic invariant separately from its running-time recurrence.

questions.title: Question 2. Recursive reverse-stride copying
questions.text: Question 2. Recursive reverse-stride copying Authentic examination · English translation MS CS 1393 · Q167 · PDF page 34 . Independently derived solution; not an official key. Copy every other element of an N -element array a , starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0) . Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure. 1. if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1); 2. if(n<i)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1); 3. if(n<i)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+1); 4. if(n<0)return; b[i++]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+2); Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. After t calls, the intended state is n = N - 1 - 2 t and i = t . Thus the next recursive call must decrease the source index by two and increase the destination by one. Option 1 preserves this state and stops precisely when the source index becomes negative. It writes ⌈ N / 2 ⌉ elements. Option 2 leaves b[0] unwritten and stops too early through an unrelated comparison. Option 3 uses stride one. Option 4 also uses source stride one and has incompatible destination updates. The source lists pseudocode resembling C without parameter type declarations; it is not a strictly compilable C17 function. We assess its specified indexing algorithm, not missing declarations. Transfer rule. Express the intended source and destination indices as functions of recursion depth.

questions.title: Question 3. Leaf weights in a binary tree
questions.text: Question 3. Leaf weights in a binary tree Authentic examination · English translation Phd CE 1405 · Q3 · PDF page 2 . Independently derived solution; not an official key. For each leaf x at depth d of a binary tree T , put w ( x ) = 2 - d . If L is the set of all leaves and α = ∑ x ∈ L w ( x ) , which is always correct? 1. α = 1 . 2. α ≤ 1 . 3. α > 1 . 4. α < 1 . Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Assign mass one to the root and half of a node's mass to each possible child. Missing children leave unused mass; a leaf receives exactly 2 - d . Leaf masses are disjoint allocations of the root mass, so their sum is at most one. This can also be proved by structural induction on the two subtrees. Equality occurs in a finite full binary tree, including a single root leaf. A root with just one leaf child has sum one half, so equality is not guaranteed. These examples eliminate the always-equal and always-strict alternatives; the greater-than alternative contradicts conservation of mass. Transfer rule. An upper bound can be universal even when equality depends on fullness of the structure.

questions.text: Question 5. Backward substitution through a quadratic Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Over exact integers, execute x = x + 3 . What is the weakest precondition for final x 2 = 25 ? 1. x = 5 or x = - 5 2. x = 2 or x = - 8 3. x = 8 or x = - 2 4. x = 2 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. questions.title: Question 6. Sequence order changes the precondition
questions.text: Question 6. Sequence order changes the precondition Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Execute x=x+1; y=2*x; x=y-3 over integers. Which initial condition is weakest for final x = 7 ? 1. x = 4 2. x = 5 3. y = 10 4. x = 10 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Work backward. The final assignment requires old y - 3 = 7 , hence y = 10 . The middle assignment requires 2 x = 10 . The first assignment then requires 2 ( x + 1 ) = 10 , so initial x = 4 . Initial y is unconstrained because the middle statement overwrites it. A forward trace from four gives five, ten and seven, confirming the derivation. Option 2 omits the increment; option 3 constrains an overwritten value; option 4 mistakes an intermediate value for the input.

questions.text: Question 7. Simultaneous versus sequential assignment Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Initially ( x , y ) = ( 5 , 8 ) . Compare simultaneous (x,y)=(y,x+y) with sequential x=y; y=x+y . What are their respective results? 1. ( 8 , 13 ) and ( 8 , 13 ) 2. ( 8 , 16 ) and ( 8 , 13 ) 3. ( 8 , 13 ) and ( 8 , 16 ) 4. questions.title: Question 8. Conditional weakest precondition
questions.text: Question 8. Conditional weakest precondition Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived analogue: Cambridge conditional verification, PDF pages 52–53 For integer x , execute if x<0: x=-x; else: x=x+2 . Which condition is weakest for final x ≥ 3 ? 1. x ≠ 0 2. x ≥ 1 3. x ≤ - 3 4. x ≤ - 3 or x ≥ 1 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 4. In the negative branch, - x ≥ 3 means x ≤ - 3 , which already implies the branch guard. In the nonnegative branch, x + 2 ≥ 3 means x ≥ 1 . Combine the guarded branches by disjunction to obtain x ≤ - 3 or x ≥ 1 . Inputs negative one and negative two refute option 1. Options 2 and 3 each omit one valid branch. The postcondition must be proved on both paths, including the otherwise branch.

questions.title: Question 9. Which consequence direction is sound?
questions.text: Question 9. Which consequence direction is sound? Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem A known triple has precondition x ≥ 0 and postcondition r = x 2 . Which replacement is always justified by consequence alone? 1. Precondition true; postcondition r = x 2 2. Precondition x ≥ 2 ; postcondition r ≥ 0 3. Precondition x ≥ 0 ; postcondition r > x 4. Precondition x < 0 ; postcondition r ≥ 0 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The stronger precondition x ≥ 2 implies x ≥ 0 , and the exact square postcondition implies r ≥ 0 over real or integer values. Therefore option 2 follows. Option 1 expands the input domain; option 4 changes it to an unproved domain. Option 3 strengthens the output assertion and fails at x = 0 or x = 1 . Consequence moves assumptions toward greater restriction and conclusions toward weaker requirements.

questions.title: Question 10. Array aliasing is a logical condition
questions.text: Question 10. Array aliasing is a logical condition Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived analogue: Cambridge array updates, PDF pages 19–22 Both indices are valid. Execute A[i]=1; A[j]=2 . Which is the weakest condition on indices for final A [ i ] = 1 and A [ j ] = 2 ? 1. i < j 2. i > j 3. i ≠ j 4. No condition Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. If indices differ, the second write cannot change the first cell, so both desired values hold. If they coincide, the last write leaves that single cell equal to two, contradicting its required equality to one. Thus inequality is both necessary and sufficient. Either strict-order alternative is sufficient but not weakest because it excludes the opposite order. The no-condition alternative assumes separate array syntax means separate memory.

Invariant strength can fail at an unreachable state Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original state-machine analogue informed by MIT §5.4 Start at ( x , y ) = ( 0 , 0 ) and repeatedly assign both coordinates simultaneously to ( x + 1 , y + 1 ) . Is I : x ≥ 0 by itself inductive under the transition, and is it sufficient to prove final x = y ? 1. Inductive and sufficient 2. Inductive but insufficient 3. Not inductive but sufficient 4. Neither Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Every state with nonnegative x produces nonnegative x + 1 , so the predicate is inductive. However, it admits ( 3 , 8 ) and gives no relationship between the coordinates. Adding x = y yields a useful invariant and proves the equality at any termination checkpoint. Truth of a weak invariant does not supply an unrelated postcondition. The reachable states happen to satisfy equality, but the annotation must express it.

questions.text: Question 12. Reachable truth need not be inductive Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard Original state-machine analogue informed by MIT §5.4 Start at x = 0 . The transition maps zero to zero and maps every positive x to - 1 . Which describes I : x ≥ 0 ? 1. False on a reachable state 2. True on every reachable state but not inductive 3. Inductive but false initially 4. A proof that every state is reachable Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The only reachable value is zero, because zero maps to itself. Thus the predicate holds on every reachable state. Yet the state x = 1 satisfies the predicate and its successor - 1 does not; this refutes preservation over all invariant states. Strengthening to x = 0 removes the unreachable counterexample. Option 1 confuses possible integers with reachable ones, and option 3 reverses the failed obligation.
