questions.title: Question 13. A defective annotation does not condemn a program
questions.text: Question 13. A defective annotation does not condemn a program Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived analogue: Cambridge Exercise 45, PDF page 58 Annotate while False: x=0 with invariant False , initial assertion True , and final assertion True . Which claim is correct? 1. The program diverges 2. The final assertion is false 3. Initialization of the chosen invariant fails, although the program is correct 4. Every chosen invariant proves every loop Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The loop executes zero bodies and terminates with the state unchanged, so the stated partial and total result is true. Nevertheless, initialization asks whether true implies false, which is invalid. A failed annotation can be repaired by using invariant true. This separates a proof artifact from program behavior. The preservation implication is vacuous here, but it cannot repair failed initialization.

questions.text: Question 14. A loop with exact iteration count Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem For positive integer n , initialize x = n and execute while x>0: x=max(0,x-3) . How many body executions occur? 1. ⌊ n / 3 ⌋ 2. ⌈ n / 3 ⌉ 3. n 4. ⌈ ( n - 1 ) / 3 ⌉ Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. After t bodies, x = max ( 0 , n - 3 t ) . questions.text: Question 15. Strict decrease over reals is insufficient Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original termination analogue informed by MIT §5.4 Start x = 1 and repeat while x>0: x=x/2 in exact real arithmetic. Which is correct? 1. The loop terminates after one step 2. It terminates after finitely many steps because x decreases 3. It does not terminate; nonnegative real strict descent is not well-founded 4. It violates x ≥ 0 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. After t steps, x = 2 - t > 0 for every finite integer t , so the guard never becomes false. Strict decrease and nonnegativity hold throughout. A real measure therefore does not justify termination without an additional well-founded ordering or a fixed minimum decrease. Floating-point underflow would create a different execution model and must not be inserted into the exact-real problem.

questions.title: Question 16. Lexicographic descent and step bounds
questions.text: Question 16. Lexicographic descent and step bounds Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard Original termination analogue informed by MIT §5.4 A nonnegative pair starts at ( 1 , 0 ) . A step may replace it by ( 0 , B ) for any finite nonnegative integer B , after which the second coordinate decreases to zero. Which is true? 1. Every execution terminates, but there is no uniform step bound from the initial pair alone 2. Some execution has infinitely many decrements after the reset 3. Every execution has at most one step 4. The pair does not decrease lexicographically Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The first step strictly decreases the first coordinate, so any finite reset is permitted by lexicographic descent. Thereafter exactly B unit decrements reach zero, making total length B + 1 . Each particular execution is finite, but choosing arbitrarily large finite B defeats any uniform bound depending only on the initial pair. Infinite reset values are not admitted. Option 4 wrongly applies componentwise ordering rather than lexicographic ordering.

questions.title: Question 19. A monotone invariant can coexist with nontermination
questions.text: Question 19. A monotone invariant can coexist with nontermination Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Replace lo=mid+1 by lo=mid in half-open lower bound. Which smallest array/target pair demonstrates failure? 1. [ 2 ] , target three 2. [ 2 ] , target one 3. [ ] , target three 4. [ 2 , 4 ] , target one Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. On the one-element interval [ 0 , 1 ) , midpoint zero has value two below target three. The defective update leaves the lower boundary at zero, so the state repeats forever. Its classification invariant remains true; the decreasing-width obligation fails. The target-one case moves the upper boundary to zero and terminates, and an empty array executes no body. A minimal counterexample isolates the faulty branch rather than relying on a large random test.

questions.title: Question 20. Lower bound requires sortedness
questions.text: Question 20. Lower bound requires sortedness Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Run correct lower-bound code on the unsorted array [ 4 , 1 , 3 ] with target three. Which result and conclusion are correct? 1. It returns zero and is correct 2. It returns two; sortedness was needed to discard earlier positions 3. It returns one; the duplicate rule failed 4. It raises an index error Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The first midpoint is one, whose value is one, so the lower boundary becomes two. questions.text: Question 21. Array lower bound versus upper bound Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem For [ 1 , 2 , 2 , 2 , 5 ] and target two, the leftmost index satisfying A [ i ] ≥ 2 and the leftmost satisfying A [ i ] > 2 are respectively what? 1. One and one 2. Three and four 3. One and four 4. Zero and three Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The first eligible index for the non-strict comparison is one. questions.title: Question 22. A conditional interval bound
questions.text: Question 22. A conditional interval bound Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem At a true lower-bound guard, let interval length be L . Which is the tightest listed common upper bound on new length in both branches with the floor midpoint? 1. L - 1 only; no tighter bound is valid 2. ⌊ L / 2 ⌋ 3. ⌈ L / 2 ⌉ + 1 4. L and no strict decrease Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The left-keeping branch has length ⌊ L / 2 ⌋ . The right-keeping branch has length L - ⌊ L / 2 ⌋ - 1 = ⌈ L / 2 ⌉ - 1 , at most ⌊ L / 2 ⌋ . For L = 1 both new lengths are zero. Option 1 gives a true but weaker bound rather than the requested common halving bound; option 3 is loose; option 4 misses strict progress.

questions.title: Question 23. Insertion shifts and inversions
questions.text: Question 23. Insertion shifts and inversions Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived insertion analogue: Stanford Lecture 2, PDF pages 1–2 Sort [ 4 , 2 , 3 , 1 ] by the displayed insertion sort. How many assignments of the form a[j+1]=a[j] execute? 1. Three 2. Four 3. Five 4. Six Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Key two shifts four once. Key three shifts four once. Key one shifts four, three and two three times. Total shifts are 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 . Independently, the strict inversions are ( 4 , 2 ) , ( 4 , 3 ) , ( 4 , 1 ) , ( 2 , 1 ) , ( 3 , 1 ) , also five. Placements of the saved key are different assignments and are not counted. questions.title: Question 24. The temporary array is not a permutation
questions.text: Question 24. The temporary array is not a permutation Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original refinement of Stanford insertion-sort proof During insertion of key two into [ 1 , 4 , 2 ] , after shifting four right and before restoring the key, the physical array is [ 1 , 4 , 4 ] . Which conservation statement is correct? 1. The physical array alone preserves the input multiset 2. Ignore the hole at index one and include the saved key two 3. Ignore the last element and discard the key 4. Only the sum of physical array values is preserved Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. After the shift, the logical hole is index one: that old value has moved right and its stale duplicate must not count twice. The other positions contain one and four; the external saved key is two. Their multiset is exactly the original prefix multiset. Filling the hole restores physical permutation. The physical sum changes from seven to nine, refuting option 4. A correct inner invariant accounts for temporary storage instead of demanding an assertion that the code does not preserve.

questions.title: Question 25. Stability is independent of sortedness
questions.text: Question 25. Stability is independent of sortedness Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Insertion sort compares keys and moves entire records. If its inner comparison becomes a[j].key >= key.key , what happens to records ( 2 , a ) , ( 2 , b ) ? 1. They remain in order ( a , b ) 2. Their order becomes ( b , a ) ; sortedness and multiplicity still hold 3. The keys become unsorted 4. A record is lost Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. When inserting the second record, the equal first key satisfies the modified guard. The first record shifts right, and the saved second record fills index zero. The result is ( 2 , b ) , ( 2 , a ) , sorted by key and a permutation of the input but unstable. The example shows why proving only key order and multiset preservation does not establish stability. A strict greater-than shift preserves equal-key order.

questions.title: Question 26. Exact stable-merge comparisons
questions.text: Question 26. Exact stable-merge comparisons Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived merge analogue: Stanford Lecture 2, PDF pages 3–4 Merge sorted lists [ 1 , 4 , 7 ] and [ 2 , 3 , 8 ] , comparing heads while both lists are nonempty and taking the left on a tie. How many head comparisons occur? 1. Three 2. Four 3. Five 4. Six Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The compared head pairs are ( 1 , 2 ) , ( 4 , 2 ) , ( 4 , 3 ) , ( 4 , 8 ) , ( 7 , 8 ) . The emissions are one, two, three, four and seven; the left list is then exhausted and eight is appended without a head comparison. Thus five comparisons occur. Six counts tail copying as another comparison; three assumes each list element pair aligns by index. The merge proof must cover the unpaired tail explicitly.

questions.title: Question 27. Sorted output without preservation
questions.text: Question 27. Sorted output without preservation Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem A routine replaces every input entry by zero. Which verifier incorrectly accepts it as a sorting algorithm for arbitrary integer inputs? 1. Check nondecreasing output only 2. Check output multiset equals input multiset only 3. Check both order and multiset 4. Check a bijection of record indices and ordered keys Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. A zero-filled array is nondecreasing, so an order-only verifier accepts every such output. For input [ 3 , 1 ] , the multiset differs, and the other listed checks reject it. A permutation-only check is also insufficient in general, but it rejects this particular corrupting routine unless the input already consists entirely of zeros. This question distinguishes what the verifier tests from the complete contract it ought to establish.

questions.title: Question 28. Recursive size must strictly decrease
questions.text: Question 28. Recursive size must strictly decrease Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original boundary completion of Stanford recursive proof A purported merge sort stops only at length one and splits length n into ⌊ n / 2 ⌋ and ⌈ n / 2 ⌉ . What happens on an empty input? 1. It terminates with an empty list automatically 2. Both child sizes are zero, so the recursion has no decreasing measure 3. It calls a child of size one 4. It produces a sorted nonempty list Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. At length zero the stated base case does not apply. Both children again have length zero, so recursive calls reproduce the same unhandled size indefinitely. Correcting the base condition to length at most one covers empty input and makes both children strictly smaller for every remaining length. Runtime formulas derived only for positive sizes cannot repair a missing functional base case.

questions.text: Question 29. Three-way partition trace Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Run the displayed three-way partition on [ 3 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 0 ] with pivot two. What final boundary pair ( lt , gt ) is returned? 1. ( 1 , 2 ) 2. ( 2 , 3 ) 3. ( 3 , 4 ) 4. ( 0 , 5 ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. There are two values below two (one and zero), one equal value and two greater values. Preservation plus the final region invariant requires less region length two and equal region length one, giving boundaries ( 2 , 3 ) . A concrete trace produces [ 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 3 ] with these boundaries, though the order within outer regions is not promised. Counting only distinct keys instead of records would give the wrong lengths.

questions.text: Question 30. Skipping an incoming unknown value Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Modify the greater-than branch of three-way partition to increment i after the swap. Which two-element input with pivot two exposes failure? 1. [ 1 , 3 ] 2. [ 2 , 3 ] 3. [ 3 , 1 ] 4. [ 1 , 2 ] Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. On [ 3 , 1 ] , decrement the upper boundary from two to one and swap index zero with index one, producing [ 1 , 3 ] . The defective increment makes the scan index one, ending the loop with less boundary zero. It therefore classifies the first value as equal even though one is less than two. The incoming unknown value needed inspection. The correct code keeps the scan index zero and moves that value into the less region on the next iteration.

questions.title: Question 31. An exact partition work count
questions.text: Question 31. An exact partition work count Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem For the displayed three-way partition on an array of length n , how many loop bodies execute regardless of key distribution? 1. n 2. n - 1 3. 2 n 4. The count depends on the number of distinct keys Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Initially the unknown-region length is gt - i = n . In each branch exactly one boundary moves by one in the direction that reduces this length, and no branch changes it by another amount. The loop stops precisely at unknown length zero. Hence there are exactly n body executions, including zero for empty input. This does not mean equal numbers of key comparisons or swaps: those depend on which branches execute.

  2. In each branch exactly one boundary moves by one in the direction that reduces this length, and no branch changes it by another amount.

  3. The loop stops precisely at unknown length zero.

  4. Hence there are exactly n body executions, including zero for empty input.

  5. This does not mean equal numbers of key comparisons or swaps: those depend on which branches execute.

questions.title: Question 32. Conservation does not imply stability
questions.text: Question 32. Conservation does not imply stability Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Partition tagged records ( 3 , a ) , ( 3 , b ) , ( 1 , c ) around pivot two using swaps. Which complete claim is valid? 1. Every partition is stable 2. Only keys, not records, are preserved 3. The algorithm preserves the record multiset but may reverse equal-key records 4. The algorithm sorts each outer region Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The first greater-than swap exchanges ( 3 , a ) with ( 1 , c ) , yielding ( 1 , c ) , ( 3 , b ) , ( 3 , a ) . The two equal-key three records now appear in reverse original order. Swaps preserve whole records, so multiplicity and payloads survive. Region membership is established, but stability and internal sorting are not part of the contract. The trace provides a precise counterexample to option 1.

questions.title: Question 33. Quotient and remainder as a certificate
questions.text: Question 33. Quotient and remainder as a certificate Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived division analogue: Cambridge verification examples and Exercise 53 Repeated subtraction divides 47 by six with initial ( q , r ) = ( 0 , 47 ) . What final pair and body count result? 1. ( 7 , 5 ) and seven 2. ( 8 , - 1 ) and eight 3. ( 6 , 11 ) and six 4. ( 7 , 6 ) and seven Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The remainder sequence is 47 , 41 , 35 , 29 , 23 , 17 , 11 , 5 . Seven subtractions occur, and the quotient reaches seven. Conservation gives 47 = 7 · 6 + 5 , and the exit range 0 ≤ 5 < 6 proves this is the unique division result. The negative-remainder option performs one extra subtraction after the guard is false; the third option stops too early; the fourth violates conservation.

questions.title: Question 34. A valid identity with an invalid termination proof
questions.text: Question 34. A valid identity with an invalid termination proof Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived domain repair: Cambridge Exercise 53, PDF page 72 Use repeated subtraction with X = 5 , Y = 0 . Which statement explains the defect? 1. The conservation identity fails initially 2. The remainder becomes negative 3. The invariant remains true, but the guard remains true and the remainder does not decrease 4. The algorithm returns quotient zero and remainder five Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Initialization gives 5 = 0 · 0 + 5 . Every body leaves the remainder five while increasing the quotient, so conservation continues to hold. The guard tests 5 ≥ 0 forever. A nonnegative remainder that is merely constant is not a decreasing variant. This is precisely why total correctness needs a positive divisor even though the algebraic partial-correctness equations can still be written.

questions.title: Question 35. Sequential updates in Euclid
questions.text: Question 35. Sequential updates in Euclid Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem With input ( 21 , 15 ) , what does defective code while b!=0: a=b; b=a%b return, and what should correct Euclid return? 1. Fifteen and three 2. Three and three 3. Six and fifteen 4. Zero and three Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The first statement overwrites the dividend with fifteen. The second uses the new dividend and computes 15 mod 15 = 0 , so the defective loop returns fifteen. Correct simultaneous steps are ( 21 , 15 ) → ( 15 , 6 ) → ( 6 , 3 ) → ( 3 , 0 ) , returning three. The gcd invariant fails on the defective first step, because the old gcd is three but the new gcd is fifteen. Preserving old operands is essential.

questions.text: Question 37. Power algorithm intermediate state Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived exponentiation analogue: CMU Contracts For exact power(3,13) , what is ( r , b , e ) after two complete loop bodies? 1. ( 3 , 81 , 3 ) 2. ( 9 , 81 , 3 ) 3. ( 3 , 9 , 6 ) 4. ( 81 , 3 , 3 ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Initially ( 1 , 3 , 13 ) . The odd first body multiplies the accumulator by three, squares the base to nine and halves the exponent to six: ( 3 , 9 , 6 ) . The even second body leaves the accumulator three, squares nine to 81 and halves six to three. The invariant checks 3 · 81 3 = 3 13 . Option 3 is only the first checkpoint; option 2 incorrectly multiplies the accumulator on an even exponent.

questions.title: Question 38. Two multiplication counts
questions.text: Question 38. Two multiplication counts Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem For exponent 45, count accumulator multiplications and base squarings in the displayed exact power implementation. 1. Six and four 2. Four and six 3. Five and five 4. Four and five Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Binary 45 is 101101, with six bits and four one bits. The loop executes six bodies, squaring once per body; the accumulator multiplication executes only on the four odd-exponent checkpoints. The exact counts are therefore four and six. Avoid silently deleting the final square when analyzing this displayed code. An optimized version could have five squarings, corresponding to option 4 but not to this implementation.

questions.title: Question 39. The old base matters
questions.text: Question 39. The old base matters Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Move b=b*b before the odd-exponent accumulator update in power . What does the resulting code return for ( x , y ) = ( 2 , 1 ) ? 1. One 2. Two 3. Four 4. Eight Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The loop begins with base two and exponent one. Squaring first makes the base four. The odd branch then multiplies the accumulator one by four, and halving the exponent ends the loop. The result four differs from the required two. The even/odd invariant derivation uses the old base in the accumulator factor; changing execution order invalidates that derivation.

questions.title: Question 40. Exponent zero and modulus one
questions.text: Question 40. Exponent zero and modulus one Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived modular extension: CMU Exercise 1 A correct modular power routine allows M ≥ 1 and exponent zero. For modulus one, which initialization yields the canonical final residue? 1. Accumulator one, without reduction 2. Accumulator 1 mod M 3. Accumulator equal to the base 4. Reject every exponent-zero input Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The canonical residues modulo one contain only zero. With exponent zero no bodies execute, so the accumulator itself is returned. Initialization 1 mod 1 = 0 yields the correct residue; unnormalized one is congruent to zero but is not the canonical value required by the contract. This distinguishes congruence from normalized output range.

questions.title: Question 41. Reduction after overflow is too late
questions.text: Question 41. Reduction after overflow is too late Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard Course-derived overflow extension: CMU Exercises 1–2 For eight-bit unsigned wrapping arithmetic, compute (200*200)%251 using an eight-bit wrapped product. Compare it with exact modular multiplication. 1. Both are 91 2. Wrapped result 64; exact result 91 3. Wrapped result 91; exact result 64 4. Both are 64 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Exact product is 40000. Modulo 256 it becomes 64 because 40000 = 156 · 256 + 64 . Reducing that wrapped value modulo 251 still gives 64. Exact reduction gives 40000 = 159 · 251 + 91 , hence 91. Wrapping modulo a power of two before reducing modulo a different modulus changes the arithmetic. A wide intermediate or an overflow-safe multiplication algorithm is required.

questions.title: Question 42. Permutation index certificate
questions.text: Question 42. Permutation index certificate Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Input records have keys [ 5 , 1 , 5 ] and claimed sorted output keys [ 1 , 5 , 5 ] . Which zero-based source-index certificate additionally establishes stability? 1. [ 1 , 0 , 2 ] 2. [ 1 , 2 , 0 ] 3. [ 1 , 0 , 0 ] 4. [ 0 , 1 , 2 ] Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Indices one, zero and two form a bijection and map the output to keys one, five and five. The equal-five records keep original index order zero before two, proving stability. Option 2 is a bijection and preserves keys but reverses equal records. Option 3 duplicates a source record; option 4 gives the wrong output ordering. A certificate must check index range, uniqueness, key consistency and the additional tie rule.

questions.title: Question 43. Meeting witness and bound proves optimum
questions.text: Question 43. Meeting witness and bound proves optimum Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem In a minimization problem, a feasible solution has value 17, while a proved lower bound for every feasible solution is 17. What follows? 1. The optimum is at most 17 only 2. The optimum is at least 17 only 3. The optimum equals 17 4. The result depends on the search algorithm runtime Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The feasible witness establishes optimum at most 17. The universal lower bound establishes optimum at least 17. Together they force equality. Feasibility alone would not exclude a cheaper solution, and the lower bound alone would not supply an attaining solution. Runtime is irrelevant to this logical certificate, although finding or checking the witness may have a cost.

questions.title: Question 44. Distance edge inequalities are necessary
questions.text: Question 44. Distance edge inequalities are necessary Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard Original certificate problem Graph edges are s → a of weight two, a → b of weight three, and s → b of weight four. Claimed distances are ( 0 , 2 , 5 ) with parent path through a . Which check detects failure? 1. Parent path existence 2. Root distance zero 3. The edge inequality on s → b 4. Nonnegative distances Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. The supplied parents give a real root-to- b path of weight five, so feasibility succeeds. But the direct edge gives d ( b ) ≤ d ( s ) + 4 , requiring 5 ≤ 4 , which is false. There is a shorter path of weight four. Thus parent paths alone certify reachable distances, not shortest distances. This example isolates the optimality-bound component of the certificate.

questions.title: Question 45. Parent cycles can pass local equalities
questions.text: Question 45. Parent cycles can pass local equalities Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard Original certificate counterexample Graph edges are s → a of weight five, a → b of weight zero and b → a of weight zero. A certificate sets d ( s ) = d ( a ) = d ( b ) = 0 , and chooses parents parent ( a ) = b , parent ( b ) = a . What is missing? 1. All edge inequalities already fail 2. A requirement that parent chains reach the root 3. The root distance must be five 4. A requirement that weights be positive Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. All edge inequalities hold: zero is at most five on the root edge, and equal zero distances satisfy both zero edges. Both parent equalities also hold. Yet the parent cycle provides no path from the root attaining distance zero; the actual distances to the other vertices are five. Requiring every parent chain to end at the root excludes this false certificate. Strictly positive weights would be an unnecessary domain restriction rather than the general repair.

Negative weights do not automatically defeat a certificate Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard Original certificate problem Graph edges are s → a of weight four, s → b of weight five and a → b of weight negative three. questions.title: Question 47. A negative cycle contradicts finite labels
questions.text: Question 47. A negative cycle contradicts finite labels Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard Original certificate problem A reachable directed cycle has edge weights two, negative five and one. What do shortest-path edge inequalities imply when summed around the cycle? 1. 0 ≤ - 2 , a contradiction 2. 0 ≤ 2 , a proof of optimality 3. d ( s ) = 0 only 4. A cycle is allowed whenever one edge is positive Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. Each inequality bounds the next distance by the previous distance plus its edge weight. Summing cancels every distance from both sides and requires zero at most total cycle weight 2 - 5 + 1 = - 2 . This is impossible, so no finite assignment satisfying all cycle-edge inequalities exists. The contradiction depends on the negative total, not on which individual edges have which sign.

questions.title: Question 48. Greedy feasibility is not optimality
questions.text: Question 48. Greedy feasibility is not optimality Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem For unweighted interval scheduling, choosing the earliest-start interval selects [ 0 , 10 ) and rejects [ 1 , 2 ) , [ 2 , 3 ) , [ 3 , 4 ) . Which conclusion is justified? 1. It is optimal because chosen intervals never overlap 2. The output is feasible but may be suboptimal 3. No greedy algorithm can be correct 4. Endpoint conventions do not matter Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The chosen singleton is feasible. Under half-open intervals, the three short intervals are mutually compatible and yield three selections instead of one. Therefore a non-overlap invariant proves feasibility but not maximal cardinality. An optimality proof needs an exchange or dominance argument for the chosen rule. This counterexample does not refute every greedy rule; earliest finish is a different rule. Endpoint conventions matter to whether adjacent intervals are compatible.

questions.title: Question 49. Structural mass with missing children
questions.text: Question 49. Structural mass with missing children Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem A binary tree has leaves at depths one, two and three, with no other leaves. What is the leaf mass ∑ 2 - d , and does it alone prove fullness? 1. 7 / 8 ; it does not prove fullness 2. 1 ; it proves fullness 3. 3 / 8 ; it proves fullness 4. 7 / 8 ; it proves fullness Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 1. The mass is 1 / 2 + 1 / 4 + 1 / 8 = 7 / 8 . In a finite full binary tree root mass splits completely and all mass reaches leaves, so total mass is one. A mass below one means some possible child branches are missing. The given depths can occur in a tree with a chain containing missing branches. This certificate argument distinguishes a universal bound from its equality condition.

An accumulator formula for dependent loops Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem For integer n ≥ 1 , increment an accumulator once for each 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ k ≤ n , starting from c 0 . What final formula follows? 1. c 0 + ( n 3 ) 2. c 0 + n 3 3. c 0 + ( n + 2 3 ) 4. ( n + 2 3 ) Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 3. Each weakly increasing triple corresponds to a multiset of size three drawn from n values. The count is ( n + 3 - 1 3 ) = ( n + 2 3 ) . questions.text: Question 51. Recursion depth as an index invariant Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Copy indices N - 1 , N - 3 , … from an input into consecutive output cells starting at zero. For N = 10 , what final copied source index and output length occur? 1. Source zero; length five 2. Source one; length five 3. Source one; length six 4. Source zero; length ten Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. The source indices are nine, seven, five, three and one. At depth t , the source is N - 1 - 2 t and destination is t . After five writes, the next source is negative one and recursion stops. Generally the output length is ⌈ N / 2 ⌉ and the last source is one for even positive lengths, zero for odd lengths. This state formula proves indexing and termination together.

questions.text: Question 52. An exact invariant determines a nonlinear sum Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived summation analogue: Cambridge for-loop verification, PDF pages 57–58 Initialize s=0, k=1 . While k<=n , execute s += 2*k-1; k += 1 , with exact integers and n ≥ 0 . Which invariant at the checkpoint just before the guard is correct? 1. s = k 2 2. s = ( k - 1 ) 2 3. s = 2 k - 1 4. s = n 2 Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Before iteration one, the sum is zero, equal to ( 1 - 1 ) 2 . If the invariant holds before k , adding 2 k - 1 gives ( k - 1 ) 2 + 2 k - 1 = k 2 , which is the required assertion before iteration k + 1 . At exit k = n + 1 , it yields s = n 2 . The empty range for n = 0 leaves zero, agreeing with the formula. Option 1 places the assertion after the body rather than before it.

questions.title: Question 53. An induction hypothesis must include preservation
questions.text: Question 53. An induction hypothesis must include preservation Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard Original strengthening of Stanford recursive proof For a recursive sorting proof, the induction hypothesis says only that each child output is sorted. Which additional assertion is essential to establish the complete parent sorting contract? 1. The child runtime is linear 2. Each child output preserves its input multiset 3. The recursion tree is balanced 4. Every input key is positive Read the complete solution and option analysis Correct option: 2. Sorted child outputs could both be empty, satisfying the weak induction hypothesis while destroying all input records. Preservation of each child multiset plus preservation by merge proves preservation for the parent. Balance affects cost and strict size reduction affects termination, but neither implies value preservation. Positive keys are unnecessary because ordering works over any totally ordered key domain.

Independently derived answer; not an official key. The probability that a family has n children is 2 - n - 1 for n ≥ 0 . Independently, each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl. Independently derived answer; not an official key. Player A tosses a fair coin 25 times and player B tosses a fair coin 20 times, independently. ( 45 15 ) 2 - 20 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. Sum over their common head count k : P = 2 - 45 ∑ k = 0 20 ( 25 k ) ( 20 k ) . 2. Replace ( 20 k ) by ( 20 20 - k ) and apply Vandermonde's identity. The sum is ( 45 20 ) . 3. Alternatively, equal heads means the heads in A's tosses plus the tails in B's tosses total 20. Those 45 independent fair indicators give the same binomial coefficient. 4. The denominator counts all 45 tosses; 2 20 is insufficient. The index 15 represents the wrong combined target. Transfer rule. Convert equality between two counts into one count by complementing one group's successes.

questions.html:
Question 4. Heads in a conditional second toss

Authentic examination · checked English translation

MS CE 1405 · Q35 · PDF page 8. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Four fair coins are tossed. Every coin that showed heads is tossed again. If Y is the number of heads in the second toss, what is P(Y=2)?

1.
1/2
2.
3/4
3.
17/128
4.
27/128
Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Correct option: 4.

  1. Model each coin by two independent fair tosses, with the second revealed only when the first is heads. A coin contributes one to Y exactly on the outcome heads-heads, which has probability 1/4.
  2. The four contribution indicators are independent, so Y is binomial with parameters 4 and 1/4. Exactly two successes have probability
(42)(1/4)2(3/4)2=27/128

, option 4. 3. An independent derivation conditions on the number K of first-round heads. Sum (4k)2-4(k2)2-k for k=2,3,4. The contributions are 3/32,3/32,3/128, whose sum is 27/128. 4. Treating the second round as four unconditional fair tosses ignores that only first-round heads qualify. Fixing the random number of qualifying coins at its expected value also changes the distribution.

Transfer rule. Replace a multistage selection experiment by independent per-object indicators when eligibility and success can be combined into one event.

questions.title: Question 5. Unequal retained masses
questions.text: Question 5. Unequal retained masses Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Four atoms have weights ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ) . Event A contains atoms one and three; B contains atoms one and two. Find both reversed conditionals and the conditional weight of each atom given B . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The total weight ten cancels in each ratio. The common intersection has weight one; B has weight three and A has weight four. Thus P ( A ∣ B ) = 1 / 3 and P ( B ∣ A ) = 1 / 4 . Given B , the four atom weights become ( 1 / 3 , 2 / 3 , 0 , 0 ) . Counting two retained atoms as equally likely would give an incorrect answer because conditioning preserves their original weight ratio. The conditional weights sum to one and the two joint identities each recover original probability 1 / 10 .

questions.title: Question 6. Reconstruct every cell
questions.text: Question 6. Reconstruct every cell Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Given P ( B ) = 2 / 5 , P ( A ∣ B ) = 3 / 4 , and P ( A ∣ B c ) = 1 / 6 , reconstruct all four joint cells, find P ( A ) , and decide whether A , B are independent. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Multiply each conditional by its stratum mass. In the order both, A only, B only, neither, the cells are 3 / 10 , 1 / 10 , 1 / 10 , 1 / 2 . They are nonnegative and sum to one, so the data define a valid model. Summing the A row gives P ( A ) = 2 / 5 . Independence would require intersection ( 2 / 5 ) ( 2 / 5 ) = 4 / 25 , while the actual value is 3 / 10 . The events are dependent and positively associated. Equal marginals explain the equal reversed conditionals but do not imply independence.

questions.title: Question 7. An impossible conditional specification
questions.text: Question 7. An impossible conditional specification Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Can P ( A ) = 1 / 5 , P ( B ) = 3 / 5 , and P ( A ∣ B ) = 1 / 2 hold simultaneously? Give a precise reason. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The last two numbers force joint mass P ( A ∩ B ) = ( 3 / 5 ) ( 1 / 2 ) = 3 / 10 . However an intersection is contained in A and cannot have probability greater than P ( A ) = 1 / 5 . Equivalently the A-only cell would be 1 / 5 - 3 / 10 = - 1 / 10 , violating nonnegativity. Therefore no probability model satisfies these premises. It is inappropriate to continue computing a reverse conditional from inconsistent data; the feasibility check must precede inference.

questions.title: Question 8. Sharp range of a conditional
questions.text: Question 8. Sharp range of a conditional Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem If P ( A ) = 7 / 10 and P ( B ) = 3 / 5 , determine the smallest and largest possible P ( A ∣ B ) and construct cells attaining each. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The joint mass x lies between 7 / 10 + 3 / 5 - 1 = 3 / 10 and 3 / 5 . Dividing by 3 / 5 gives the sharp interval [ 1 / 2 , 1 ] . At the lower endpoint the cells are ( 3 / 10 , 2 / 5 , 3 / 10 , 0 ) ; at the upper endpoint they are ( 3 / 5 , 1 / 10 , 0 , 3 / 10 ) . Each construction is nonnegative and normalized, so both endpoints are attainable. The upper endpoint says B implies A almost surely; the lower endpoint makes the neither cell empty in probability.

questions.title: Question 9. Recover an unknown stratum weight
questions.text: Question 9. Recover an unknown stratum weight Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Events satisfy P ( A ∣ B ) = 4 / 5 , P ( A ∣ B c ) = 1 / 5 , and P ( A ) = 1 / 2 . Find the unknown stratum weight P ( B ) and the reversed conditional P ( B ∣ A ) . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Let b be the unknown stratum mass. Total probability gives 1 / 2 = ( 4 / 5 ) b + ( 1 / 5 ) ( 1 - b ) , hence b = 1 / 2 . The joint mass is b ( 4 / 5 ) = 2 / 5 , and reversing the conditional gives ( 2 / 5 ) / ( 1 / 2 ) = 4 / 5 . The four cells are ( 2 / 5 , 1 / 10 , 1 / 10 , 2 / 5 ) , confirming feasibility. The equality of reversed conditionals is explained by equal marginals, not by an automatic symmetry of conditional probability. All denominators in this reconstructed model are positive.

questions.title: Question 10. Equal reversed conditionals without equal marginals
questions.text: Question 10. Equal reversed conditionals without equal marginals Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For positive marginal probabilities, characterize when P ( A ∣ B ) = P ( B ∣ A ) . Can they be equal when the marginals differ? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Write x for the intersection. Equality is x / b = x / a , equivalent after multiplication by positive ab to x ( a - b ) = 0 . Therefore either x is zero or the marginals are equal. Positive-probability disjoint events supply unequal-marginal examples: take A mass 1 / 4 and disjoint B mass 1 / 2 . Both conditionals are zero. Dividing one conditional by the other would wrongly discard this case because that step would divide by zero.

questions.title: Question 11. Association changes in both directions
questions.text: Question 11. Association changes in both directions Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Adapted proof structure: CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.8 Assume positive marginals and P ( A ∣ B ) > P ( A ) . Prove the corresponding strict inequality for P ( B ∣ A ) , and identify the quantity that controls both signs. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The given inequality is x / b > a , which is equivalent to x - a b > 0 because b is positive. Dividing that same inequality by a gives x / a > b , the desired P ( B ∣ A ) > P ( B ) . More precisely the two differences are ( x - a b ) / b and ( x - a b ) / a . Their magnitudes can differ but their signs agree. If one marginal is zero its corresponding conditional is undefined, so the positive-marginal premise cannot be dropped.

questions.title: Question 12. A conditional union uses one universe
questions.text: Question 12. A conditional union uses one universe Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Inside a positive event C , suppose P ( A ∣ C ) = 2 / 3 , P ( B ∣ C ) = 1 / 2 , and P ( A ∩ B ∣ C ) = 1 / 3 . Find the conditional union, exactly one, and neither. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Apply inclusion-exclusion to the conditional probability measure. The union is 2 / 3 + 1 / 2 - 1 / 3 = 5 / 6 . Exactly one subtracts both copies of the intersection from the sum, giving 2 / 3 + 1 / 2 - 2 / 3 = 1 / 2 . Neither is the complement of the union, giving 1 / 6 . The both, A-only, B -only, neither cells within C are ( 1 / 3 , 1 / 3 , 1 / 6 , 1 / 6 ) . Their sum is one; mixing an unconditional intersection into this calculation would break the common universe.

questions.title: Question 13. Implication in probability versus literal containment
questions.text: Question 13. Implication in probability versus literal containment Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Construct events with P ( A ∣ B ) = 1 but B ⊈ A as sets. Explain why there is no contradiction. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Use three outcomes with weights ( 1 / 2 , 1 / 2 , 0 ) . Let A contain only outcome one, and let B contain outcomes one and three. Then P ( B ) = 1 / 2 and P ( A ∩ B ) = 1 / 2 , so the conditional is one. Nevertheless outcome three belongs to B but not A . The formula proves only P ( B ∖ A ) = 0 . It establishes almost-sure containment; literal containment follows only with additional support assumptions such as strictly positive weights on every finite outcome.

Nested information Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem For weights ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ) , let A = { 1 , 4 } , B = { 1 , 2 , 4 } , and C = { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } . Verify the nested-conditioning identity numerically. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The total weight is fifteen, but ratios can use unnormalized weights. The intersection B with C is B , of weight seven; its intersection with A has weight five. Thus P ( A ∣ B ∩ C ) = 5 / 7 . Inside C , P ( A ∩ B ∣ C ) = 5 / 10 and P ( B ∣ C ) = 7 / 10 , whose ratio is again 5 / 7 . The cancellation is valid because both C and its intersection with B have positive mass. Averaging P ( A ∣ B ) and P ( A ∣ C ) would have no justification.

questions.text: Question 15. A zero last factor is allowed Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Suppose P ( A ) = 2 / 5 , P ( B ∣ A ) = 3 / 4 , and P ( C ∣ A ∩ B ) = 0 . Find the triple probability and explain why the chain rule remains defined. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The prefix A has positive mass 2 / 5 , and the second prefix has mass ( 2 / 5 ) ( 3 / 4 ) = 3 / 10 . Both denominators used in the chain exist. The last conditional factor is zero, so the triple mass is zero. Positive final mass is not required; it is only a sufficient way of guaranteeing positive prefixes. If a further factor conditioned on the zero-mass triple were written, it would be undefined. A tree should stop that branch rather than multiply an undefined number by zero.

questions.title: Question 16. Dropping history changes a joint answer
questions.text: Question 16. Dropping history changes a joint answer Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For independent fair bits let A = { X = 1 } , B = { Y = 1 } , and C = { X = Y } . Compare the correct chain product with the product that conditions C only on B . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The joint event is the single bit pair 11, so its mass is 1 / 4 . The full factors are 1 / 2 , 1 / 2 , 1 , giving 1 / 4 . Conditioning C only on B leaves two possibilities 01 and 11, so the abbreviated last factor is 1 / 2 and the product becomes 1 / 8 . The error assumes that observing X adds no information after Y , which is false for the equality event. Pairwise independence of some event pairs does not license this history deletion.

questions.text: Question 19. Minimum and maximum of two rolls Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Completed written example: MIT 6.041SC Lecture 2, PDF page 1 Two independent fair four-sided dice show X and Y . Given min ( X , Y ) = 2 , determine the distribution of max ( X , Y ) . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The condition retains ordered pairs ( 2 , 2 ) , ( 2 , 3 ) , ( 3 , 2 ) , ( 2 , 4 ) , ( 4 , 2 ) . They each had probability 1 / 16 , so the conditional universe has five equal atoms. The maximum is two in one atom, three in two atoms, and four in two atoms, giving probabilities 1 / 5 , 2 / 5 , 2 / 5 . A maximum of one is impossible under the condition. Counting unordered pairs as three equal alternatives would ignore that off-diagonal pairs represent two ordered outcomes.

Find the probability of red-blue-red without replacement, then the probability of exactly two reds in three draws. questions.title: Question 21. Condition on a coarse color history
questions.text: Question 21. Condition on a coarse color history Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem From the same urn, condition on the first two draws having different colors. Find the probability that the third is red. Explain why ignoring the order is valid here. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The two retained histories RB and BR each remove one red and one blue. In either case the remaining urn has three red and two blue objects, so the third-red conditional is 3 / 5 . Total conditional probability over the two histories is a weighted average of two identical rates, hence still 3 / 5 regardless of their weights. One may discard the history order only after establishing this equality of remaining compositions. A different condition, such as at least one red, would retain histories with different compositions.

questions.text: Question 22. A mixture of remaining urns Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Draw three times without replacement from four red and three blue objects. Given at least one red in the first two draws, what is the probability the third is red? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The conditioning event has mass 1 - ( 3 / 7 ) ( 2 / 6 ) = 6 / 7 . The joint target can be calculated by subtracting the excluded history from the third-red marginal. By exchangeability the third-red marginal is 4 / 7 . The excluded blue-blue-red path has mass ( 3 / 7 ) ( 2 / 6 ) ( 4 / 5 ) = 4 / 35 . Thus the joint mass is 16 / 35 , and the conditional is ( 16 / 35 ) / ( 6 / 7 ) = 8 / 15 . Assuming exactly one red has been removed would give 3 / 5 and overlook the retained RR history.

questions.title: Question 23. A conditional arrangement erases p
questions.text: Question 23. A conditional arrangement erases p Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Eight independent trials have common success probability p ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) . Given exactly three successes, find the probability that positions one and two are both successes. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Every three-success pattern has the same original mass p 3 ( 1 - p ) 5 , so the conditional patterns are uniform among ( 8 3 ) = 56 possibilities. Fixing successes at positions one and two leaves one success to place in six positions. The ratio is 6 / 56 = 3 / 28 . Equivalently use ( 3 / 8 ) ( 2 / 7 ) . The separate conditional marginals are each 3 / 8 , whose product 9 / 64 is different; fixing the total introduced dependence. The restriction on p ensures the conditioning count has positive probability.

questions.title: Question 24. A conditional streak count
questions.text: Question 24. A conditional streak count Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Adapted counting structure: CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.24(a); changed trial and success counts Six independent trials share p ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) . Given exactly three successes, what is the probability they contain a run of three consecutive successes? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Conditioning makes the ( 6 3 ) = 20 three-success strings equally likely. With exactly three successes, a run of three uses all successes, so its start can be one, two, three, or four. These four patterns are distinct and no pattern contains two different length-three runs. The answer is 4 / 20 = 1 / 5 . Counting starts by multiplication without checking overlap would fail when more successes were allowed. Here the fixed count makes the events disjoint and makes the answer independent of p .

questions.title: Question 25. Birthday-type chain with nonuniform labels
questions.text: Question 25. Birthday-type chain with nonuniform labels Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original nonuniform analogue of CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.10 Three independent label draws take values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1 / 2 , 1 / 3 , 1 / 6 . Find the probability that all three labels differ. Read the complete derivation and reasoning All labels differ precisely when the ordered triple is a permutation of 123. There are six disjoint permutations. Each has mass ( 1 / 2 ) ( 1 / 3 ) ( 1 / 6 ) = 1 / 36 , so the answer is 1 / 6 . The usual uniform birthday product would be invalid because the labels are not equiprobable. An alternative chain must condition on which labels have already appeared, not only their count: remaining probability mass depends on their identities. Direct disjoint enumeration avoids an unjustified reduction of the state.

questions.text: Question 26. Random eligibility with unequal stages Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Five objects independently have entry probability 2 / 3 , and conditional success probability 3 / 4 given entry. Find the probability that exactly two objects succeed overall. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each complete object history contributes success with probability ( 2 / 3 ) ( 3 / 4 ) = 1 / 2 by the multiplication rule. The independent-history premise makes these five composite indicators mutually independent. A specified two-success pattern therefore has probability ( 1 / 2 ) 5 , and ten choices of success positions give 10 / 32 = 5 / 16 . Replacing the eligible count by 10 / 3 would not even define the original integer-count experiment. Independence of entry and later success within an object was not required; the latter probability was already conditioned on entry.

The source proportion increases from 1 / 4 to 2 / 5 after success because the type-one success likelihood is larger.

questions.text: Question 29. A countably infinite mixture Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem P ( N = n ) = ( 1 - r ) r n for n ≥ 0 , with 0 < r < 1 . Conditional on N , N independent checks all pass with per-check probability q ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) . Given that all pass, find the probability that N is positive. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The all-pass probability is the convergent sum ∑ n ≥ 0 ( 1 - r ) ( r q ) n = ( 1 - r ) / ( 1 - r q ) . The distinction between all-pass and at least one pass matters: the latter would exclude the zero-count case from the information itself.

questions.text: Question 30. Determine whether overlapping cases double-count Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Events B and C cover the whole space but overlap with positive probability. Is P ( A ∣ B ) P ( B ) + P ( A ∣ C ) P ( C ) necessarily P ( A ) ? Derive the correction. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The displayed sum equals P ( A ∩ B ) + P ( A ∩ C ) . Since the union of B and C covers the space, inclusion-exclusion makes this P ( A ) + P ( A ∩ B ∩ C ) . Subtract the overlap mass to obtain the correct result. Thus covering is insufficient for the simple total-probability sum; the cases also need to be disjoint in probability, or their target overlap must vanish. For A equal to the whole space, the overcount is exactly P ( B ∩ C ) .

Simpson reversal in exact fractions Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem A has success rates 9 / 10 , 2 / 5 in easy and hard cases; B has rates 4 / 5 , 3 / 10 . A receives easy cases with weight 1 / 10 and B with weight 9 / 10 . Calculate the aggregate rates and prove that common weights would prevent this reversal. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Weighted addition gives A rate ( 1 / 10 ) ( 9 / 10 ) + ( 9 / 10 ) ( 2 / 5 ) = 9 / 20 . B rate ( 9 / 10 ) ( 4 / 5 ) + ( 1 / 10 ) ( 3 / 10 ) = 3 / 4 . A is better within both strata but worse in the aggregate. With a common easy weight w , subtracting the aggregate rates gives w ( 1 / 10 ) + ( 1 - w ) ( 1 / 10 ) = 1 / 10 > 0 . More generally a common convex combination preserves each within-stratum inequality. Different weights, not a failure of probability laws, produced the reversal.

questions.text: Question 32. Disjoint does not normally mean independent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Two disjoint events have probabilities a and b . questions.title: Question 33. Nested independent events
questions.text: Question 33. Nested independent events Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem A ⊆ B , P ( A ) = a , and P ( B ) = b . Characterize independence. Does the answer change if containment holds only almost surely? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The intersection has mass a . Independence requires a = a b , or a ( 1 - b ) = 0 , giving a = 0 or b = 1 . The same mass identity holds if the set difference A ∖ B has probability zero, so almost-sure containment gives the same characterization. For a nonnull A and a B with probability strictly below one, nesting forces dependence. If B is certain, observing it adds no probability information and independence holds for every A .

Complement closure without conditional division Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Adapted proof extension: CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.16 Prove that independence of A and B implies independence of A c and B c , including zero and one marginal probabilities. questions.title: Question 35. An event independent of itself
questions.text: Question 35. An event independent of itself Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Find every possible probability of an event A independent of itself. Then explain how a nonempty event can satisfy the zero case. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The intersection of A with itself is A , so independence requires P ( A ) = P ( A ) 2 . Factoring gives P ( A ) ( 1 - P ( A ) ) = 0 , hence probability zero or one. A nonempty null set, such as an individual point under a uniform continuous law, satisfies the zero case. The event need not be empty as a set. This result concerns probability factorization, not logical independence; an event perfectly determines its own truth even when its indicator is almost surely constant.

Pairwise independent, not mutually independent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Adapted counterexample structure: CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.18 Two independent fair bits define A = { X = 1 } , B = { Y = 1 } , and C = { X ≠ Y } . Triple factorization is not sufficient Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Constructed counterexample for CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.15 On eight equal atoms, let A = B = { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } and C = { 1 , 5 } . Check the full triple product and a failed pair condition. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The marginal probabilities are 1 / 2 , 1 / 2 , 1 / 4 . The triple intersection is just atom one and has mass 1 / 8 , equal to the product of all three marginals. Yet AB has mass 1 / 2 , while the product of its marginals is 1 / 4 . questions.title: Question 38. Counting independence constraints
questions.text: Question 38. Counting independence constraints Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem For five events, how many nontrivial product equalities are required by mutual independence, and how many are checked by pairwise independence alone? Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are 2 5 - 1 = 31 nonempty subsets. The five singleton equalities state a probability equals itself and impose no new condition. Thus mutual independence involves 31 - 5 = 26 nontrivial equations. Pairwise independence checks only ( 5 2 ) = 10 equations; the other sixteen involve three or more events. Counting constraints does not prove they are logically independent equations, but it precisely describes what the definition requires one to verify or derive.

Exactly one heterogeneous success Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Three mutually independent events have probabilities 1 / 2 , 1 / 3 , 1 / 4 . questions.title: Question 40. Pairwise information cannot fix an all-failure rate
questions.text: Question 40. Pairwise information cannot fix an all-failure rate Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Compare three independent fair bits with the triple X , Y , X ⊕ Y generated by two fair bits. In both models the three success events are pairwise independent with probability one half. What are their all-failure probabilities? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Three independent fair bits give eight equal states and all failure has mass 1 / 8 . The two-bit parity construction gives four equal triples: 000, 011, 101, 110. Every coordinate is fair and every pair is independent, but all failure is one of four states and has mass 1 / 4 . Thus the pairwise data do not determine the joint complement event. The product of three failure probabilities requires mutual independence, including subfamilies beyond pairs.

questions.title: Question 41. Selection on equality creates dependence
questions.text: Question 41. Selection on equality creates dependence Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Explicit numerical example for CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.19 Independent fair bits X , Y are conditioned on equality. Compute the two success marginals, their conditional joint probability, and the factorization error. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The retained states 00 and 11 each have conditional mass 1 / 2 . Hence both success marginals are 1 / 2 and their conditional joint is 1 / 2 . The product of the marginals is 1 / 4 , leaving a factorization difference of 1 / 4 . Observing equality did not change either individual success rate; it changed their relationship. Thus unchanged single-event marginals alone do not imply that their joint independence survived selection.

questions.text: Question 43. Hidden type makes independent checks dependent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Type one and type two each have prior weight one half. Given the type, two checks are independent and have rates 9 / 10 , 9 / 10 for type one and 1 / 10 , 1 / 10 for type two. Find the marginal joint and the second-check rate after first success. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Weighted joint addition gives ( 1 / 2 ) ( 9 / 10 ) 2 + ( 1 / 2 ) ( 1 / 10 ) 2 = 41 / 100 . Each unconditional success marginal is 1 / 2 . Therefore the checks are not marginally independent, since 41 / 100 ≠ 1 / 4 . Dividing the joint by the first-success marginal gives 41 / 50 . First success changes the relative type weights to 9 / 10 and 1 / 10 ; weighting the unchanged within-type second rates by these new weights yields the same result.

Conditional factorization and its ratio equivalent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independently proved equivalent formulation: CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.21 Assume P ( C ) > 0 and P ( B ∩ C ) > 0 . Prove that P ( A ∩ B ∣ C ) = P ( A ∣ C ) P ( B ∣ C ) is equivalent to P ( A ∣ B ∩ C ) = P ( A ∣ C ) . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Within the measure conditioned on C , the multiplication rule gives P ( A ∩ B ∣ C ) = P ( A ∣ B ∩ C ) P ( B ∣ C ) . The final factor is positive by the stated intersection condition. Divide by it to obtain the ratio characterization from factorization. Conversely multiply the ratio equality by this factor to recover factorization. If B has zero mass within C , factorization is automatically satisfied but the ratio conditioned on its intersection is undefined, so the positive premise is indispensable.

questions.text: Question 47. When a mixture remains independent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem In two strata with nonzero weights w and 1 - w , A and B are conditionally independent, with rates u 1 , u 2 and v 1 , v 2 . Because the two weights are positive, the difference is zero precisely when u 1 = u 2 or v 1 = v 2 . Thus at least one target rate must be constant across the two strata. This is a two-stratum result; with three or more strata, positive and negative covariance contributions can cancel even if neither list is constant.

In two strata with nonzero weights w and 1-w, A and B are conditionally independent, with rates u1,u2 and v1,v2. Give the exact criterion for marginal independence.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Expand the joint-minus-product expression. It simplifies to

w(1-w)(u1-u2)(v1-v2)

. Because the two weights are positive, the difference is zero precisely when u1=u2 or v1=v2. Thus at least one target rate must be constant across the two strata. This is a two-stratum result; with three or more strata, positive and negative covariance contributions can cancel even if neither list is constant.

questions.title: Question 48. A truthful report has two different answers
questions.text: Question 48. A truthful report has two different answers Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original protocol analogue motivated by Berkeley STAT 134 Lecture 2, PDF page 12 Two independent fair sensors are active or inactive. Compare the probability both are active given a report under two protocols: report whenever at least one is active; or choose one sensor uniformly and report if it is active. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first message has probability 3 / 4 and its joint probability with both active is 1 / 4 , yielding 1 / 3 . In the second protocol, the single-active states report with probability 1 / 2 while the both-active state reports with probability one. The message mass is ( 1 / 4 ) ( 1 / 2 ) + ( 1 / 4 ) ( 1 / 2 ) + 1 / 4 = 1 / 2 , giving answer 1 / 2 . Both protocols tell the truth, but the retained state weights differ. The reporting process must be included in the model.

questions.title: Question 49. Two-sided cards and face multiplicity
questions.text: Question 49. Two-sided cards and face multiplicity Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Fully specified adaptation: Berkeley STAT 134 Lecture 2, PDF page 11 Cards RR, RB, BB are selected uniformly and then shown on a uniformly chosen face. Given a red face, find the probability the hidden face is red. Contrast a procedure that selects uniformly among cards containing red and deliberately shows red. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first procedure has six equally likely card-face outcomes. Three show red, two of them on RR. The hidden face is therefore red with probability 2 / 3 . In the second procedure there are two equally likely card choices RR and RB, each guaranteed to show red. The hidden-red probability is 1 / 2 . Counting retained card types without their observation likelihoods produces the wrong answer for the first experiment because RR has twice as many red faces.

questions.title: Question 50. A biased informed host
questions.text: Question 50. A biased informed host Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original tie-breaking extension of CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.22 The prize is uniformly behind one of three doors and you chose door one. An informed host always reveals an unchosen empty door. When the prize is at door one, the host opens door three with probability t . Given that door three is opened, find the switching success probability and its feasible range. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The joint weights for prize at one, two, three and opening door three are t / 3 , 1 / 3 , 0 . The observation mass is ( 1 + t ) / 3 , positive for every t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] . Switching to door two succeeds with conditional probability 1 / ( 1 + t ) , ranging from one when t is zero to one half when t is one. At fair tie-breaking t equals one half, the result is two thirds. Aggregate switching before seeing a named opened door still succeeds with probability two thirds; the named-message conditional can depend on t .

questions.title: Question 51. A host who does not know the prize
questions.text: Question 51. A host who does not know the prize Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem After choosing door one, a host independently opens door two or three uniformly without inspecting the prize. Given that the opened door is empty, should switching to the remaining closed door have probability two thirds of winning? Read the complete derivation and reasoning If the prize is behind door one, the host reveals an empty door with probability one, contributing mass 1 / 3 . If the prize is behind either other door, the host reveals empty with probability one half, each contributing 1 / 6 . The empty-reveal event has mass 2 / 3 . Given it, the initial door is winning with probability ( 1 / 3 ) / ( 2 / 3 ) = 1 / 2 . Switching succeeds exactly in the two other retained cases, with total conditional probability one half. The informed always-reveal calculation answers a different protocol.

questions.title: Question 52. Shared-edge paths are dependent
questions.text: Question 52. Shared-edge paths are dependent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Three independent edges E , F , G each work with probability p . Paths EF and EG connect a system. Find the reliability and quantify the error from treating the paths as independent. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The union of path events has mass p 2 + p 2 - p 3 = 2 p 2 - p 3 , since their intersection requires all three edges. The false independent-path formula would use joint mass p 4 and give 2 p 2 - p 4 . Its excess is p 3 - p 4 = p 3 ( 1 - p ) , positive for interior p . At p one half, correct reliability is 3 / 8 and the false value is 7 / 16 . Independent components do not make paths sharing a component independent.

questions.title: Question 53. Bridge reliability by conditioning
questions.text: Question 53. Bridge reliability by conditioning Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original explicit network instance motivated by Berkeley STAT 134 Lecture 3, PDF pages 5–7; board-only derivations not used Use the five-edge bridge network described in the lesson, with all edge states independent and working probability p . Derive its reliability and evaluate at p one half. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Condition on the bridge. With it failed, the two disjoint series paths give 2 p 2 - p 4 . With it working, the network needs at least one of two source edges and at least one of two destination edges; their disjoint coordinate blocks give ( 2 p - p 2 ) 2 . Total probability weights these by 1 - p and p . At one half the case reliabilities are 7 / 16 , 9 / 16 and the average is 1 / 2 . This reduction avoids treating overlapping full-network paths as independent and passes both zero and one endpoint checks.

questions.title: Question 54. Edge-disjoint two-hop alternatives
questions.text: Question 54. Edge-disjoint two-hop alternatives Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Independently explained model: CMU Chapter 2, Section 2.4 network discussion Eight edge-disjoint two-hop paths each use two independent edges with working probability p , and all sixteen edge states are mutually independent. Derive the system reliability. Why is 8 p 2 usually wrong? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each path works with probability p 2 . Because their edge coordinate blocks are disjoint under a mutually independent primitive model, the path events are mutually independent. All paths fail with probability ( 1 - p 2 ) 8 , so system reliability is 1 - ( 1 - p 2 ) 8 . Adding path probabilities would overcount states with several working paths. The sum 8 p 2 is only a union bound and can exceed one; it is exact here only at p zero. At p one the reliability must be one rather than eight.

questions.title: Question 55. Conditional independence is not supplied by equal rates
questions.text: Question 55. Conditional independence is not supplied by equal rates Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Two bits have joint masses P ( 00 ) = P ( 11 ) = 3 / 8 and P ( 01 ) = P ( 10 ) = 1 / 8 . Each bit is fair. Find the chance the second is one given the first is one and quantify the departure from independence. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first-one mass is 1 / 2 , and the both-one mass is 3 / 8 . The conditional is therefore 3 / 4 , not the marginal one half. Product independence would require the both-one mass to be 1 / 4 , whereas its excess is 1 / 8 . Fairness describes each marginal separately and places no requirement on the joint arrangement. A valid joint-table calculation, rather than equal rates or symmetry of labels, settles the independence question.

questions.title: Question 56. Conditional geometry on a triangle
questions.text: Question 56. Conditional geometry on a triangle Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For a uniform point on the unit square, find P ( X ≤ 1 / 2 ∣ X + Y ≤ 1 ) and explain why a one-dimensional length ratio is invalid. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The condition is a triangle of area one half. Its portion with X at most one half has area ∫ 0 1 / 2 ( 1 - x ) d x = 3 / 8 . Dividing the areas gives 3 / 4 . The horizontal projection has length one, but the vertical cross-section decreases with x , so equal horizontal lengths do not represent equal conditional masses. The conditioned density is uniform over area in the triangle, not uniform over its horizontal projection.

questions.text: Question 57. An exact observation requires a density model Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original smooth-density example motivated by Oxford Part B Applied Probability, Section 2.2 The joint density is two on 0 < x < y < 1 and zero elsewhere. For 0 < y < 1 , find the conditional density of X given Y=y , and P ( X ≤ y / 3 ∣ Y = y ) . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Integrate the joint density over x to obtain marginal density f Y ( y ) = 2 y . The conditional density version is 2 / ( 2 y ) = 1 / y on 0 < x < y and zero outside. It integrates to one. Integrating from zero to y/3 gives probability one third. This uses a density ratio at a point with positive marginal density; it does not divide by the event probability P ( Y = y ) , which is zero. Boundary values require a stated version rather than this interior division.

questions.text: Question 58. A shrinking strip calculation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For the preceding triangular density, fix 0 < y < 1 and 0 < ε < 1 - y . Calculate P ( X ≤ y / 2 ∣ y ≤ Y ≤ y + ε ) and its limit as the strip shrinks. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The strip mass is ∫ y y + ε 2 u d u = 2 y ε + ε 2 . The target rectangle inside it has width y/2 and height epsilon, entirely inside the triangle; its mass is y ε . Their ratio simplifies to y / ( 2 y + ε ) and tends to one half. Each finite strip has positive mass, so its ratio is defined. The limit supplies the natural continuous conditional version in this regular model; the zero-mass line itself never becomes a valid elementary denominator.

questions.title: Question 59. How little does pairwise data identify?
questions.text: Question 59. How little does pairwise data identify? Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Three fair events are pairwise independent. Let t be their triple-intersection probability. Determine every feasible t and construct the full eight-cell table. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The 111 cell is t . Each two-success-only cell is 1 / 4 - t because each pair intersection is one quarter. Each one-success-only cell is t after subtracting those cells from its one-half marginal. Normalization leaves the 000 cell 1 / 4 - t . All eight cells are nonnegative exactly when 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 / 4 . They sum to one and recover every specified pair, so this interval is sharp. Mutual independence selects t = 1 / 8 , but the pairwise premises alone allow the entire interval.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning The cells in row-column order are b u , ( 1 - b ) v , b ( 1 - u ) , ( 1 - b ) ( 1 - v ) . The calculation links an algebraic matrix criterion to the statement that knowing B leaves the A rate unchanged.

questions.title: Question 1. A conditional probability with random family size
questions.text: Question 1. A conditional probability with random family size Authentic examination · checked English translation Phd CS 1404 · Q69 · PDF page 15 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. The probability that a family has n children is 2 - n - 1 for n ≥ 0 . Independently, each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl. Given that the family has no boys, what is the probability it has at least one child? 1. 1/3 2. 1/2 3. 3/4 4. 1/4 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. Let G mean no boys. Conditional on n children its probability is 2 - n , including value one for n = 0 . The total probability of G is ∑ n ≥ 0 2 - n - 1 2 - n = 1 2 ∑ n ≥ 0 4 - n = 2 / 3 . 3. The joint probability of G and at least one child is 2 / 3 - 1 / 2 = 1 / 6 . Divide by P ( G ) = 2 / 3 to obtain 1 / 4 , option 4. 4. The reverse conditional, no boys given at least one child, would be 1 / 3 , option 1. That tempting distractor demonstrates why the conditioning direction must be preserved in translation. Transfer rule. Name the conditioning event, include the zero-size case where appropriate, and divide the joint event by that event's probability.

The total probability of G is ∑ n ≥ 0 2 - n - 1 2 - n = 1 2 ∑ n ≥ 0 4 - n = 2 / 3 . 3. The joint probability of G and at least one child is 2 / 3 - 1 / 2 = 1 / 6 . Divide by P ( G ) = 2 / 3 to obtain 1 / 4 , option 4. 4. The reverse conditional, no boys given at least one child, would be 1 / 3 , option 1. That tempting distractor demonstrates why the conditioning direction must be preserved in translation. Transfer rule. Name the conditioning event, include the zero-size case where appropriate, and divide the joint event by that event's probability.

1/4

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Correct option: 4.

  1. Let G mean no boys. Conditional on n children its probability is 2-n, including value one for n=0.
  2. The total probability of G is
∑n≥02-n-12-n=12∑n≥04-n=2/3

. 3. The joint probability of G and at least one child is 2/3-1/2=1/6. Divide by P(G)=2/3 to obtain 1/4, option 4. 4. questions.title: Question 3. Three competing sources
questions.text: Question 3. Three competing sources Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Original problem Three mutually exclusive sources have priors ( 1 / 2 , 1 / 3 , 1 / 6 ) . An alert has conditional probabilities ( 1 / 10 , 1 / 5 , 3 / 5 ) . Find the evidence rate, complete posterior, and most likely source. Read the complete derivation and reasoning First multiply each prior by its own likelihood. The joint alert masses are ( 1 / 20 , 1 / 15 , 1 / 10 ) = ( 3 , 4 , 6 ) / 60 . Because the sources form a partition, their sum 13 / 60 is the evidence probability. Divide every mass by this same denominator to obtain ( 3 / 13 , 4 / 13 , 6 / 13 ) . The third source is most probable after the alert, although its prior was smallest. Check that the posterior components sum to one. An unweighted average of the likelihoods would ignore unequal source frequencies; choosing the largest prior would ignore the observation.
