questions.title: Question 47. A tiny pivot under declared rounding
questions.text: Question 47. A tiny pivot under declared rounding Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Course-derived task: Stanford CME108/MATH114, Permuted LU, rounding example Solve 10 - 4 x + y = 1 , x + y = 2 exactly. Then show unpivoted elimination with rounding to three significant decimal digits after every scalar operation can fail. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Exactly, subtracting the equations gives x = 10000 / 9999 , then y = 9998 / 9999 . Without pivoting the multiplier is 10000 . The lower coefficient 1 - 10000 = - 9999 rounds to - 10000 , and the lower load 2 - 10000 = - 9998 also rounds to - 10000 . Their quotient gives y ^ = 1 , and back substitution gives x ^ = 0 . Swapping equations first makes the multiplier 10 - 4 . The lower coefficient 0.9999 and load 0.9998 both round to one, so y ^ = 1 and x ^ = 1 . The exact and rounded models are different; the pivoted rounded answer is near the exact solution, whereas the unpivoted answer is not.

Small residual does not imply small forward error Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For A = [ 1 1 1 1 + ε ] , b = ( 2 , 2 + ε ) T , compare the exact solution with x ^ = ( 2 , 0 ) T , where ε > 0 is small. questions.title: Question 49. Pivoting is a stability strategy, not a rank theorem
questions.text: Question 49. Pivoting is a stability strategy, not a rank theorem Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Does choosing the largest available coefficient pivot prove that every numerical rank decision is exact or that every computed solution is accurate? Give precise limits. Read the complete derivation and reasoning No. In exact arithmetic a nonzero available pivot permits elimination and an all-zero available column must be skipped. In floating-point arithmetic, comparisons use perturbed values and a tolerance depends on scaling and the problem. Partial pivoting bounds multiplier magnitudes by one in ordinary real/complex arithmetic, but trailing growth and conditioning still affect accuracy. Near-singular input may have a tiny true pivot whose status cannot be inferred from a universal fixed threshold. Verify residuals, inspect scale and conditioning, and distinguish exact algebraic classification from a numerical estimate. The chapter laboratory deliberately uses exact rational arithmetic rather than claiming numerical rank certification.

questions.text: Question 50. Magnitude of multipliers under partial pivoting Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Prove | l i k | ≤ 1 after partial pivot selection, and explain why this does not bound every entry of U by the largest original entry. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The selected pivot has magnitude at least that of every entry below it in the current column. Hence | a i k / a k k | ≤ 1 whenever the pivot is nonzero. However an updated entry is a i j - l i k a k j , whose magnitude can be as large as the sum of the two current magnitudes. Repeated stages can cause growth. The multiplier bound controls one source of error amplification, not all intermediate entries. It also requires the maximum to be taken from the current transformed column, not from the original input.

questions.title: Question 51. Binary-field elimination changes the arithmetic
questions.text: Question 51. Binary-field elimination changes the arithmetic Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Over F 2 , solve x + y = 1 , y + z = 0 , x + z = 1 . Compare with the same equations over the reals. Read the complete derivation and reasoning In the binary field, subtraction equals addition. Add the first two rows to the third: its left side and right side become zero. Set z = t ∈ { 0 , 1 } ; then y = t and x = 1 + t . There are two solutions, ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) and ( 0 , 1 , 1 ) . Over the reals, the first two equations give y = - z and x = 1 + z , and the third requires 1 + 2 z = 1 , so z = 0 and the unique solution is ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) . Rank and compatibility depend on the field; division by two is legal over the reals and impossible in F 2 .

questions.text: Question 52. A parameter family over a finite field Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Over F 5 , solve x + 2 y = 1 and 2 x + 4 y = 2 . List all solutions. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The second row is twice the first and reduces to zero. For every y = t ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } , x = 1 - 2 t modulo five. The solutions are ( 1 , 0 ) , ( 4 , 1 ) , ( 2 , 2 ) , ( 0 , 3 ) and ( 3 , 4 ) . A single free field coordinate gives five solutions, not infinitely many. The exact rational laboratory does not operate modulo five; this task uses explicitly declared finite-field arithmetic. Modulo five, every nonzero coefficient has an inverse; for instance two has inverse three. This field property permits the same reversible division logic as ordinary elimination.

questions.title: Question 54. An invariant for a correct in-place implementation
questions.text: Question 54. An invariant for a correct in-place implementation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Explain why an elimination implementation must save the old multiplier before overwriting its pivot-column entry with zero. Give a failing two by two example. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For [ A ∣ b ] = [ 2 1 3 4 3 7 ] , the multiplier is two. The correct lower row is ( 0 , 1 , 1 ) . If code first overwrites a 21 = 0 and then recomputes a 21 / a 11 , it uses zero and leaves the trailing entries ( 3 , 7 ) unchanged. The corrupted row gives y = 7 / 3 rather than one. Store the factor, use the unchanged pivot row for every trailing update, and only then assign the known zero. The invariant is equality to a reversible row transform of the original augmented matrix.

questions.title: Question 55. A linear dependence among equations is a load test
questions.text: Question 55. A linear dependence among equations is a load test Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Rows satisfy r 3 = 2 r 1 - r 2 . What condition on loads is necessary for consistency, and is it sufficient if the first two rows are independent? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Any solution must satisfy b 3 = 2 b 1 - b 2 by the same linear combination. If the first two coefficient rows are independent, the map defined by those two rows has full row rank and can realize any pair of real loads; solving those two equations yields at least one vector. The compatibility equality then makes the third equation automatic, so it is sufficient. If the first two rows themselves are dependent, additional compatibility conditions may exist. Every dependence in the coefficient rows must have the corresponding dependence in the load vector.

questions.title: Question 56. A linear constraint after elimination
questions.text: Question 56. A linear constraint after elimination Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem The general solution is x = ( 1 , 0 , 2 ) T + s ( 1 , 1 , 0 ) T + t ( 0 , 1 , - 1 ) T . Add the conditions x 1 - x 2 = 0 and x 2 + x 3 = 4 and solve. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first condition gives 1 + s - ( s + t ) = 0 , so t = 1 . The second gives ( s + t ) + ( 2 - t ) = 4 , so s = 2 . Hence x = ( 3 , 3 , 1 ) T . The original affine parametrization is retained and the additional constraints become a smaller linear system in free parameters. Substitution checks both new equations. This method avoids re-eliminating all original equations and makes independence of the extra restrictions explicit. The two new conditions act independently on the two parameter coordinates. Their unique parameter solution proves that no second point in the original affine plane meets both.

questions.title: Question 57. Row space is preserved; column space generally moves
questions.text: Question 57. Row space is preserved; column space generally moves Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For A = [ 1 0 1 0 ] , apply R 2 ← R 2 - R 1 . Compare row spaces, column spaces and kernels. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The new matrix is R = [ 1 0 0 0 ] . Both row spaces are the span of ( 1 , 0 ) , and both kernels are the span of ( 0 , 1 ) T . But the original column space is the span of ( 1 , 1 ) T , while the new column space is the span of ( 1 , 0 ) T . The invertible left transformation maps the column space to a different subspace of the same dimension. questions.title: Question 59. No equations and no variables are distinct boundaries
questions.text: Question 59. No equations and no variables are distinct boundaries Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Classify a system with zero equations and n real unknowns. Then classify one with m equations and zero unknowns. Read the complete derivation and reasoning With no equations, every vector in ℝ n satisfies the empty conjunction, so the solution set is all of that space. With no unknowns, the only possible variable vector is the empty vector; every equation reads 0 = b i . There is one solution if every load is zero and none otherwise. When both counts are zero, there is exactly one empty vector. These mathematical boundaries need not be accepted by a practical input interface, but they prevent mistaken claims that zero pivots always mean infinitely many solutions.

Nonnegative real solutions in an affine family Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Find all nonnegative real solutions of x + y + z = 4 , x - y = 0 , and the extreme points of their solution set. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The second equation gives x = y = t . The first gives z = 4 - 2 t . Nonnegativity is exactly 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 . Therefore the feasible set is the line segment joining ( 0 , 0 , 4 ) and ( 2 , 2 , 0 ) . Row reduction alone gives an entire affine line with unrestricted real t ; the inequalities cut it to a bounded segment. The endpoints, not all points on the affine line, are its extreme points.

questions.text: Question 64. Block elimination with a matrix pivot Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Let A = [ B C D E ] with square invertible B . Substitute into the lower equation to obtain ( E - D B - 1 C ) y = g - D B - 1 f . Once this subsystem is solved, recover x from the upper formula. The order of matrix factors is fixed by dimensions and cannot be commuted. In computation, solve systems with B to obtain the needed products instead of explicitly forming its inverse. questions.title: Question 65. A lower-triangular inverse by a finite series
questions.text: Question 65. A lower-triangular inverse by a finite series Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For L = [ 1 0 0 2 1 0 - 1 3 1 ] , compute its inverse and distinguish it from negating all subdiagonal entries. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Write L = I + N , where N is strictly lower triangular and N 3 = 0 . Thus L - 1 = I - N + N 2 . Here N 2 has only entry ( 3 , 1 ) = 6 , so L - 1 = [ 1 0 0 - 2 1 0 7 - 3 1 ] . Negating the subdiagonal alone would give entry ( 3 , 1 ) = 1 instead of seven and fail multiplication. The cross term records the indirect path through row two. Direct multiplication in both orders gives the identity. The third-row first-column product is - 1 - 6 + 7 = 0 . This checks the entry most likely to be missed when the indirect lower-triangular cross term is omitted.

questions.title: Question 66. A Gauss transform has a simple inverse for a reason
questions.text: Question 66. A Gauss transform has a simple inverse for a reason Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Course-derived proof task: Stanford CME108/MATH114, LU, Gauss-transform prompt Let G = I - g e k T with g i = 0 for every i ≤ k . Prove G - 1 = I + g e k T and identify the assumption that makes this true. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Because e k T g = g k = 0 , the rank-one matrix N = g e k T satisfies N 2 = g ( e k T g ) e k T = 0 . Therefore ( I - N ) ( I + N ) = I - N 2 = I in both orders. The inverse formula depends on the zero kth coordinate, not merely on the rank-one appearance. If g k ≠ 0 , the square is generally nonzero and this inverse expression fails. The elimination multipliers lie strictly below the pivot position, precisely supplying the required condition. The nonzero entries of an elimination multiplier vector occur strictly below the pivot, so the zero kth coordinate follows from its construction rather than an extra numerical coincidence.

questions.title: Question 67. Why multiple contradictions add only one augmented rank
questions.text: Question 67. Why multiple contradictions add only one augmented rank Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem An eliminated single-load system has several coefficient-zero rows with nonzero right sides. Can the augmented rank exceed the coefficient rank by more than one? Read the complete derivation and reasoning No. Appending one column can increase rank by at most one. All coefficient-zero augmented rows have the form ( 0 , … , 0 , c i ) and are scalar multiples of the same last-coordinate row when their entries are nonzero. They expose inconsistency but add only one independent augmented direction. In full augmented RREF, there is one right-side pivot row, not several independent right-side pivots. For a matrix of several right sides, rank can increase by more than one because several columns are appended.

questions.title: Question 68. Same kernel need not mean the same nonhomogeneous solutions
questions.text: Question 68. Same kernel need not mean the same nonhomogeneous solutions Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Let A = [ 1 0 ] and C = [ 2 0 ] . Compare the systems A x = 1 and C x = 1 , and their homogeneous kernels. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Both kernels are the y -axis because each homogeneous equation requires only x 1 = 0 . But the first nonhomogeneous solution set is x 1 = 1 , while the second is x 1 = 1 / 2 . Row-equivalent coefficient matrices preserve the kernel, but preserving a nonhomogeneous solution set requires transforming the right side too. Scaling the first equation by two should produce C x = 2 , not C x = 1 . The homogeneous kernel records allowable differences between solutions. It does not specify the affine offset required by a particular nonzero load.

questions.title: Question 69. A complete elimination certificate for an asserted solution family
questions.text: Question 69. A complete elimination certificate for an asserted solution family Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem A proposed family for x + y + z = 2 , 2 x - y + z = 1 is ( 1 , 1 , 0 ) + t ( 1 , 1 , - 2 ) . Accept or reject it and repair the result. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The proposed particular point satisfies both equations. The proposed direction satisfies the first homogeneous equation but gives 2 ( 1 ) - 1 - 2 = - 1 in the second, so it is not a null direction. Subtract the first equation from the second to get x - 2 y = - 1 , hence x = 2 y - 1 and z = 3 - 3 y . Taking y = 1 + t gives the correct family ( 1 , 1 , 0 ) + t ( 2 , 1 , - 3 ) . Checking the particular point alone would miss the defect; every spanning direction must satisfy every homogeneous equation.

Question 69. A complete elimination certificate for an asserted solution family

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard

Original problem

A proposed family for x+y+z=2, 2x-y+z=1 is (1,1,0)+t(1,1,-2). Accept or reject it and repair the result.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The proposed particular point satisfies both equations. The proposed direction satisfies the first homogeneous equation but gives 2(1)-1-2=-1 in the second, so it is not a null direction. Subtract the first equation from the second to get x-2y=-1, hence x=2y-1 and z=3-3y. Taking y=1+t gives the correct family (1,1,0)+t(2,1,-3). Checking the particular point alone would miss the defect; every spanning direction must satisfy every homogeneous equation.

questions.title: Question 70. Minimum-length member of an affine line
questions.text: Question 70. Minimum-length member of an affine line Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem The solutions are x = ( 1 , 2 ) T + t ( 1 , - 1 ) T . Find the unique solution of minimum Euclidean norm using the parametrization. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The squared norm is ( 1 + t ) 2 + ( 2 - t ) 2 = 5 - 2 t + 2 t 2 . Completing the square gives 2 ( t - 1 / 2 ) 2 + 9 / 2 , whose minimum occurs at t = 1 / 2 . Thus x = ( 3 / 2 , 3 / 2 ) T . Its inner product with the null direction is zero, which is the geometric optimality condition. This extension selects one representative but does not change the full solution set of the original equations; minimum norm is an additional criterion, not a claim that free variables must be zero.

questions.title: Question 71. Deterministic pivot search versus maximum-magnitude search
questions.text: Question 71. Deterministic pivot search versus maximum-magnitude search Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem In exact rational arithmetic, must one select the largest available pivot to obtain the correct RREF? Discuss work and the canonical result. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Any nonzero available pivot is algebraically valid because its row scaling and row additions are reversible. Different selections can produce different intermediate fractions and different REF matrices, but the RREF is canonical. A largest-magnitude rule is primarily a floating-point stability strategy; in exact arithmetic one may prefer a pivot reducing fraction growth. The correctness conditions are that a chosen pivot is nonzero, that its column is cleared correctly, that the full augmented row is transformed, and that skipped columns contain no eligible pivot. There is no magnitude order intrinsic to an arbitrary field.

questions.title: Question 1. Explicit rank-theorem revisit: Dimension with simultaneous constraints
questions.text: Question 1. Explicit rank-theorem revisit: Dimension with simultaneous constraints Authentic examination · checked English translation MS CS 1405 · Q41 · PDF page 9 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. Let W be the real vector space of symmetric 4 × 4 matrices with trace zero. What is dim W ? 1. 10 2. 9 3. 8 4. 7 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. A symmetric matrix is determined by four diagonal entries and six entries above the diagonal, giving ten free coordinates before the trace condition. The trace equation is one nonzero homogeneous linear constraint. It permits the fourth diagonal entry to be determined by the first three. Three diagonal degrees of freedom and six off-diagonal degrees of freedom remain, giving nine. A basis consists of six symmetric off-diagonal pair matrices and three diagonal matrices E i i - E 44 for i = 1 , 2 , 3 . Ten ignores trace; eight and seven subtract additional constraints that are not independent requirements of this space. Transfer rule. Count independent parameters, then subtract the rank of the imposed linear constraints, not the number of times a constraint is written.

questions.title: Question 2. Explicit rank-theorem revisit: A lower norm bound does not imply positivity
questions.text: Question 2. Explicit rank-theorem revisit: A lower norm bound does not imply positivity Authentic examination · checked English translation Phd CS 1404 · Q30 · PDF page 8 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. A real square matrix A satisfies ‖ A x ‖ ≥ θ ‖ x ‖ for every real x , with θ > 0 . Which assertion is false? 1. ‖ A - 1 ‖ ≤ θ - 1 for the induced norm. 2. A is positive definite. 3. A is nonsingular. 4. If λ is an eigenvalue of A , then | λ | ≥ θ . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. If A x = 0 , the inequality forces x = 0 . A square matrix with trivial kernel is invertible. Put x = A - 1 y : ‖ A - 1 y ‖ ≤ ‖ y ‖ / θ . Taking the supremum gives the inverse norm bound. For the Euclidean norm, the real inequality extends to complex vectors by applying its squared form to real and imaginary parts. For an eigenvector, ‖ A x ‖ = | λ | ‖ x ‖ , giving the eigenvalue modulus bound. Positivity does not follow: A = - I satisfies the norm bound with θ = 1 , but x T A x = - ‖ x ‖ 2 < 0 for nonzero x . Thus option 2 is false. Model note. The source uses the standard matrix/vector norm convention; the eigenvalue discussion above explicitly uses the Euclidean induced norm. Norm preservation of magnitude says nothing about the sign of a quadratic form.

questions.html:
Question 2. Explicit rank-theorem revisit: A lower norm bound does not imply positivity

Authentic examination · checked English translation

Phd CS 1404 · Q30 · PDF page 8. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

A real square matrix A satisfies ‖Ax‖≥θ‖x‖ for every real x, with θ>0. Which assertion is false?

1.

‖A-1‖≤θ-1 for the induced norm.

2.

A is positive definite.

3.

A is nonsingular.

4.

If λ is an eigenvalue of A, then |λ|≥θ.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Correct option: 2.

  1. If Ax=0, the inequality forces x=0. A square matrix with trivial kernel is invertible.
  2. Put x=A-1y: ‖A-1y‖≤‖y‖/θ. Taking the supremum gives the inverse norm bound.
  3. For the Euclidean norm, the real inequality extends to complex vectors by applying its squared form to real and imaginary parts. For an eigenvector, ‖Ax‖=|λ|‖x‖, giving the eigenvalue modulus bound.
  4. Positivity does not follow: A=-I satisfies the norm bound with θ=1, but xTAx=-‖x‖2<0 for nonzero x. Thus option 2 is false.

Model note. The source uses the standard matrix/vector norm convention; the eigenvalue discussion above explicitly uses the Euclidean induced norm. Norm preservation of magnitude says nothing about the sign of a quadratic form.

questions.text: Question 3. Original columns versus transformed columns Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Find bases of all four fundamental spaces for A = [ 1 2 1 2 4 0 0 0 1 ] State their ambient spaces, dimensions, and the complete conditions for an arbitrary load to be attainable. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Row 2 minus (2) times row 1. [ 1 2 1 0 0 - 2 0 0 1 ] Skip coefficient column 2: no available pivot. [ 1 2 1 0 0 - 2 0 0 1 ] Divide row 2 by -2. [ 1 2 1 0 0 1 0 0 1 ] Row 1 minus (1) times row 2. [ 1 2 0 0 0 1 0 0 1 ] Row 3 minus (1) times row 2. [ 1 2 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 ] Coefficient reduction complete. [ 1 2 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 ] There are 2 pivots at one-based columns 1, 3. Column space. Use those columns of the ORIGINAL matrix. The columns of this matrix form its basis: C = [ 1 1 2 0 0 1 ] . Row space. The nonzero reduced rows form its basis. They are the rows of R * = [ 1 2 0 0 0 1 ] . Kernel. Solve the pivot equations with one unit free coordinate at a time. The resulting basis is the column list of N = [ - 2 1 0 ] . Left kernel. Reduce the transpose by the same procedure. Its basis is the column list of Y = [ - 1 1 2 1 ] . The four dimensions are 2, 2, 1, 1, respectively. Each null vector is annihilated by its matrix; independent free-coordinate patterns and the rank–nullity counts prove completeness. For any load b , compatibility is exactly the vanishing of its dot product with every listed left-kernel vector. The second original column is twice the first. The independent third column is not replaced by its transformed standard vector when answering a column-space question.

questions.title: Question 15. The rank–nullity proof cannot skip independence
questions.text: Question 15. The rank–nullity proof cannot skip independence Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Let a kernel basis of a linear map from an n -dimensional space be extended by v 1 , … , v r to a domain basis. Prove that the images of the added vectors form an image basis. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Every input has a unique expansion in the full basis. Its kernel part maps to zero, so every output is a combination of the A v i . For independence, suppose ∑ c i A v i = 0 . Then ∑ c i v i lies in the kernel and is a combination of the original kernel basis. Move that combination to the left: independence of the DOMAIN basis forces every c i and every kernel coefficient to vanish. Hence the images are independent and spanning. Their number is r = n - dim ker A , proving the theorem. Counting a spanning list without this independence step would not establish rank.

questions.title: Question 16. Which claimed rank values are possible?
questions.text: Question 16. Which claimed rank values are possible? Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem A real 5 × 8 matrix has a four-dimensional kernel. Find its rank and left nullity; decide whether every load is attainable. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Apply rank–nullity in the input space: r + 4 = 8 , so r = 4 . Apply it separately to the transpose: left nullity is 5 - 4 = 1 . The image is a four-dimensional proper subspace of ℝ 5 , so not every load is attained. Four kernel dimensions do not imply four compatibility conditions: input ambiguity and output restrictions live in different ambient spaces.

Explain without constructing a matrix. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Nullity three would give rank 7 - 3 = 4 . But rank cannot exceed the number of rows, which is three. Therefore no such matrix exists. Equivalently every map from seven input coordinates to three outputs must lose at least four independent directions. The argument is valid over any field.

questions.title: Question 18. One load versus every load
questions.text: Question 18. One load versus every load Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem A 6 × 4 matrix gives a unique solution for one compatible load. Does this establish injectivity, surjectivity, or both? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Any nonzero kernel vector could be added to that solution and produce a second solution for the SAME load. Uniqueness therefore forces the kernel to be zero, so rank is four and the map is injective. Surjectivity onto F 6 is impossible because the image dimension is at most four. Thus uniqueness for one compatible load proves uniqueness for all compatible loads, but never existence for all six-component loads.

questions.title: Question 19. When a fiber is a subspace
questions.text: Question 19. When a fiber is a subspace Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Prove that a nonempty solution set of A x = b is a linear subspace precisely when b = 0 . Read the complete derivation and reasoning If the set is a linear subspace it contains zero, so substituting zero gives b = A 0 = 0 . Conversely, for b = 0 the set is the kernel, which is closed under linear combinations. When b ≠ 0 and a solution exists, it is the affine set x p + ker A , whose direction space is a subspace but whose translated points do not generally close under addition.

Two parallel fibers Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For A = ( 1 , 1 ) , describe the fibers for loads three and five and their intersection. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The kernel is span ( 1 , - 1 ) T . The first fiber is ( 3 , 0 ) T + t ( 1 , - 1 ) T and the second is ( 5 , 0 ) T + s ( 1 , - 1 ) T . A point in both would have coordinate sum both three and five, a contradiction. The fibers are disjoint affine lines with identical direction space. Neither coordinate is individually ignored: the map preserves their sum and loses their difference.

questions.title: Question 21. Finite-field counting
questions.text: Question 21. Finite-field counting Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem A compatible system over a field of nine elements has six unknowns and rank four. How many solutions exist? Contrast the real case. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are two free field coordinates, each with nine independently available values. Every assignment determines all pivot coordinates uniquely, so the count is 9 2 = 81 . Over ℝ the same pivot structure gives an affine plane with infinitely many points. The rank–nullity theorem is unchanged; only the cardinality of the field changes the number of assignments.

A left-kernel compatibility certificate Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem The rows of A satisfy row three equal to row one plus twice row two. Rank is two. Give a necessary and sufficient condition on a three-component load. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The vector y = ( - 1 , - 2 , 1 ) T satisfies y T A = 0 . Left nullity is 3 - 2 = 1 , so this nonzero vector spans the left kernel. Compatibility is therefore precisely - b 1 - 2 b 2 + b 3 = 0 . Necessity follows by combining the original equations. Sufficiency follows because this is every independent left-kernel condition. Without the stated rank two, one relation alone would not establish sufficiency.

questions.title: Question 23. One appended column can increase rank only once
questions.text: Question 23. One appended column can increase rank only once Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Prove the possible rank differences between A and [ A ∣ b ] and interpret both outcomes. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Appending b changes the column span from U to U + span ( b ) . If b ∈ U , no basis vector is added and the difference is zero. If b ∉ U , append it to a basis of U to obtain an independent spanning list with exactly one additional member. The difference is then one. Each of the two columns of any correction must lie in that kernel, so every right inverse is R 0 + v ( s , t ) with arbitrary real s , t . Conversely each such correction is annihilated. questions.title: Question 30. One-sided inverse of a square matrix
questions.text: Question 30. One-sided inverse of a square matrix Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Let square A , B satisfy A B = I . Prove B A = I without determinant multiplication. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The relation A B = I makes A onto: every y equals A ( B y ) . In finite equal dimensions, rank–nullity forces A to be injective and invertible. Multiply A B = I on the left by A - 1 to get B = A - 1 . Then B A = I . The finite-dimensional square hypothesis is the essential link between onto and one-to-one; it cannot be omitted.

questions.title: Question 31. An infinite-dimensional counterexample
questions.text: Question 31. An infinite-dimensional counterexample Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem On all real sequences, let S prepend zero and D delete the first coordinate. Compute both compositions. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For any sequence x , prepending zero and then deleting the first entry recovers x , so D S = I . Deleting first and then prepending zero gives ( 0 , x 2 , x 3 , … ) , which differs from x when x 1 ≠ 0 . Thus S D ≠ I . The first-coordinate sequence is a nonzero kernel vector of D , while D is onto. This explicitly locates the failure of finite-dimensional rank–nullity arguments.

questions.text: Question 35. Row operations change column-space position Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For A = ( 1 , 0 ) T swap its two rows. Which of rank, kernel and column space is preserved? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The new matrix is ( 0 , 1 ) T . Both have rank one and trivial kernel in the one-dimensional input space. Their column spaces are distinct coordinate axes in the two-dimensional output space. The row swap acts as an invertible output-coordinate map, so dimensions and input dependencies are preserved while the image position moves. Therefore row equivalence is not equality of column spaces.

Sharp sum bounds with complete cancellation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For matrices of the same shape derive a lower bound on the rank of their sum and show that cancellation can attain zero. Rearranging gives the first difference bound; exchanging A , B gives the opposite difference. Combine them to obtain the absolute rank difference. If B = - A , the sum vanishes while both original ranks can be arbitrarily large within the shape bounds. Individual nonzero ranks do not prevent cancellation.

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard

Original problem

Construct two maps with disjoint nonzero images but whose sum rank is smaller than their rank sum.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Let both maps have one-dimensional input and two-dimensional output: A=(1,0)T, B=(0,1)T. Their images are different coordinate axes with intersection zero. Each has rank one, but the sum has a single nonzero column (1,1)T and rank one. A shared scalar controls both outputs; independent image directions do not provide independent input degrees of freedom. This explains the missing hypothesis in the tempting rank-additivity assertion.

Recover an intersection dimension Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Column basis matrices C , D each have rank three, while [ C D ] has rank five. questions.title: Question 43. Stacking versus concatenating
questions.text: Question 43. Stacking versus concatenating Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem If A , B both have three input columns, interpret the kernel of their vertical stack. If both have three output rows, interpret the column space of their horizontal concatenation. Read the complete derivation and reasoning A stacked equation requires both A x = 0 and B x = 0 for the same input, so its kernel is the intersection of the two kernels. A horizontal concatenation maps independent inputs x , y to A x + B y , so its image is the sum of the two images. These are different constructions. Use the input dimension minus the stack rank for the first intersection, and the dimension formula with the concatenation rank for the second.

questions.title: Question 45. Frobenius with numbers
questions.text: Question 45. Frobenius with numbers Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Compatible matrices have rank B = 5 , rank ( A B ) = 4 and rank ( B C ) = 3 . Bound the rank of A B C . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Frobenius gives rank ( A B C ) ≥ 4 + 3 - 5 = 2 . The product upper bound gives at most three, because the image of B C has dimension three. Thus only two or three are possible. The intermediate loss from applying A to the full image of B is one; its restriction to the image of B C can lose at most that one direction. The argument explains why merely multiplying three ranks is meaningless.

questions.title: Question 46. A two-parameter rank stratification
questions.text: Question 46. A two-parameter rank stratification Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Find the rank of A ( s , t ) = [ 1 1 1 1 1 + s 1 1 1 1 + t ] for every real pair. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Subtract row one from rows two and three to obtain rows ( 0 , s , 0 ) and ( 0 , 0 , t ) . The first row is always independent of any nonzero later row because its first entry is one. Rank is therefore 1 plus the number of nonzero members of s , t : three when both are nonzero, two when exactly one is nonzero, and one when both vanish. This uses branch-safe row subtraction and no illegal parameter division.

Exceptional load compatibility Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For the preceding matrix family with s = 0 and t ≠ 0 , give all compatible loads and all inputs. questions.title: Question 49. A vanished determinant does not establish rank one
questions.text: Question 49. A vanished determinant does not establish rank one Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem At t = 0 , the matrix diag ( 1 , 1 , t ) has determinant zero. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first two columns are distinct standard vectors, so they are independent and give rank at least two. The third column is zero and gives rank at most two. Hence rank is exactly two. Determinant zero proves only rank less than three. The upper-left two-by-two minor is nonzero and supplies the missing lower-bound evidence.

questions.title: Question 51. Constant off-diagonal rank family
questions.text: Question 51. Constant off-diagonal rank family Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Find all ranks of a real 4 × 4 matrix with diagonal d and all off-diagonal entries c . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Write M = ( d - c ) I + c J . On the one-dimensional all-ones line the action is multiplication by d + 3 c ; on the three-dimensional zero-sum space it is multiplication by d - c . If both scalars are nonzero, rank is four. If only the first is nonzero, rank is one. If only the second is nonzero, rank is three. If both vanish, subtracting the two equations yields 4 c = 0 , so c = d = 0 over the reals and rank is zero. Rank two is impossible.

questions.title: Question 53. Complex transpose is not a positive Gram construction
questions.text: Question 53. Complex transpose is not a positive Gram construction Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Let C = ( 1 , i ) T . Compare the ranks of C , C T C and C * C . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The column is nonzero, so rank is one. Plain transpose gives C T C = 1 + i 2 = 0 , a zero scalar of rank zero. Conjugate transpose gives C * C = 1 + ( - i ) i = 2 , rank one. This refutes the plain-transpose Gram rank identity over complex scalars while confirming the Hermitian version. An argument using a sum of squares must use absolute squares in the complex case.

questions.title: Question 55. A Schur complement computation
questions.text: Question 55. A Schur complement computation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Find the rank of [ 2 1 3 0 1 1 2 2 t ] for every real t . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Use the top-left block P = [ 2 1 0 1 ] , which is invertible. Solving P z = ( 3 , 1 ) T gives z = ( 1 , 1 ) T . The bottom-left row is ( 2 , 2 ) , so its product with z is four. The Schur complement is t - 4 . Reversible block elimination gives rank two plus the rank of this scalar: three if t ≠ 4 , two if t = 4 . The block inversion is legal for every parameter because P is fixed and invertible.

questions.title: Question 60. Rank can increase by only one under an outer-product update
questions.text: Question 60. Rank can increase by only one under an outer-product update Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Let A be any rectangular matrix and let u and v have compatible coordinate lengths. questions.title: Question 61. An oblique projection
questions.text: Question 61. An oblique projection Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For P = [ 1 2 0 0 ] find its image, kernel and rank, and decide whether its decomposition is orthogonal. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Multiplication gives P 2 = P . The image is the first coordinate line and the kernel is spanned by ( - 2 , 1 ) T . These lines intersect only at zero, so they give a direct decomposition of ℝ 2 . Rank and trace are both one. Their spanning vectors have dot product minus two, not zero, so the decomposition is not orthogonal. Idempotence alone does not imply a symmetric orthogonal projection.

questions.title: Question 62. Why projection rank equals trace over the reals
questions.text: Question 62. Why projection rank equals trace over the reals Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Prove rank–trace equality for a real idempotent matrix without assuming an orthonormal eigenbasis. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For each x , write x = P x + ( x - P x ) . The first term is in the image; applying P to the second gives zero. A vector in both spaces satisfies P y = y and P y = 0 , so it is zero. Choose any basis of each and combine them. In that basis the matrix is diag ( I r , 0 ) , with trace r and rank r . Trace is unchanged by a basis change because tr ( X Y ) = tr ( Y X ) follows by exchanging the two finite entry sums.

questions.title: Question 63. Kernel stabilization controls every later power
questions.text: Question 63. Kernel stabilization controls every later power Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Prove that if ker A k = ker A k + 1 , then all later kernels are the same. Read the complete derivation and reasoning If A k + 2 x = 0 , then A x ∈ ker A k + 1 = ker A k , giving A k + 1 x = 0 and hence x ∈ ker A k . The reverse containment follows by applying an extra power. Thus the next two kernels also coincide. Repeating this argument proves stabilization for every later power. Equal consecutive ranks imply equal kernels because the kernels are nested and their dimensions are equal by rank–nullity.

Ranks of powers of a nilpotent chain Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem On five standard basis vectors let A e 1 = 0 and A e j = e j - 1 for j = 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 . Find ranks and nullities of powers one through five. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Applying the map k times sends e j to e j - k when j > k and to zero otherwise. The image is spanned by the first 5 - k standard vectors for 1 ≤ k ≤ 5 . These are independent, so ranks are four, three, two, one and zero. Kernels are spanned by the first k input basis vectors, giving nullities one through five. The paired dimensions always sum to five.

questions.title: Question 65. A rank bound from an annihilating power
questions.text: Question 65. A rank bound from an annihilating power Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem If A 3 = 0 on an n -dimensional space, prove rank A ≤ ⌊ 2 n / 3 ⌋ . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Sylvester applied to A 2 gives rank A 2 ≥ 2 r - n . Applying it to A A 2 = 0 gives 0 ≥ r + rank A 2 - n . Combining yields 0 ≥ 3 r - 2 n , so r ≤ 2 n / 3 and integrality gives the floor. This bound does not require a Jordan form; it follows directly from two composition inequalities with the same intermediate dimension.

questions.title: Question 67. Two independent matrix constraints
questions.text: Question 67. Two independent matrix constraints Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem On symmetric real 4 × 4 matrices impose trace zero and entry a 12 = 0 . Find the dimension and justify independence. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The trace functional uses diagonal coordinates; the second uses one off-diagonal coordinate. questions.text: Question 68. Symmetric matrices with every row sum zero Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Find the dimension of symmetric real n × n matrices whose row sums vanish. The row-sum map sends diagonal matrices to arbitrary row-sum vectors, so it is onto and has rank n . Rank–nullity leaves n ( n + 1 ) / 2 - n = n ( n - 1 ) / 2 dimensions. Off-diagonal entries can be chosen freely and each diagonal entry is then the negative sum of the other entries in its row. Symmetry adds no extra row-sum redundancy.

questions.text: Question 71. Differentiation on a finite polynomial space Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For D : p ↦ p ′ from degree-at-most-four polynomials to degree-at-most-three polynomials over the reals, find rank and kernel. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Constants are exactly the polynomials with zero derivative, so the kernel is the one-dimensional span of one. Every degree-at-most-three polynomial has an antiderivative of degree at most four, so the map is onto a four-dimensional codomain and has rank four. The monomial images are zero, one, 2 x , 3 x 2 , 4 x 3 . Their nonzero members span the codomain. In positive characteristic some of these integer coefficients may vanish, so the real-field assumption matters.

Constraints encoded by a graph incidence matrix Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For a connected graph on n vertices, orient each edge and let its incidence column be one standard vector minus another. Along a path from the root to any other vertex, add signed incidence columns; intermediate coordinates cancel and give that vertex unit vector minus the root unit vector. Connectivity provides these n - 1 independent vectors, which span the zero-sum subspace. Hence rank is n - 1 . The left kernel consists of constant vertex vectors.

questions.title: Question 75. Equality of kernels and row spaces
questions.text: Question 75. Equality of kernels and row spaces Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem For real matrices with the same number of columns, prove that equal kernels imply equal row spaces. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Their row spaces are respectively the orthogonal complements of their kernels. Equal kernels therefore give equal orthogonal complements and equal row spaces. Conversely equal row spaces give equal kernels by the same relation. The matrices may have different numbers of rows, so they need not be related by an invertible square row transformation of a common size. The statement concerns the spaces of restrictions, not the literal arrays.

questions.title: Question 76. A useful equal-rank composition criterion
questions.text: Question 76. A useful equal-rank composition criterion Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem If rank ( A B ) = rank B , prove that A is injective on the image of B . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The exact composition formula subtracts the dimension of Col B ∩ ker A from the rank of B . Equal ranks force that intersection to have dimension zero. Thus the restriction of A to the image of B has trivial kernel and is injective. It may still have a nontrivial kernel elsewhere in the intermediate space. The criterion is a restricted injectivity statement, not global invertibility.

questions.title: Question 77. A lower-rank product equality condition
questions.text: Question 77. A lower-rank product equality condition Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem Assume the Sylvester lower expression rank A + rank B - n is nonnegative. Characterize equality for A B . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The restriction formula gives rank of A B as rank of B minus the dimension of the intersection of its image with the kernel of A . Equality with the stated lower expression requires that intersection dimension equal n - rank A , the full kernel dimension. Since the intersection is contained in the kernel, equal finite dimensions mean the entire kernel is contained in the image of B . Conversely that containment supplies equality. If the formal bound is negative, equality with the sharp bound zero is a different condition.

questions.title: Question 79. Ranks of complementary projections
questions.text: Question 79. Ranks of complementary projections Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem If P 2 = P over the reals, prove rank P + rank ( I - P ) = n . Explain the image of the complementary projection and state whether symmetry is required. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The image of I - P is exactly the kernel of P : applying P to ( I - P ) x gives zero, and any kernel vector z equals ( I - P ) z . Its dimension is therefore n - rank P by rank–nullity. This gives the desired sum. No symmetry assumption is needed because the direct decomposition is algebraic; orthogonality is an additional condition.

questions.title: Question 81. A constrained rank factorization cannot exceed its bottleneck
questions.text: Question 81. A constrained rank factorization cannot exceed its bottleneck Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original problem If A = U V W with respective shapes 8 × 3 , 3 × 2 and 2 × 7 , give the best dimension-only rank bound. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Every image of the product passes through the two-dimensional intermediate space after the right factor, so rank is at most two. The left intermediate dimension three gives only a weaker bound. To attain two, choose W onto the two-dimensional space, V injective from two to three coordinates, and U injective on that image. Thus two is both an upper bound and attainable. The bound does not assert that arbitrary such factors attain it.

questions.title: Question 82. A shifted span fails the zero test
questions.text: Question 82. A shifted span fails the zero test Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived: CMU 21-241, Day 9 pp. 1–2 Compare the line t ( 1 , 2 ) T with t ( 1 , 2 ) T + ( 1 , 1 ) T . Which is a subspace? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first is a span and is closed under every linear combination. In the second, obtaining zero would require t = - 1 from the first coordinate and t = - 1 / 2 from the second, which is impossible. It is therefore an affine line, not a subspace. Both have one-dimensional direction space, but only the first can be a kernel or image of a linear map.

questions.title: Question 83. A nonlinear sign constraint is not a null space
questions.text: Question 83. A nonlinear sign constraint is not a null space Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived: CMU 21-241, Day 9 p . 2 Is { ( x , y ) : x y ≥ 0 } a real subspace? Explain with a closure counterexample. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The vectors ( 1 , 0 ) and ( 0 , - 1 ) each satisfy the condition because their products are zero. Their sum ( 1 , - 1 ) has product minus one and violates the condition. Closure under addition fails even though zero belongs and multiplying an individual vector by a scalar preserves the product sign. Consequently this set cannot be the kernel of any real linear map.

questions.title: Question 85. Membership in a full row space
questions.text: Question 85. Membership in a full row space Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Course-derived: CMU 21-241, Days 9–10, row-space prompt Is ( 1 , 1 ) in the row space of [ 3 4 1 2 ] ? Find explicit row coefficients. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Solve 3 s + t = 1 and 4 s + 2 t = 1 . Subtract twice the first equation from the second to get - 2 s = - 1 , so s = 1 / 2 and t = - 1 / 2 . Thus half the first row minus half the second is ( 1 , 1 ) . Both rows are independent because these coefficient equations have nonzero determinant, so they span all of ℝ 2 . Membership can be certified by the explicit combination rather than inferred from a sketch.

A polynomial basis statement needs its ambient space Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Course-derived: CMU 21-241, Day 24 p . 2 For x 2 - x + 1 , x + 10 , and 3 , decide whether the list is a basis of P 2 and of P 3 , where subscripts denote maximum degree. questions.title: Question 88. Extend two polynomial vectors to a basis
questions.text: Question 88. Extend two polynomial vectors to a basis Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Course-derived: CMU 21-241, Day 24 p . 2 Extend 1 + x and 1 - x to a basis of real P 2 . Read the complete derivation and reasoning A zero combination gives constant coefficient a + b = 0 and linear coefficient a - b = 0 , forcing a = b = 0 . They are independent and span all degree-at-most-one polynomials because half their sum is one and half their difference is x . Add x 2 , which is outside that span. Coefficient comparison now proves independence of all three, and the standard monomials are in their span. Thus the enlarged list is a basis. In characteristic two the original pair coincides and this extension argument changes.

questions.title: Question 90. Oxford row-space membership with a linear certificate
questions.text: Question 90. Oxford row-space membership with a linear certificate Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Course-derived: Oxford M1, Example 121, printed pp. 42–43 For rows ( 1 , 2 , - 1 , 0 ) , ( 2 , 1 , 0 , 3 ) and ( 0 , 1 , 1 , 1 ) , determine when x = ( x 1 , x 2 , x 3 , x 4 ) lies in their span. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Exact reduction gives row basis ( 1 , 0 , 0 , 8 / 5 ) , ( 0 , 1 , 0 , - 1 / 5 ) and ( 0 , 0 , 1 , 6 / 5 ) . Thus a combination with first three coordinates x 1 , x 2 , x 3 has fourth coordinate ( 8 x 1 - x 2 + 6 x 3 ) / 5 . Membership is exactly 8 x 1 + 6 x 3 = x 2 + 5 x 4 . This condition is sufficient as well as necessary because the three pivot coordinates freely determine the combination. It is the single left-annihilator restriction on this three-dimensional row space in four coordinates.

Copy every other element of an N -element array a , starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0) . Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure. 1. Start destination at i , decrease source n by two, increase destination i by one, and stop when n<0 . 2. questions.title: Question 2. A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation
questions.text: Question 2. A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation Authentic bridge revisit · checked English adaptation Phd CE 1405 · Q9 · PDF page 3 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. For an array of distinct values, SplitSort chooses its median m , recursively processes R = { x : x > m } and L = { x : x < m } , and returns concatenate(SplitSort(R), [m], SplitSort(L)) ; arrays of length at most one are returned unchanged. What is the output order? 1. Descending up to the median, then ascending. 2. Approximately random. 3. Ascending. 4. Descending. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. The base cases of zero or one value are descending. Assume recursive outputs are descending. Every value in the first block is greater than m , and every value in the final block is less than m . Concatenating the descending greater block, m , and the descending smaller block therefore produces a descending whole array. Strong induction establishes the claim for every length. Median selection controls balance, not ascending direction. Option 1 misreads one recursive block; option 2 ignores determinism; option 3 would require left–median–right concatenation. Transfer rule. Prove a recursion's semantic invariant separately from its running-time recurrence.\ n \ n Call boundary interpretation. The returned greater and smaller blocks must be kept with the appropriate median continuation; reversing their concatenation changes semantics even though the calls have the same types. For an array of distinct values, SplitSort chooses its median m, recursively processes R={x:x>m} and L={x:x<m}, and returns concatenate(SplitSort(R), [m], SplitSort(L)); arrays of length at most one are returned unchanged. What is the output order?

1.

Descending up to the median, then ascending.

2.

Approximately random.

3.

Ascending.

4.

Descending.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

Correct option: 4.

  1. The base cases of zero or one value are descending.
  2. Assume recursive outputs are descending. Every value in the first block is greater than m, and every value in the final block is less than m.
  3. Concatenating the descending greater block, m, and the descending smaller block therefore produces a descending whole array. Strong induction establishes the claim for every length.
  4. Median selection controls balance, not ascending direction. Option 1 misreads one recursive block; option 2 ignores determinism; option 3 would require left–median–right concatenation.

questions.text: Question 3. Two copies and one returned result Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For mathematical integers, f(x)=3x -2 and g(y)=2y+5 . A caller with a=4 computes b=g ( f(a) ) but never assigns to a . Find a , b and derive the general returned map. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first invocation binds its local x to 4 and returns 10. The second binds its local y to 10 and returns 25. Neither parameter is the caller object a , so the final caller pair is (4,25). Substitution gives g ( f ( u ) ) = 2 ( 3 u - 2 ) + 5 = 6 u + 1 . This relation specifies b , not a mutation of a . The reversed composition gives f ( g ( u ) ) = 6 u + 13 , which shows that exchanging the order is not harmless. A finite C implementation additionally requires every intermediate to fit its type.

questions.title: Question 4. An output inequality through two helpers
questions.text: Question 4. An output inequality through two helpers Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Let f(x)=2x+1 and g(y)=3y -4 over integers. Find all x for which g ( f(x) ) is between 17 and 41 inclusive. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Substitute the first postcondition into the second: g ( f ( x ) ) = 6 x - 1 . The double inequality becomes 18 ≤ 6 x ≤ 42 , hence 3 ≤ x ≤ 7 . Both endpoints are allowed and yield 17 and 41. The integer solutions are 3,4,5,6,7. Using f ( g ( x ) ) would instead yield 6 x - 7 , which is a different interface order. Check C range restrictions separately rather than treating mathematical integers as a machine type.

questions.title: Question 5. Repeated returned assignment
questions.text: Question 5. Repeated returned assignment Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem T(x)=2x+3 . Starting at x=1 , assign x=T(x) five times. Derive a formula for k assignments. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Write x k + 1 = 2 x k + 3 and add 3 to both sides: x k + 1 + 3 = 2 ( x k + 3 ) . Therefore x k + 3 = 2 k ( x 0 + 3 ) , so x k = 4 · 2 k - 3 . The values after five assignments are 5,13,29,61,125. A repeated call with discarded return would leave the caller at 1 instead. The shifted-variable derivation handles every nonnegative k and exposes the required intermediate representability.

questions.title: Question 6. A shrinking returned recurrence
questions.text: Question 6. A shrinking returned recurrence Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For nonnegative integers, h(x)=x/2 using integer division. Starting with x=83 , repeatedly assign x=h(x) until x=0 . Count calls and list results. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The successive values are 41,20,10,5,2,1,0, so seven calls are executed. For positive input n , after k assignments the value is ⌊ n / 2 k ⌋ ; this follows by induction using nested floor division by positive two. The first zero is reached at k = ⌊ log 2 n ⌋ + 1 . With input zero the loop makes no calls, so that boundary must be stated separately. This is a sequential loop of calls, not seven simultaneously active helper frames.

questions.title: Question 7. Inverse composition with a negative coefficient
questions.text: Question 7. Inverse composition with a negative coefficient Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Let f(x)= - 2x+7 and g(x)=3x -1. Solve f ( g(x) ) = 9 over integers. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Composition gives - 2 ( 3 x - 1 ) + 7 = - 6 x + 9 . Equating this to 9 gives x=0 . At that input g returns -1 and f returns 9. The reversed composition is - 6 x + 20 , which would not solve the same equation. A negative coefficient reverses an inequality if the problem is changed from equality; it does not reverse equality. The result belongs to the caller only if it is assigned or otherwise used.

questions.title: Question 8. A helper called inside a summation
questions.text: Question 8. A helper called inside a summation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A pure helper f(k)=2k+1 is called once for each k from 0 through n -1. Derive the sum of returned values and the call count. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are exactly n invocations, including zero when n=0 . The returned sum is ∑ k = 0 n - 1 ( 2 k + 1 ) = 2 n ( n - 1 ) / 2 + n = n 2 . The sum formula follows from pairing the arithmetic progression or induction: adding the next odd number changes n 2 into ( n + 1 ) 2 . A persistent counter inside the helper would require a different specification. Calls are sequential, so their cumulative count does not measure simultaneous depth.

questions.title: Question 9. Nested calls and live depth
questions.text: Question 9. Nested calls and live depth Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Let inc( x ) =x+1 and twice( x ) =2x . Evaluate twice(inc(twice(3))) and count total helper calls and maximum helper depth. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The innermost twice receives 3 and returns 6. inc receives 6 and returns 7. The outer twice receives 7 and returns 14. Three helper invocations occur, but argument evaluation completes before the outer callee body begins. Thus these helper bodies are not three simultaneously active frames; maximum active helper depth is one, excluding the enclosing caller. Syntactic parenthesis nesting is not the same as nested active bodies. This differs from a helper body that itself invokes another helper.

questions.title: Question 10. A genuinely nested helper body
questions.text: Question 10. A genuinely nested helper body Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem f(x) computes y=g(x) , then returns y+g(y) , where g(x)=2x+1 . Evaluate f(3) , total calls, and peak helper depth. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first g frame receives 3 and returns 7. It ends before the second g frame begins with argument 7 and returns 15. f then returns 22. The call tree contains f and two g invocations, three in total. While either g is active, f is paused and remains active, giving peak helper depth two. The general result is ( 2 x + 1 ) + ( 4 x + 3 ) = 6 x + 4 . Treating both g calls as simultaneously active overcounts memory.

questions.title: Question 11. The exact common domain of a composite
questions.text: Question 11. The exact common domain of a composite Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For mathematical reals, f(x)=1 /( x -2) and g(y)=1 /( y+1 ). Find the domain and formula of g ( f(x) ). Read the complete derivation and reasoning The inner call requires x ! = 2. The outer denominator requires 1 / ( x - 2 ) + 1 ≠ 0 , which excludes x=1 . On the remaining domain, combining fractions yields ( x - 2 ) / ( x - 1 ) . The simplified expression is defined at x=2 , but the original composition is not: simplification cannot remove an inner-call precondition. Therefore the domain is all reals except 1 and 2. This is an original interface-domain problem, not a C integer-division trace.

questions.title: Question 12. A function that counts but does not accumulate caller changes
questions.text: Question 12. A function that counts but does not accumulate caller changes Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A void C helper changes its parameter using x += 4. The caller passes the same a=7 in a loop of 13 iterations. What is final a and how many local assignments occur? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each invocation initializes a fresh parameter object with 7, changes that object to 11, and ends without writing any caller object. Final a is still 7. There are thirteen local assignments, but they affect thirteen different invocation objects. Summing the local increments to obtain caller value 59 confuses accumulated work with persistent storage. A pointer version or assignment of a returned result would change the state transition and must be analyzed separately.

questions.title: Question 14. A machine-safe affine contract
questions.text: Question 14. A machine-safe affine contract Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Using C17 int, f(x)=2 * x+1 . Derive a safety precondition rather than assuming every int input is valid. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Check operations in their actual order. First 2 x must lie in [INT_MIN,INT_MAX]; then 2 x+1 must also lie there. Together require INT\_MIN ≤ 2 x and 2 x ≤ INT\_MAX - 1 . Thus integer x lies from ⌈ INT\_MIN / 2 ⌉ through ⌊ ( INT\_MAX - 1 ) / 2 ⌋ . These are mathematical floor/ceiling operations, not blindly substituted C negative division. For the explicitly stated 32-bit range, this is [-1073741824,1073741823]. The lower endpoint doubles exactly to INT_MIN, then safely adds one.

questions.title: Question 15. Lexical scope defeats caller shadowing
questions.text: Question 15. Lexical scope defeats caller shadowing Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard MIT 6.0001 Lecture 4 scope family; original C adaptation int x = 12; int f(void) { return x + 1; } int g(void) { int x = 4; return f() + x; } Find g (). Read the complete derivation and reasoning f is defined at file scope, where its x denotes the file-scope object containing 12. g has a distinct local x containing 4, but that local declaration is not visible in f . Therefore f returns 13 and g returns 17. The two objects remain 12 and 4 during the calculation. Searching the active caller frame would implement dynamic scope, which C does not use. This task adapts the environment distinction in MIT Lecture 4 with new constants.

questions.text: Question 16. An inner block changes only its own object Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem int x = 5; int result; { int x = 2; x += 3; result = x; } x += result; Find final x and result. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The inner declaration creates a new x=2 , then changes it to 5. result belongs to the enclosing scope and receives 5. Exiting the block ends the inner automatic object, while the outer x is still 5. The last statement adds result, yielding outer x=10 . Identical spelling does not make the two x declarations one object. The stored result survives because its object is outside the inner block.

questions.title: Question 17. Self-initialization is not an outer copy
questions.text: Question 17. Self-initialization is not an outer copy Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem int x = 8; { int x = x; /* then use x */ } Does the inner object reliably become 8? Read the complete derivation and reasoning No. The inner identifier is in scope before its initializer expression is evaluated. The initializer therefore reads the newly declared automatic object before it has an initialized value. The fragment cannot be assigned the guaranteed numeric answer 8. The outer initialized object still exists but is hidden by the declaration. To preserve it, copy it to another named initialized object before declaring the inner x , or use different identifiers. This is a declaration-point question, not a question about random stack leftovers.

questions.title: Question 18. Two functions have separate static objects
questions.text: Question 18. Two functions have separate static objects Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem int f(void) { static int s; return ++s; } int g(void) { static int s; s += 2; return s; } Calls in separate statements are f (), g (), f (), g (). Find returns. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The two static declarations denote different objects because they are distinct declarations in distinct function bodies. Both are initially zero. f returns 1, g returns 2, f returns 2, and g returns 4. Static persistence operates within each identity; equal names do not merge them. A single shared file-scope counter would produce another sequence. The separate-statement condition removes any argument-evaluation ordering ambiguity.

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard

Original examination-style problem

int f(void) { static int s; return ++s; }
int g(void) { static int s; s += 2; return s; }

Calls in separate statements are f(),g(),f(),g(). Find returns.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The two static declarations denote different objects because they are distinct declarations in distinct function bodies. Both are initially zero. f returns 1, g returns 2, f returns 2, and g returns 4. Static persistence operates within each identity; equal names do not merge them. A single shared file-scope counter would produce another sequence. The separate-statement condition removes any argument-evaluation ordering ambiguity.

questions.title: Question 19. Automatic reset versus static persistence
questions.text: Question 19. Automatic reset versus static persistence Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Cambridge Programming in C , Lecture 2 static-storage family; original mixed trace int f(int d) { int a = 1; static int s = 1; a += d; s += a; return s; } Call f(2) , f(3) , f(-1) in separate statements. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The automatic a starts at 1 each time, so its values are 3,4,0. Static s begins at 1 once and becomes 4,8,8, which are the three returned values. Negative d in the last call does not reset s ; it adds zero through the freshly initialized a . The caller argument objects are copies and are not modified. This problem extends Cambridge Lecture 2 static storage with a mixed local/static trace.

questions.title: Question 20. Recursive locals and one shared static
questions.text: Question 20. Recursive locals and one shared static Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem int f(int n) { static int s = 0; if (n == 0) return s; ++s; int t = f(n - 1); return t + n; } Start with a fresh program and call f(3) . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Descent increases the one shared s to 1,2,3. The n=0 frame returns 3. Ascent then adds 1,2,3, giving returned values 4,6,9. Each n and t is a separate automatic object, while s is one object. Final shared s is 3 and the result is 9. A second f(3) would start from s=3 and return 12. The additive formula after c prior increments is c + 3 + 3 · 4 / 2 , so persistent history belongs in the input state.

questions.title: Question 21. Returning a value versus returning a local address
questions.text: Question 21. Returning a value versus returning a local address Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Compare a function returning local int x=9 by value with a function returning & x . May the caller use both results? Read the complete derivation and reasoning A copied returned integer value can safely initialize a live caller object after the callee ends. The address identifies an automatic local whose lifetime ends with its invocation. Dereferencing that expired object’s address is invalid; returning an address does not extend the object’s lifetime. The cases differ in what crosses the boundary: a value versus a designation of storage. A static local or caller-owned object has different lifetime and must be stated explicitly.

questions.title: Question 22. Scope is not storage duration
questions.text: Question 22. Scope is not storage duration Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A function has static int saved = 0 inside its body. Is saved visible to unrelated functions, and is it recreated on every invocation? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Its identifier has block scope, so unrelated functions cannot access it by that name. Its object has static storage duration, so it is not recreated on each call. The name’s visibility and the object’s existence answer different questions. If the function returns a pointer to saved, a caller may access the live object through that pointer, without gaining lexical access to the identifier saved. Calling that arrangement a global name would obscure the distinction.

questions.title: Question 23. Prototype names do not create caller variables
questions.text: Question 23. Prototype names do not create caller variables Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Consider int mix(int left,int right); followed by a definition int mix(int a ,int b ){return a-b;}. Is it compatible, and are left and right available afterward? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The declarations agree on return type and the two parameter types, so different parameter names do not create an incompatibility. Prototype parameter names have prototype scope and are not variables available to the caller after the declaration. The definition creates a and b for each invocation. Renaming these bound names consistently does not change the function’s behavior. Compatibility concerns the types, not matching identifier spellings.

questions.title: Question 24. File static versus block static
questions.text: Question 24. File static versus block static Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Explain the different meanings of static in a file-scope helper function declaration and a block-scope integer declaration. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For a file-scope function, static gives internal linkage: its declaration is not an externally linked interface shared by independently compiled units. For a block-scope object, static gives the object static storage duration while the identifier keeps block scope. Neither use means “pass parameters by reference.” A header with static helper definitions can create separate functions in different translation units; a single external definition is a different arrangement. Scope, duration, and linkage must be named separately.

questions.title: Question 25. Two independent targets: case 1
questions.text: Question 25. Two independent targets: case 1 Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem void step(int *p, int *q) { *p += 2; *q *= 3; } Call with distinct target objects initialized to 4 and 7. Derive the exact transition and explain the incorrect distinct/alias alternative. Read the complete derivation and reasoning p and q designate different live objects. The first statement changes only the p target to 6; the q target remains 7 until the second statement changes it to 21. Final target values are (6, 21). The general transition is ( u , v ) ↦ ( u + 2 , 3 v ) . Sharing pointer-value type does not make the targets aliases; object identity decides that. Both results are representable in every C17 int.

questions.title: Question 26. One aliased target: case 2
questions.text: Question 26. One aliased target: case 2 Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem void step(int *p, int *q) { *p += 2; *q *= 3; } Call with both pointers designating one integer initialized to 4. Derive the exact transition and explain the incorrect distinct/alias alternative. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first full statement changes the single target from 4 to 6. The next statement reads that same updated object and triples it to 18. There is one result object, not two independent outputs. In general the map is u ↦ 3 u + 6 ; reversing the two statements gives 3 u + 2 , differing by four. Applying the distinct-target formula would falsely read the old value through q . The pointer parameters themselves remain distinct copied pointer objects.

questions.title: Question 29. Local pointer redirection does not redirect the caller
questions.text: Question 29. Local pointer redirection does not redirect the caller Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem void choose(int *p, int *q) { p = q; *p = 9; } int a=2, b=5; int *r=&a; choose(r,&b); Find a , b and the target of r . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The parameter p initially copies r’s address of a . Assigning p=q changes only the local pointer to address b . The following write through p changes b to 9. Caller r still points to a , whose value remains 2. Final a=2 , b=9 , r= & a . Do not draw the caller pointer arrow moving when only a copied parameter was assigned. This contrast motivates the pointer-to-pointer interface.

questions.title: Question 32. Arithmetic swap is an unsafe general replacement
questions.text: Question 32. Arithmetic swap is an unsafe general replacement Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem The sequence * p= * p+ * q ; * q= * p -* q ; * p= * p -* q attempts a swap. Analyze distinct safe targets and identical targets initialized to 6. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For distinct targets u , v and representable intermediates, the states are ( u+v , v ), then ( u+v , u ), then ( v , u ), so it swaps. With one aliased object initially 6, the first write produces 12, the second computes 12- 12=0 , and the third computes 0- 0=0 . Thus it destroys the value. Even for distinct targets, u+v can overflow signed C , so the identity over mathematical integers does not make the implementation universally safe. A temporary avoids both failures.

questions.text: Question 33. The arithmetic relation 23=4 * 5+3 is valid, but the interface cannot leave both 4 and 3 in the same integer object. A contract promising * q=4 and * r=3 needs q ! =r .
