questions.title: Question 34. An output may alias the original input object
questions.text: Question 34. An output may alias the original input object Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem void qr(int n,int d,int *q,int *r) { *q=n/d; *r=n%d; } int n=23,rem; qr(n,5,&n,&rem); Are the original n overwrite and remainder calculation safe? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The argument n’s value 23 is copied into the callee parameter before the body starts. The first write changes the caller n object to 4, but the callee parameter n remains 23. The remainder expression still uses that parameter and yields 3, stored in the distinct rem object. Final caller n=4 ,rem = 3. This is permitted input/output aliasing, unlike q and r sharing one output object. Tracking identifier spelling instead of object identity would incorrectly use 4%5.

questions.title: Question 35. Sequential aliases yield an affine recurrence
questions.text: Question 35. Sequential aliases yield an affine recurrence Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem void step(int *p,int *q) { *p=2* *p+1; *q=*q+*p; } Both pointers designate one object. Derive the result after k calls from x0=2 , assuming all intermediates fit. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Inside one call the first write gives y=2x+1 . The second reads that same object twice and writes 2y=4x+2 . Thus x k + 1 = 4 x k + 2 . Iterating gives x k = 4 k x 0 + 2 ( 4 k - 1 ) / 3 , so with x0=2 the first values are 10,42,170. There is no simultaneous old-state assignment in these statements. The numerator is divisible by three because 4 k ≡ 1 ( mod 3 ) .

questions.title: Question 37. Output contract for a maximum and minimum
questions.text: Question 37. Output contract for a maximum and minimum Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Design a two-output interface for integers u , v and state whether the output pointers may alias. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Compute the two mathematical values before writing: low is the smaller input and high is the larger. questions.title: Question 38. Two next calls inside a difference
questions.text: Question 38. Two next calls inside a difference Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Use counter = 0 and next() returning ++ counter in C17. Determine all results of difference(next(),next()), where difference( a , b ) = a-b. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The two called function bodies are indeterminately sequenced, so each increment completes before the other body runs. If the left call runs first, its value is 1 and the right value is 2, giving -1. If the right runs first, the values are 2 and 1, giving 1. Final counter is 2 in both cases. The permitted result set is {-1,1}. This is unspecified order with defined alternatives, not unsequenced direct argument modifications.

questions.text: Question 41. Separate statements impose an order Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem int i=0; int a=i++; int b=i++; int r=a-b; Find a , b , i , r . Recombining the increments as function arguments would discard that guarantee.

Return conversion follows expression evaluation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem double ratio(int a,int b) { return a/b; } Find ratio(9,4), then propose a corrected fractional implementation. A missing return value Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem int f(int x) {if( x>0 )return x ;} is called as int y=f(0) ;. The special initial-main fallthrough rule does not apply to f .

questions.title: Question 45. A non-returning branch is not a numeric result
questions.text: Question 45. A non-returning branch is not a numeric result Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A helper loops forever for x<0 and returns x * x otherwise. What domain supports a total mathematical function? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Under mathematical unbounded integer arithmetic, the helper terminates exactly on nonnegative inputs, producing their squares. A total-function contract therefore restricts x>= 0. Over C17 int, further restrict x so x * x is representable. Negative inputs do not return an unspecified number; they do not normally return at all under the stated model. Termination and arithmetic safety are separate obligations.

questions.text: Question 46. Function versus repeated-evaluation macro Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Cambridge Programming in C , Lecture 2 macro family; original comparison Compare twice( i++ ) with TWICE( i++ ) for initially i=3 , using the lesson definitions. questions.text: Question 47. A macro can be defined but surprising Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem #define MAX(a,b) ((a)>(b)?(a):(b)) int i=3; int r=MAX(i++,2); Find i and r in C17. questions.title: Question 48. Default promotions versus prototype conversion

Default promotions versus prototype conversion Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Contrast a float argument passed to a declared float parameter with one passed as a trailing variadic argument. For a trailing variadic argument, default argument promotions convert float to double and apply integer promotions to narrow integer types. A variadic callee must retrieve values using a compatible promoted type. A cast of the call result does not change how the argument was passed. The ellipsis is not an arbitrary exemption from type compatibility.

questions.title: Question 49. Printing and returning are separate observations
questions.text: Question 49. Printing and returning are separate observations Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard MIT 6.0001 Lecture 4 return/print family; original trace Python f(x) prints x+1 then returns x *2. With x=4 , the caller prints f(x) . Give the output and returned value. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The inner print produces the line 5. f then returns 8, which the caller print writes as the second line. The returned value is 8, not 5. If the return were omitted, the second line would be None; printing inside the callee does not return the printed object. The two output events occur in execution order. This task adapts the return-versus-print distinction in MIT Lecture 4.

This supplies the missing modular claim in the source exercise.

Use an invariant that every integer candidate larger than the current d up to min(a,b) has already been ruled out as a common divisor, together with d>=1. This supplies the missing modular claim in the source exercise.

questions.title: Question 55. Unused arithmetic can still overflow
questions.text: Question 55. Unused arithmetic can still overflow Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A repeated-squaring power helper unconditionally squares b on its last loop iteration even when e becomes zero. questions.text: Question 56. Quotient-remainder uniqueness Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For n=47 , d=6 , find q , r satisfying n=qd+r and 0 <=r<d , then prove uniqueness generally. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Integer division gives q=7 , r=5 and 47=7 * 6+5 . If another pair q2,r2 satisfied the bounds, subtracting gives ( q - q 2 ) 6 = r 2 - r . A function contract must additionally guarantee that the two output objects retain these values after its writes.

questions.title: Question 57. Signed division needs a different remainder statement
questions.text: Question 57. Signed division needs a different remainder statement Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem In C17, find q , r for n= -23, d=5 . Is 0 <=r<d the right contract? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The quotient truncates toward zero, giving q= -4. The remainder is n -q d= - 23+20= -3. The identity n=q d+r holds, but the remainder is negative, so the nonnegative Euclidean contract fails. For nonzero r , C remainder has the numerator sign and magnitude below the denominator magnitude. To obtain Euclidean r=2 , q= -5 with positive d , adjust the negative remainder and quotient explicitly. Do not copy Python floor-division results into C .

questions.title: Question 58. A frame condition makes replacement reasoning possible
questions.text: Question 58. A frame condition makes replacement reasoning possible Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Two helpers both return x * x . One also increments a global counter. Can a caller substitute either when only the numerical postcondition is stated? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The returned relation alone does not make the helpers observationally equivalent. If the caller later reads the counter, replacing one helper by the other changes behavior. A contract intended to permit pure substitution must specify that no relevant external state is modified, alongside termination and input-range obligations. Treat the function as a transition on result and state. A name such as square is not evidence of purity.

questions.title: Question 60. Two callback applications are not one doubled argument
questions.text: Question 60. Two callback applications are not one doubled argument Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem int apply(int (*f)(int),int x) { int y=f(x); return f(y); } int step(int x) { return 3*x-2; } Find apply(step,4) and its general formula. Both calls occur in a definite order because the first result assignment is a separate full expression.

Reference and value in the same C++ interface Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Stanford CS106B reference family; original mixed-parameter problem void change(int &x,int y) { x+=y; y=0; } int a=4,b=7; change(a,b); Find final a , b . Two C++ references can designate one object Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem void change(int &x,int &y) { x+=2; y*=3; } int a=4; change(a,a); Find a . Call by name re-evaluates an expression Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Under an explicitly defined mathematical call-by-name model, parameter p denotes the caller expression i+1 . A repeated static triangular counter Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A helper adds its argument d to one static s initially zero and returns s . Call with d=1 ,..., n in separate loop iterations. Derive the sum of all returns. Read the complete derivation and reasoning After the k -th call, s equals 1 + 2 + … + k = k ( k + 1 ) / 2 . Summing the returns gives ∑ k = 1 n k ( k + 1 ) / 2 = n ( n + 1 ) ( n + 2 ) / 6 . Derive it from the formulas for sums of k and k squared, or by induction on n . At n=4 , returns 1,3,6,10 sum to 20. The helper is stateful: substituting return =d would give the wrong sum 10. C representability must hold for both counter and accumulated total.

questions.title: Question 87. Independent counters versus one shared counter
questions.text: Question 87. Independent counters versus one shared counter Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Two Python make-counter closures increment by one. One is called twice and the other once, then the first again. Find the four returns and explain storage identities. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each factory call allocates a distinct retained binding initialized to zero. Calls a(),a(), b (),a() therefore return 1,2,1,3. There are two persistent states, not one state per invocation and not one module-wide counter. The activation stack can empty between calls while both retained environments remain reachable. This is the same identity reasoning needed for separate C static declarations, despite different lifetime mechanisms.

questions.title: Question 88. A returned reference is not a lifetime cure
questions.text: Question 88. A returned reference is not a lifetime cure Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A C++ function returns int& referring to its ordinary automatic local. Does reference syntax keep the local alive? Read the complete derivation and reasoning No. The automatic local still ends its lifetime when the invocation ends. A returned reference designating that expired object cannot safely be used to read or write it. References do not own or extend the lifetime of arbitrary automatic locals. Return by value, refer to a caller-owned live object, or use a suitable longer-lived object with explicit sharing requirements. A reference-to-temporary lifetime rule is not permission to return a local this way.

questions.title: Question 89. Array parameter size does not recover array length
questions.text: Question 89. Array parameter size does not recover array length Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A C17 function is declared void f(int a[10]) ;. Does it receive a copied ten-element array, and can sizeof(a) inside reliably compute ten times sizeof(int)? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The parameter declaration is adjusted to a pointer type, so it receives a pointer value rather than a copied array. Inside, sizeof(a) is the size of that pointer object, not the caller array’s total size. The bracket 10 is not a runtime length field automatically passed with the address. Communicate length separately and preserve valid bounds. The distinction is introduced here to prevent a parameter-model mistake; detailed indexing belongs to the arrays chapter.

questions.title: Question 90. Two expressions with the same value need not be interchangeable
questions.text: Question 90. Two expressions with the same value need not be interchangeable Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A pure helper returns 7; another returns 7 but increments global s . A caller evaluates the helper twice and then tests s . Are they interchangeable? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Both calls supply the same numeric results, so an expression using only those saved integers may agree. However, with initial s=0 , the stateful helper leaves s=2 and the pure one leaves s=0 . The later test distinguishes them. Equality of returned values is only one part of observational equivalence. Require matching state effects and termination behavior, or restrict observations explicitly before replacing a function.

questions.title: Question 91. C++ reference argument alias with a copied value
questions.text: Question 91. C++ reference argument alias with a copied value Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem void f(int &a,int b) { a+=b; b+=a; } int x=3; f(x,x); Find final x and local b . Read the complete derivation and reasoning At entry the reference a denotes x and the separate parameter b copies the initial value 3. First a+=b changes x to 6. Next b+= a reads current x=6 and changes only local b from 3 to 9. Final x is 6; b is 9 before the function ends. Passing the same expression twice does not mean every parameter aliases. The declared passing mode decides which argument creates a copy.

questions.title: Question 1. Recursive reverse-stride copying
questions.text: Question 1. Recursive reverse-stride copying Authentic bridge revisit · checked English adaptation MS CS 1393 · Q167 · PDF page 34 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. Copy every other element of an N -element array a , starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0) . Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure. 1. if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1); 2. if(n<i)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1); 3. if(n<i)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+1); 4. if(n<0)return; b[i++]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+2); Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. After t calls, the intended state is n = N - 1 - 2 t and i = t . Thus the next recursive call must decrease the source index by two and increase the destination by one. Option 1 preserves this state and stops precisely when the source index becomes negative. It writes ⌈ N / 2 ⌉ elements. Option 2 leaves b[0] unwritten and stops too early through an unrelated comparison. Option 3 uses stride one. Option 4 also uses source stride one and has incompatible destination updates. The source lists pseudocode resembling C without parameter type declarations; it is not a strictly compilable C17 function. We assess its specified indexing algorithm, not missing declarations. Transfer rule. Express the intended source and destination indices as functions of recursion depth.

Authentic bridge revisit · checked English adaptation

MS CS 1393 · Q167 · PDF page 34. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Copy every other element of an N -element array a, starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0). Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure.

1.

if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

2.

if(n<i)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

3.

questions.title: Question 2. Expected running-minimum updates
questions.text: Question 2. Expected running-minimum updates Authentic bridge revisit · checked English adaptation Phd CS 1404 · Q72 · PDF page 16 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. An array contains n distinct values in a uniformly random permutation. Set min to positive infinity, scan from index 1 to n , and replace it whenever the next value is smaller. If Y counts replacements, which expression is closest to its mean for large n ? 1. 1 2. ln n 3. n 4. n ln n Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. Let I i indicate that position i contains the smallest of the first i values. Uniform permutation symmetry gives P ( I i = 1 ) = 1 / i . Linearity of expectation requires no independence between these indicators: E [ Y ] = ∑ i = 1 n 1 / i = H n . Integral bounds give ln ( n + 1 ) ≤ H n ≤ 1 + ln n , so ln n is the listed large- n approximation. The exact mean is H n , not exactly ln n . One counts only the first update; n assumes every position is a record; n ln n multiplies counts that should be summed. Transfer rule. Distinguish the number of loop tests (always n ) from the number of successful updates (random).

questions.title: Question 3. A lower bound is not the first value
questions.text: Question 3. A lower bound is not the first value Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A flat representation declares indices -3 through 8 inclusive, four-byte elements and base address 1600 for the first element. Find the address of index 5, total storage and final occupied byte. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are 8 - ( - 3 ) + 1 = 12 positions. Index 5 is eight positions after the first, regardless of the values stored. Its address is 1600 + 4 ( 5 + 3 ) = 1632 . Storage is 12 · 4 = 48 bytes, so the last occupied byte is 1647 and the one-past boundary is 1648. Using 1600+4 ·5 would silently treat the lower bound as zero. The final byte and final element start differ by three. These are numerical layout statements; the negative declaration bound is not ordinary C array syntax.

questions.title: Question 4. Invert a two-dimensional row-major address
questions.text: Question 4. Invert a two-dimensional row-major address Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A matrix has row indices 2..6 and column indices -1..5. Each element occupies eight bytes; its first element starts at 4096. Which element starts at address 4312? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The byte difference is 216, divisible by eight, so the element offset is 27. There are seven columns. Divide 27 = 3 · 7 + 6 : normalized row 3 and column 6 recover declared row 5 and column 5. Both lie in bounds. Thus the requested element is (5,5). The total extent is 35 elements, so 27 is valid. Dividing by the number of rows instead would invert a column-major representation. Address 4313 would be inside this element but not its start, so it would fail the element-start divisibility check.

questions.title: Question 5. Recover a missing column extent
questions.text: Question 5. Recover a missing column extent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem In row-major storage of four-byte elements, A[1,2] starts at 1028 and A[3,1] starts at 1064. Both dimensions start at zero. Determine the number of columns, then the base address. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Subtract the addresses to eliminate the base. The offset difference is 2 C - 1 elements, so 4 ( 2 C - 1 ) = 36 and C=5 . Substitute the first observation: 1028 = B + 4 ( 5 + 2 ) , giving B=1000 . A necessary consistency check is that columns 1 and 2 fit within five columns; at least four rows must exist because row 3 is present. The pair of observations does not determine the total row count. An answer that reports a unique complete matrix shape goes beyond the evidence.

questions.title: Question 6. Distinguish row-major from column-major numerically
questions.text: Question 6. Distinguish row-major from column-major numerically Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A 4×6 matrix begins at 800, uses two-byte elements and zero-based indices. Calculate the address of (2,3) in each layout and explain why the addresses need not differ at every index. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Row-major offset is 2 · 6 + 3 = 15 , yielding 830. Column-major offset is 3 · 4 + 2 = 14 , yielding 828. Equality of the two layouts at an index requires i ( C - 1 ) = j ( R - 1 ) ; here 5 i = 3 j . Both layouts start at the same address for (0,0), and the last element also occupies their common final slot. Therefore a single matching address does not identify the layout. The two formulas describe separately declared representations, not two legal interpretations of one C rectangular-array object.

questions.title: Question 7. Three-dimensional mixed-radix recovery
questions.text: Question 7. Three-dimensional mixed-radix recovery Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A row-major array has extents 3×4×5 , base 2000 and four-byte elements. Find the address of (2,1,3), then recover the indices of element offset 47. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The selected offset is ( 2 · 4 + 1 ) 5 + 3 = 48 , giving address 2192. To invert 47, first divide by five: final index 2 and quotient 9. Divide 9 by four: middle index 1 and first index 2. Thus 47 belongs to (2,1,2), the immediate predecessor in the final axis. There are 60 elements, so both offsets are valid. A common error sums the three indices without strides, which loses the complete earlier planes and rows. The product-of-extents bound is a separate part of the inverse proof.

questions.title: Question 8. A transpose changes the destination shape
questions.text: Question 8. A transpose changes the destination shape Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A 2×5 row-major matrix is copied into a 5×2 transpose. Where does original flat offset 7 move, and where does offset 9 move? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Divide by the original column count five: offset 7 is original (1,2). Transpose to destination (2,1), whose new row-major offset is 2 · 2 + 1 = 5 . Offset 9 is original (1,4), which moves to (4,1), destination offset 9. A fixed last element therefore does not imply that the whole transpose is unchanged. The destination stride uses two columns, not five. The mapping i C + j ↦ j R + i is a bijection because transposing the recovered destination coordinates returns the original pair.

A fixed last element therefore does not imply that the whole transpose is unchanged. The destination stride uses two columns, not five. The mapping i C + j ↦ j R + i is a bijection because transposing the recovered destination coordinates returns the original pair.

The destination stride uses two columns, not five. The mapping iC+j↦jR+i is a bijection because transposing the recovered destination coordinates returns the original pair.

Affine strides with a reversed axis Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A numerical view has row stride 40 bytes and column stride -4 bytes. questions.title: Question 10. Packed lower triangle and symmetric lookup
questions.text: Question 10. Packed lower triangle and symmetric lookup Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A zero-based symmetric 6×6 matrix stores its lower triangle including the diagonal, in row order, with eight-byte elements and base 3000. Find the stored address for logical (1,4). Read the complete derivation and reasoning Symmetry redirects (1,4) to lower-triangle position (4,1). Four earlier rows contain 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 elements. Add column offset one to obtain flat offset 11 and address 3088. The full packed length is 6 · 7 / 2 = 21 , not 36. Applying the lower-triangle formula directly to an upper-triangle coordinate would violate its domain and can collide with another row. This answer assumes symmetry of values and the specified storage convention; a general matrix cannot discard its upper half this way.

questions.title: Question 11. Packed upper triangle cannot reuse the lower formula
questions.text: Question 11. Packed upper triangle cannot reuse the lower formula Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem An upper-triangular 5×5 matrix includes its diagonal and is packed by rows. Within row two, column four is two positions after its first column two, so the offset is 11. Offset 9 is the beginning of row two and therefore belongs to (2,2). questions.title: Question 13. Diagonal offsets and loop count
questions.text: Question 13. Diagonal offsets and loop count Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For an n×n dense row-major matrix, derive the diagonal offsets and their sum, then evaluate for n=5 . Count distinct positions selected. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Coordinate ( i , i ) has flat offset i n + i = i ( n + 1 ) for i=0 through n -1. Their sum is ( n + 1 ) n ( n - 1 ) / 2 . At n=5 the offsets are 0,6,12,18,24 and the sum is 60. There are five positions, not 25; the arithmetic progression spacing is n+1 . For n=0 the abstract selected set and sum are empty, while a C fixed zero-size declaration is a separate invalid construction. The sum of offsets does not equal the sum of matrix values unless values were specifically defined from their offsets.

questions.title: Question 14. When is a flat byte difference meaningful?
questions.text: Question 14. When is a flat byte difference meaningful? Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Two separate malloc allocations appear at numerical addresses 1000 and 1040 on one run. Each stores integers. Is their C pointer difference necessarily ten? Explain what additional facts are needed. Read the complete derivation and reasoning No portable pointer-difference result follows. C subtraction requires both pointers to be within the same array object or its one-past boundary, with a representable ptrdiff_ t result. Separate allocations fail that object relation even if they are adjacent numerically. Four-byte integers and the observed difference forty support only a numerical address calculation under that run’s representation. They do not create a shared array. If instead both pointers designate positions zero and ten of one live integer array, with legal endpoints and representable subtraction, the result is ten elements.

questions.title: Question 15. Interior negative indexing is ordinary pointer arithmetic
questions.text: Question 15. Interior negative indexing is ordinary pointer arithmetic Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For int a[7] = {2,4,6,8,10,12,14}, let p=a+4 . Evaluate p [-3], p [2], and the complete range of legal element-access offsets k . Read the complete derivation and reasoning p designates a[4]. Subtracting three selects a[1], so p [-3] = 4; adding two selects a[6], so p [2] = 14. Element access requires 0 ≤ 4 + k < 7 , hence - 4 ≤ k ≤ 2 . Offset three forms the legal one-past pointer p+3 but cannot be dereferenced. This negative index is relative to the pointer’s current position, not Python’s end-of-sequence normalization. The legality follows from the shared live array object and bounds, rather than from the sign of the written subscript.

questions.title: Question 16. Array sizeof and parameter sizeof
questions.text: Question 16. Array sizeof and parameter sizeof Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Assume sizeof(int) = 4 and sizeof(int *) = 8. For a real int a[9], evaluate sizeof a / si zeof a[0]. What does the same expression mean inside void f(int a[9]) ? Read the complete derivation and reasoning In the caller’s actual-array scope, sizeof a is 36 and sizeof a[0] is four, so the quotient is nine. In f , the array-parameter declaration is adjusted to int *, even though nine appears in its syntax. sizeof a is therefore eight and the quotient is two; it is not a runtime length computation. The length must be passed or supplied by a valid interface contract. Different pointer sizes would change the misleading quotient, while the true caller array length would remain nine. No array elements are read by these non-VLA sizeof expressions.

questions.title: Question 17. Whole-array pointer versus first-element pointer
questions.text: Question 17. Whole-array pointer versus first-element pointer Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For int a[6] and sizeof(int) = 4, compare the numerical advances of a+1 and & a+1 . Why can both begin at the same storage? Read the complete derivation and reasoning After expression conversion, a+1 has type int * and advances to the next integer, numerically four bytes in the given model. &a is a pointer to the whole six-int array, so & a+1 advances over 24 bytes to one past that entire array object. Their beginnings coincide because the first element starts at the array beginning. The identical beginning does not make their pointed-to types or strides identical. The whole-array one-past result is valid to form, but dereferencing it would ask for a nonexistent following array object.

questions.title: Question 18. A row pointer retains the inner extent
questions.text: Question 18. A row pointer retains the inner extent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For int m [3][5] with four-byte integers, let p=m . Interpret p+2 , *( p+2 ), and sizeof *( p+2 ). Is p correctly declared int **? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The converted type is pointer to a five-int row: int (* p )[5]. Adding two advances two complete rows, forty bytes, to row two. Dereferencing gives the row-array lvalue m [2]; in ordinary expressions it can then convert to an int * to that row’s first element. sizeof on this row-array operand is 20. Declaring p as int ** would falsely expect stored pointer objects where integers are actually stored. A cast cannot repair that representation mismatch. Both the row index and any subsequent column index need their own valid bounds.

questions.title: Question 19. Numerical adjacency does not erase a C subarray boundary
questions.text: Question 19. Numerical adjacency does not erase a C subarray boundary Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For int m [2][3], does a int * p=m [0] authorize p [4] merely because the matrix stores six adjacent integers? Read the complete derivation and reasoning No portable justification follows from total adjacency. p points into the first three-element row subarray. Its permitted pointer formation reaches that row’s one-past boundary, but p [4] goes beyond it. Use m [1][1], whose row and column accesses are each within their proper array objects, to select the physically corresponding integer. A separately allocated genuine six-int flat buffer would allow flat[4]. The row-major numerical offset four is useful for deriving layout; it is not a replacement for the typed object-boundary requirements of C pointer arithmetic.

questions.title: Question 20. Partial initialization and definite values
questions.text: Question 20. Partial initialization and definite values Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem At block scope consider int a[5] = {9,2}; int b [5]; static int c [5]; Which values of a[4], b [4], c [4] are determined by these declarations? This is not an array-bound error—index four fits—but an initialization problem. Correct tracing separates valid storage, valid index and a usable stored value. Changing the scope or initialization of b can change that third condition.

questions.title: Question 21. Constraint violation is not a surprise numeric output
questions.text: Question 21. Constraint violation is not a surprise numeric output Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Which declarations or statements require a C diagnostic: int a[3]; int b [3]; a=b ; int z [0];? How do you copy the contents instead? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Array assignment a=b violates a constraint because an array object is not a modifiable lvalue for assignment. A fixed array bound zero also violates the array-declaration requirements; accepting it as an extension does not make it standard C . Declare valid arrays and copy elements in a bounded loop, or use an appropriate nonoverlapping byte-copy operation for suitable objects. An array name does not become a writable pointer variable merely because it often converts to a pointer in expressions. Rebinding a separate pointer changes the reference, not the original array contents.

The legal subtraction does not require a read at the endpoint, and it does not make the endpoint into a real element.

Dereferencing it to read or write an element is invalid because there is no fifth element. a+5 exceeds even the permitted one-past boundary and is invalid pointer arithmetic. Subtracting a from a+4 is permitted within the same array relation and returns four elements if that result fits ptrdiff_t. The pointer’s permitted formation and the object’s permitted access are distinct checks. The legal subtraction does not require a read at the endpoint, and it does not make the endpoint into a real element.

questions.title: Question 23. Unsigned reverse loop trap
questions.text: Question 23. Unsigned reverse loop trap Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Explain why for(size_ t i=n -1; i>= 0; --i) use(a[ i ]); is incorrect. Give a version that also handles n=0 and prove its first and last accessed indices. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The condition i>= 0 is always true for unsigned size_ t . At n=0 , n -1 wraps before any valid index exists; at nonzero n , decrementing zero wraps to a huge value instead of stopping. Initialize i=n , test i>0 , decrement i , then access a[ i ]. For n>0 the first body decrements to n -1. Each subsequent body selects one smaller index; the final access is zero, after which the next test fails. For n=0 the body is skipped. This proves n valid accesses and avoids relying on unsigned wraparound as termination.

questions.title: Question 24. A stride count with nonzero boundaries
questions.text: Question 24. A stride count with nonzero boundaries Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A loop visits indices 3,7,11,... while i<26 . List the final index and number of visits; derive the count without simulating every iteration. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Write i=3+4t . The guard becomes 3 + 4 t < 26 , so 0 ≤ t ≤ 5 . There are six visits and the last index is 23. Equivalently the count is ⌈ ( 26 - 3 ) / 4 ⌉ = 6 . Replacing the strict guard by i<= 26 happens to give the same result here because 26 is not in the progression; that coincidence is not a general equivalence. At boundary 27 the strict and non-strict guards would differ. An array hosting the loop must contain every selected index, not merely the number of visits.

questions.title: Question 25. Two different reduction initializations
questions.text: Question 25. Two different reduction initializations Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For [5,5,2,2,7,1,1], compare the number of comparisons and successful minimum updates when initialized from the first element versus mathematical positive infinity, always using strict comparison. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Initializing from the first element leaves six later comparisons. Strict decreases occur at value two and value one, so there are two updates. Initializing from infinity performs seven comparisons and the first five is an additional update, giving three. Equal occurrences never update under strict comparison, so the selected minimum position is the first one, index five. A non-strict comparison changes tie handling and update count. The number of loop comparisons is fixed here, whereas successful assignments depend on the data and initialization policy.

questions.title: Question 26. Weighted prefix invariant
questions.text: Question 26. Weighted prefix invariant Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For mathematical integers A= [2,-1,4,3], compute S=su m (( i+1 )A[ i ]) and give a loop invariant for the weighted scan. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The contributions are 2,-2,12,12, so S=24 . At boundary i the invariant is 0 ≤ i ≤ 4 and S = ∑ k = 0 i - 1 ( k + 1 ) A [ k ] . It starts with the empty sum zero. When i<4 , reading A[ i ] is valid and adding ( i+1 )A[ i ] extends the relation through that index. Advancing i preserves the boundary condition. At exit i=4 and the invariant gives the required result. A loop that uses i rather than i+1 computes a different weighting, so an unweighted total cannot serve as its certificate.

questions.title: Question 28. Difference-array range updates
questions.text: Question 28. Difference-array range updates Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Starting from five zeros, add 4 on [1:4), then subtract 2 on [2:5). Use a six-entry boundary difference array and reconstruct the result. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first update adds four at boundary one and subtracts four at boundary four. The second subtracts two at boundary two and adds two at boundary five. D becomes [0,4,-2,0,-4,2]. Accumulating its first five entries gives [0,4,2,2,-2]. The sixth entry is a sentinel that brings the running total back to zero beyond the array; it is not a sixth data value. The signs follow from starting and ending each added constant segment. questions.title: Question 29. Rectangle inclusion–exclusion
questions.text: Question 29. Rectangle inclusion–exclusion Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For A= [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], build the boundary prefix table and find the sum of rows [0:2), columns [1:3). Read the complete derivation and reasoning Include a zero row and column to obtain P= [[0,0,0,0],[0,1,3,6],[0,5,12,21]]. The requested sum is P [ 2 , 3 ] - P [ 0 , 3 ] - P [ 2 , 1 ] + P [ 0 , 1 ] = 21 - 0 - 5 + 0 = 16 . Directly, the selected entries are 2,3,5,6, also totaling 16. The table recurrence removes the overlap already counted by the top and left accumulated rectangles. Boundary indexing avoids substituting -1 at the top edge. The same four-term relation yields zero for an empty row or column interval.

questions.title: Question 30. An in-place recurrence uses modified predecessors
questions.text: Question 30. An in-place recurrence uses modified predecessors Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For A= [1,2,3,4,5], execute A[ i ] += A[ i -1] for i=1 ..4 in increasing order. Derive the general final relation to original values. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The successive complete states are [1,3,3,4,5], [1,3,6,4,5], [1,3,6,10,5], and [1,3,6,10,15]. After processing index i , A[ i ] equals the sum of original entries zero through i . The already updated predecessor supplies the earlier prefix, so the operation implements a prefix accumulation. A formula A 0 [ i ] + A 0 [ i - 1 ] would incorrectly assume an untouched predecessor. This can be proved by induction on i : the base leaves A[0] original, and each update adds the next original value to the established prefix.

questions.title: Question 31. Reverse execution computes another map
questions.text: Question 31. Reverse execution computes another map Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Execute the same update A[ i ] += A[ i -1] on [1,2,3,4,5] for i=4 ,3,2,1. Why is the result not a prefix sum? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The reverse order yields [1,2,3,4,9], then [1,2,3,7,9], then [1,2,5,7,9], and finally [1,3,5,7,9]. At each update the predecessor index is lower and has not yet been changed. Therefore the final value for i>0 is A 0 [ i ] + A 0 [ i - 1 ] , not a growing prefix total. Index zero remains original. Both executions use valid indices and the same statement, so the difference is a data dependency rather than an undefined-behavior issue. A snapshot-based implementation would make the neighbor-sum intent explicit.

questions.text: Question 34. Leftward overlap needs the opposite direction Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Move four entries of [2,4,6,8,10,12] from source offset 1 to destination offset 0. questions.title: Question 35. Bounds alone do not prove a copy contract
questions.text: Question 35. Bounds alone do not prove a copy contract Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Course-inspired extension — CMU 15-122 Lecture 3, exercise 2 A copy_into loop has valid source/destination bounds but its postcondition compares final source and final destination segments. Explain why those bounds are insufficient if both parameters alias. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Take a= [1,2,3,4], source start zero, target start one and length three. A forward loop produces [1,1,1,1]. Its final source segment and target segment happen to be equal, yet the intended original-value copy [1,1,2,3] was not achieved. In the opposite direction, a forward move produces [2,3,4,4] and even final source/target equality can fail. Therefore a meaningful specification must refer to original source values and control interference. Require disjointness, or use a snapshot/overlap-safe move. The CMU array-copy exercise is extended here precisely to expose this missing obligation.

questions.title: Question 37. Insertion shifts and the end case
questions.text: Question 37. Insertion shifts and the end case Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A logical sequence [3,6,9,12] occupies the first four positions of capacity six. Insert 7 at index two. Give the write order, new contents and shift count; compare insertion at index four. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Move original index three to four, then index two to three, then write seven at index two. The logical result is [3,6,7,9,12], length five. There are n - k=2 shifts; descending movement preserves the original values. Insertion at boundary four uses zero shifts and writes only the new last value. Boundary n is valid for insertion although it is not a valid old element index. Capacity must permit the new length, and spare positions need not have meaningful initialized values before they are assigned.

questions.title: Question 38. Deletion changes length rather than erasing storage
questions.text: Question 38. Deletion changes length rather than erasing storage Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Delete index one from [3,6,9,12,15] using stable compaction. How many shifts occur and what may remain in the spare slot? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Move indices two, three and four left once, yielding the logical prefix [3,9,12,15] and length four. There are n -k- 1=3 shifts. The physical slot at old index four can still contain fifteen; it is outside the logical sequence and need not be zeroed for correctness. Reading it as an allocated initialized element is a different question from including it in the container’s valid logical contents. Forward copy is safe because each write is below unread source positions. Deleting the last logical element would require no shifts.

questions.title: Question 39. Reverse a half-open segment exactly
questions.text: Question 39. Reverse a half-open segment exactly Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Reverse A[1:6) in [0,1,2,3,4,5,6]. List the swapped pairs and final sequence. Why is the central element untouched? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The segment length is five, so there are floor(5/2)= 2 swaps: (1,5) and (2,4). The final array is [0,5,4,3,2,1,6]. Index three maps to itself, so writing it again is unnecessary. An invariant fixes completed pairs to the reversed original values and leaves the intervening middle original. Using r instead of r -1 for the first high index would incorrectly include index six, outside the requested segment. Length zero or one requires no swaps and is already reversed.

questions.title: Question 40. Three reversals implement left rotation
questions.text: Question 40. Three reversals implement left rotation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Rotate [0,1,2,3,4,5,6] left by three using three segment reversals. Show each intermediate state and explain the block algebra. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Reverse the first block to get [2,1,0,3,4,5,6]. Reverse the second block to get [2,1,0,6,5,4,3]. Reverse the whole sequence to obtain [3,4,5,6,0,1,2]. If the original is XY, the first two stages produce reverse( X ) reverse( Y ), and reversing that concatenation gives YX. This proves the rotation without assuming particular values. Normalize k modulo n only when n>0 . The method uses constant auxiliary element storage and linear swaps, whereas a copied result requires separate output storage.

questions.title: Question 41. Rotation cycles and visit count
questions.text: Question 41. Rotation cycles and visit count Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For a 12-element sequence rotated left by eight, determine the number and length of permutation cycles, and list the cycle beginning at index zero. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The step permutation is addition by eight modulo twelve. Since gcd(12,8)= 4, there are four cycles, each of length three. The cycle from zero is 0→8→4→0 . Distinct starting representatives can be 0,1,2,3. Repeating a cycle from another already visited member would duplicate work. The cycle length is the smallest positive t with 12 dividing 8t , namely three. All twelve indices appear across the four disjoint cycles; the direction used to move values must match whether the map denotes original-to-destination or destination-to-source.

questions.title: Question 42. A stable read/write filter
questions.text: Question 42. A stable read/write filter Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Remove odd entries from [5,2,7,4,6,9,8] in place without changing the order of retained entries. Give final logical contents and explain why writes cannot destroy unread data. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Use read r from zero upward and write w starting at zero. Copy a[ r ] to a[ w ] only when the entry is even, then increment w . Retained entries are 2,4,6,8, giving logical length four and prefix [2,4,6,8]. At every boundary 0 ≤ w ≤ r ≤ 7 , and the output prefix equals the retained original entries from the processed prefix. Because w≤r , a retained write affects the current or an earlier position, never a larger unread position. Stability follows because retained values are appended in original encounter order.

questions.title: Question 43. Dependency analysis of a two-pass difference transform
questions.text: Question 43. Dependency analysis of a two-pass difference transform Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For A= [3,5,9,10], compute the adjacent differences A[ i ]-A[ i -1] for i>0 in place while retaining A[0]. Which loop direction gives original differences? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Process from index three down to one. The writes are 10- 9=1 , then 9- 5=4 , then 5- 3=2 , so the final sequence is [3,2,4,1]. Each predecessor is still original when read. Forward processing first changes index one to two; index two then reads that changed two and becomes seven, and the final index becomes three. That wrong result is [3,2,7,3]. The desired difference map is the inverse of a forward prefix accumulation when all arithmetic is exact. Direction follows from which neighbor must remain original.

questions.title: Question 44. Python single indices and clipped slices
questions.text: Question 44. Python single indices and clipped slices Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For a=li st(range(6)), evaluate a[-2], a[-8:20:3] and a[8:20]. Which corresponding single-index access raises an exception? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The single index -2 normalizes to four and returns 4. For the second expression, start -8 clips to zero and stop 20 clips to six; step three selects indices zero and three, giving [0,3]. The third slice starts beyond the end and clips both boundaries to six, producing []. A single access a[8] raises IndexError, as does a[-8]. This difference is deliberate: slice boundaries can be clipped while an element request needs an actual element. It is incorrect to infer single-access safety from an empty slice at similar written bounds.

questions.title: Question 45. Omitted negative stop versus explicit -1
questions.text: Question 45. Omitted negative stop versus explicit -1 Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For a=li st(range(7)), evaluate a[::-1], a[:-1:-1] and a[5:0:-2]. Explain the stop semantics. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The omitted negative-step start defaults to six, and the omitted stop is a before-first sentinel, so the reversal is [6,5,4,3,2,1,0]. In a[:-1:-1], the explicitly supplied -1 normalizes to six. The start is also six, and a strict decreasing progression cannot begin above that stop, so the result is empty. The third slice visits indices 5,3,1 and returns [5,3,1]. Replacing an omitted negative stop with written -1 is therefore not a harmless spelling change. Normalize the slice before counting its selected indices.

questions.title: Question 46. Extended slice replacement count
questions.text: Question 46. Extended slice replacement count Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For a= [0,1,2,3,4,5], assign a[1:6:2] = [9,8,7]. What is the result? Why does replacing it with [9,8] fail? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The selected indices are 1,3,5, so three replacement values produce [0,9,2,8,4,7]. An extended slice whose step is not one cannot change the number of selected slots, and a two-item replacement raises ValueError instead of shrinking the list. Ordinary step-one slice assignment uses a different rule and can change length. The resulting list’s unselected values at indices zero, two and four remain unchanged. Count the normalized index progression before matching replacement length; the written difference between stop and start is not the number of selected entries.

questions.title: Question 47. Ordinary slice assignment can change length
questions.text: Question 47. Ordinary slice assignment can change length Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For a= [1,2,3,4,5], assign a[1:4] = [8,9], then a[2:2] = [6,7]. Give both states and lengths. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first replacement removes three selected entries and inserts two, giving [1,8,9,5] of length four. The empty slice at boundary two then inserts two values before the old entry there, yielding [1,8,6,7,9,5] of length six. A slice of length zero can be an insertion location; it is not an element access. The second operation uses the current list positions after the first length change. Treating both statements as updates to original indices would select the wrong position. These Python semantics are not fixed-capacity C array assignment.

questions.title: Question 48. Outer copy and inner alias
questions.text: Question 48. Outer copy and inner alias Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Course-inspired extension — UC Berkeley CS61A, Composing Programs §2.4.2 Compute the final a and b : a = [[2], [5]] b = a[:] b[0].append(7) b[1] = [9] result = (a, b) Read the complete derivation and reasoning The slice creates a distinct outer list but copies the two inner references. Appending seven changes the shared first inner list, so both outer lists observe [2,7]. Assigning b [1] = [9] changes one slot in b’s outer list and does not redirect a’s second slot. Therefore a= [[2,7],[5]] and b= [[2,7],[9]]. The two outer lists are not identical, while their first entries are identical objects. This trace separates mutation of a referenced object from replacement of a reference slot; the word copy alone does not say which level is independent.

questions.title: Question 49. Repeated rows share one inner object
questions.text: Question 49. Repeated rows share one inner object Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Compare bad = [[0]*4]*3 with good = [[0]*4 for _ in range(3)] after setting index [1][2] to nine in each. Read the complete derivation and reasoning bad contains three references to one inner row. Modifying that row through the second reference changes the displayed value in all three rows, giving three copies in appearance of [0,0,9,0]. good creates three distinct rows, so only its second row changes. Repetition copies references, not recursively referenced objects. Distinct outer slot positions can therefore share one inner identity. For a matrix whose rows should vary independently, create the row inside the comprehension. A shallow outer copy of bad still preserves the same inner sharing and cannot repair it.

questions.title: Question 50. Deletion during iteration skips shifted entries
questions.text: Question 50. Deletion during iteration skips shifted entries Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Trace: a = [2, 4, 6, 7] for x in a: if x % 2 == 0: a.remove(x) result = a Read the complete derivation and reasoning The iterator first selects two at position zero and removes it, leaving [4,6,7]. Its next index is one, which now contains six rather than four, so it removes six and leaves [4,7]. The next index is two, beyond the current list, and iteration ends. Final result is [4,7], despite four also being even. The issue is index advancement combined with leftward shifting, not a failure of the predicate. questions.title: Question 51. Identity versus equal contents
questions.text: Question 51. Identity versus equal contents Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Let a= [[1],[2]], b=a [:], c= [row[:] for row in a ]. Evaluate a==b , a is b , a[0] is b [0], and a[0] is c [0]. What later mutation distinguishes b from c ? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Initially a==b is true because the contents compare equal, but a is b is false because the outer slice made a different list. a[0] is b [0] is true because the shallow copy retained its inner references. a[0] is c [0] is false because the row slicing created distinct inner lists. questions.title: Question 52. Mapped values and filtered values are different outputs
questions.text: Question 52. Mapped values and filtered values are different outputs Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Course-inspired extension — UC Berkeley CS61A, Composing Programs §2.3.3 For a= [-2,0,3,5], compare [ x x for x in a if x>0 ] with [ x for x in a if x x>0 ], then derive the first output sum. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first expression filters original positive values three and five, then maps them to nine and twenty-five, giving [9,25] and sum 34. The second filters all nonzero original values because their squares are positive, but returns those original values, giving [-2,3,5]. The order and position of the map/filter expressions determine the result. The original input list is unchanged in this example because evaluating squares and comparisons does not mutate its integer objects. The output comprehension creates a new list but that alone does not imply deep copying for arbitrary mapped objects.

questions.title: Question 53. Code points, UTF-8 bytes and display units
questions.text: Question 53. Code points, UTF-8 bytes and display units Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For Python s= "Aé", give len(s) , len( s .encode("utf-8")), and the number of stored characters in a UTF-8 C array initialized with the same two symbols plus a terminator. State the encoding assumption. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Python counts two Unicode code points, so len(s)= 2. UTF-8 encodes A in one byte and é in two, giving three encoded bytes. questions.title: Question 54. Embedded zero separates capacity from string length
questions.text: Question 54. Embedded zero separates capacity from string length Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem In C , char s [8] = {\x27a\x27,\x27b\x27,0,\x27c\x27}; determine sizeof s , strlen( s ), s [3] and whether later initialized entries extend the string. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The real array has capacity eight bytes because sizeof(char) = 1. Its first zero is at index two, so strlen( s ) = 2. s [3] is the initialized character c , and the remaining unspecified initializer entries are zero. Later initialized bytes exist as array elements but are not part of the string beginning at s . Thus a string length does not identify the array capacity, and a terminator does not end the storage object. A bounded array access to index three is valid even though a string operation starting at index zero stops earlier.

questions.title: Question 55. An exactly filled C character array lacks a terminator
questions.text: Question 55. An exactly filled C character array lacks a terminator Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Classify char a[3] = "cat" and char b [] = "cat" in C17, then evaluate which may be passed to strlen without another change. Read the complete derivation and reasoning C permits the first initializer to fill the three-element array with c , a , t and omit the zero because there is no remaining slot. The declaration itself is allowed, but a is not a valid terminated string. strlen(a) cannot be assigned a portable result; it may read beyond its storage seeking a zero. b has four elements including the terminator and strlen( b ) = 3. The distinction is specifically C ; language variants can differ. A known capacity and initialized characters are not sufficient—the string operation requires an accessible terminating zero.

questions.title: Question 56. Writable array versus literal target
questions.text: Question 56. Writable array versus literal target Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Contrast char a[] = "cat"; const char * p= "cat"; a[0] = \x27b\x27;. What changes, and why is casting away const not permission to modify the literal? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The array a owns four writable character objects initialized from the literal, so the assignment changes its string to bat while keeping the terminator. p designates a separate string-literal array and still presents cat. A string literal is not a permitted modification target in C even if a cast changes the written pointer type. Type casts do not change storage permissions, object origin or lifetime. The caller’s array and the literal can have equal initial values without being the same modifiable object. sizeof a counts its array, whereas sizeof p counts the pointer.

questions.title: Question 57. Bounded length finds a terminator or reports absence
questions.text: Question 57. Bounded length finds a terminator or reports absence Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem For bytes [65,66,67,0,88] with capacity five, derive a safe length scan. What should the same scan report for [65,66,67,88,89]? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Initialize k=0 and continue while k<ca pacity and a[ k ]! = 0, checking the bound before the element access. The first buffer returns k=3 and reports a terminator found. The second reaches k=5 without reading a[5] and reports absence, not a valid string length for an unbounded string operation. The invariant states that every earlier position is nonzero and all tested indices were within storage. Short-circuit evaluation protects the current access at the boundary. Returning five without the absence status would confuse a buffer length with a verified string length.

Naive matching comparison count Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Search pattern "aaab" in text "aaaaab" by comparing left to right at starts zero upward, stopping each candidate at its first mismatch. Find the first match and total character comparisons. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are three candidate starts, zero through two. At start zero, the first three a characters match and the fourth comparison mismatches a against b , costing four. Start one has the same four-comparison failure. Counting only failed comparisons would report two and omit successful tests. A match stops the search, so later candidate costs would not be charged even if they existed.

questions.text: Question 59. An empty pattern and a longer pattern Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Specify first-match results for text "abc" with patterns "" and "abcd". Why should unsigned n -m not be calculated before the length comparison in C ? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Under the explicit convention, the empty pattern matches at boundary zero and requires no character comparisons. The four-character pattern cannot fit within the three-character text, so it fails immediately. If n and m are size_ t , n -m wraps when m>n and can create a huge apparent candidate count. Test the empty-pattern convention and m>n case first, then subtract. A candidate start is a boundary, whereas successful nonempty matching must keep all compared positions within actual elements. The failure case is determined by lengths and does not require examining text contents.

questions.title: Question 60. Appending requires one more slot than the visible result
questions.text: Question 60. Appending requires one more slot than the visible result Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A writable C buffer of capacity nine contains "abcd". Can it append "wxyz" with a valid final terminator? What changes if capacity is eight? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The initial length is four and the appended length is four. The result needs 4 + 4 + 1 = 9 slots, including the zero at index eight, so capacity nine is exactly enough. Capacity eight can store all eight visible characters but has no slot for the required terminator; it cannot hold that complete string. The proof must establish source termination, destination capacity and any overlap restrictions of the chosen copy operation. Counting only visible symbols is the standard off-by-one distractor. An unused spare slot before the operation is not automatically a verified terminator.

questions.title: Question 62. A signed char cannot be passed blindly to ctype
questions.text: Question 62. A signed char cannot be passed blindly to ctype Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A byte 0xE9 is stored in a char on an implementation where char is signed. Explain why toupper( s [ i ]) may violate its contract and how to prepare the argument. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The promoted char can be a negative int that is neither EOF nor representable as unsigned char. C’s character-classification and conversion functions require EOF or an unsigned-char-representable value. Convert the stored byte to unsigned char before the call, for example toupper((unsigned char) s [ i ]). This fixes the argument-domain issue, not general Unicode uppercasing. In UTF-8 the byte may be one part of a multi-byte code point, and bytewise conversion is not a full text transformation. Stating an ASCII-only domain can simplify a separate arithmetic exercise but cannot justify passing arbitrary negative char values.

questions.title: Question 63. Returned substring pointer and lifetime
questions.text: Question 63. Returned substring pointer and lifetime Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A C search returns a pointer to a matching character inside its text argument. What ownership and lifetime facts permit later use? Contrast a pointer into a local automatic buffer returned by the function. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The returned pointer designates part of the original text storage, not a new allocated copy. Later access requires that the text object remain alive and that its intended characters stay initialized and within bounds. The search cannot transfer ownership merely by returning an interior pointer; freeing that interior pointer is not equivalent to freeing an owning allocation pointer. A pointer into a local automatic buffer becomes invalid when that buffer’s lifetime ends at function return. A numerically plausible address or unchanged bytes observed later do not restore the ended object lifetime.

A C search returns a pointer to a matching character inside its text argument. What ownership and lifetime facts permit later use? Contrast a pointer into a local automatic buffer returned by the function.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

The returned pointer designates part of the original text storage, not a new allocated copy. Later access requires that the text object remain alive and that its intended characters stay initialized and within bounds. The search cannot transfer ownership merely by returning an interior pointer; freeing that interior pointer is not equivalent to freeing an owning allocation pointer. A pointer into a local automatic buffer becomes invalid when that buffer’s lifetime ends at function return. A numerically plausible address or unchanged bytes observed later do not restore the ended object lifetime.

questions.title: Question 64. Exact doubling work for a particular length
questions.text: Question 64. Exact doubling work for a particular length Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Course-inspired extension — Stanford CS106B Lecture 17, expansion model An initially empty container reserves capacity one and doubles when full. After 13 successful appends, find final capacity, total elements copied during expansions, total writes including new values and peak simultaneously allocated slots. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Expansion capacities are 2,4,8,16, copying the old live counts 1,2,4,8. Final capacity is 16 and copy work is 15. Adding the thirteen new-element writes gives 28 writes. During the final expansion, blocks of capacity eight and sixteen coexist, so the peak is 24 slots. Logical length is thirteen, distinct from both final capacity and peak capacity. An individual ninth append copies eight elements before its own write; amortized constant cost therefore does not imply constant cost for that operation.

questions.title: Question 65. General doubling bound and exact powers
questions.text: Question 65. General doubling bound and exact powers Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Prove copied-element work is c -1 when final capacity c is a power of two reached from capacity one. Relate it to final positive length n , including n=1 . Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each expansion copies its previous full capacity, so the sum is 1 + 2 + … + c / 2 = c - 1 . At c=1 no expansion occurs and the empty sum is zero, matching the formula. Choosing the least power of two at least n gives n ≤ c < 2 n , hence c - 1<2n . Including new writes gives less than 3n . If n itself is a power of two, c=n and the exact copy work is n -1. These relations assume no deletions, failed allocations or costly element copies; they count element assignments rather than every machine instruction.

questions.title: Question 66. Additive growth causes a quadratic sum
questions.text: Question 66. Additive growth causes a quadratic sum Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Initial capacity is three; whenever full it grows by three. After 12 appends, calculate copied elements and derive the order for n=3m appends. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For twelve appends, expansions copy 3,6,9 live elements and final capacity is twelve, so copy work is 18. For n=3m , expansions copy 3 , 6 , … , 3 ( m - 1 ) , totaling 3 m ( m - 1 ) / 2 . Since m=n/3 , the leading term grows quadratically in n . New-element writes add only n . A fixed additive increment therefore cannot use the same geometric bound as doubling. The exact sum depends on whether initial allocation is counted and whether a capacity expansion happens only before an append that would exceed current capacity; those conventions are stated here.

questions.title: Question 67. A growth factor other than two
questions.text: Question 67. A growth factor other than two Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Capacity begins at one and triples when full. After ten appends, find final capacity and copy work. Explain why this does not prove tripling universally better or worse than doubling. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Full capacities one, three and nine are copied before reaching capacity 27. Thus copy work is 1+3+9=13 and new writes add ten. The total is 23 element writes, but 17 final spare slots remain. With doubling, ten appends reach capacity sixteen and copy fifteen elements, so that particular comparison trades less copying for more reserved storage. Different operation counts and memory constraints can favor different factors. Both fixed factors above one give linear total copy work under the simple model; the phrase “most efficient” requires a specified objective and cost model.

questions.title: Question 68. Allocation overflow and an exact boundary
questions.text: Question 68. Allocation overflow and an exact boundary Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Assume SIZE_MAX = 65535 and an eight-byte element type. What is the largest n for which n *sizeof(element) fits, and why is checking the wrapped product afterward insufficient? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The multiplication is representable exactly when n ≤ ⌊ 65535 / 8 ⌋ = 8191 . That maximum requests 65528 bytes. n=8192 would need 65536 and wraps to zero in the stated unsigned arithmetic. Comparing a wrapped product with SIZE_MAX cannot detect the original mathematical overflow because every wrapped unsigned result already lies in the type’s range. Check n against the quotient before multiplication, then handle allocation failure. This arithmetic certificate permits a byte-count computation; it does not guarantee that memory is available or that all created elements have been initialized.

questions.title: Question 69. A failed realloc must not lose the owner
questions.text: Question 69. A failed realloc must not lose the owner Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem Explain the problem with p=re alloc( p ,new_bytes) when failure is possible. What references remain valid after a successful move versus after failure? Read the complete derivation and reasoning On allocation failure, realloc returns null while the original allocation remains valid. Assigning the result directly to the sole owner p overwrites the only saved original pointer and can leak that block. Store the result in a temporary, test success and update p only afterward. On successful reallocation, use the returned pointer; old interior pointers and references into the prior allocation are not retained as valid access handles, even if observed addresses seem unchanged. On failure, the old allocation and its existing valid interior pointers remain available. State new_bytes > 0 here to avoid version-dependent zero-size corner cases.

questions.title: Question 70. Shifts and growth costs in one insertion
questions.text: Question 70. Shifts and growth costs in one insertion Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A full dynamic sequence of length/capacity eight inserts at index two after doubling. Count old-element copies, subsequent shifts, new-element write and peak slots under an implementation that first expands then shifts. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Expansion copies all eight old live elements into capacity sixteen. Insertion then shifts n - k=6 elements from indices seven down to two, followed by one new-element write. The specified implementation therefore performs fifteen element writes: eight copies, six shifts and one new write. Peak capacity during expansion is 8+16=24 slots. A different implementation could copy directly into final shifted positions and avoid some duplicate assignments, so the count is tied to the declared execution strategy. The logical result still needs length nine and stable preservation of the old order around the inserted value.

questions.title: Question 71. Shrink threshold thrashing
questions.text: Question 71. Shrink threshold thrashing Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original examination-style problem A container of capacity eight shrinks to four as soon as length becomes four, and doubles when a fifth element is inserted. Explain the cost of repeatedly deleting and re-appending the fifth item. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each deletion reaches length four and copies four elements into a capacity-four block. The next append finds that block full, copies four elements into capacity eight and writes the new item. Repeating the pair causes eight copied elements every cycle despite the sequence length fluctuating by only one. For a scaled capacity c with shrink at c/2 , the pair can cost a linear number of copies in c . A lower shrink threshold, such as one quarter with a suitable minimum-capacity policy, leaves room for many operations before the opposite resize and prevents this immediate oscillation.
