questions.title: Question 9. Strictly below the endpoint
questions.text: Question 9. Strictly below the endpoint Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Oxford §3.4 Example 3.12 Count positive integers strictly less than 1000 divisible by at least one of 2, 3 and 5. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The endpoint is 999. Singles contribute 499, 333 and 199; pair intersections use divisors six, ten and fifteen. Those pair counts are 166, 99 and 66. The triple count uses thirty and is 33. The alternating total is 499 + 333 + 199 - 166 - 99 - 66 + 33 = 733 . The seven terms include every specified nonempty divisor intersection. The complementary count is 266. Using 1000 changes the universe and includes an additional qualifying integer. Result. 733.

questions.title: Question 10. The dice union error
questions.text: Question 10. The dice union error Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Berkeley EECS70 Note 14 §4.3 Roll three independent fair six-sided dice. Find the probability that at least one shows a specified face, and assess the claim that it equals one half. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each hit event has probability 1 / 6 . Every specified pair has probability 1 / 36 , and the triple has probability 1 / 216 by mutual independence. The union is 3 / 6 - 3 / 36 + 1 / 216 = 91 / 216 . One half is only the first-order upper bound. Alternatively all three dice miss with probability ( 5 / 6 ) 3 = 125 / 216 , whose complement is 91 / 216 . The two descriptions count the same event. The independence assumption computes intersections; inclusion-exclusion itself does not require it. Result. 91/216 .

questions.title: Question 11. Totient from actual prime events
questions.text: Question 11. Totient from actual prime events Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent numerical application of the MIT §14.9.5 and CMU §2.5 totient derivations How many integers in the closed interval from 1 to 360 are coprime to 360? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The distinct prime divisors are two, three and five. An integer is coprime precisely when it avoids all three divisibility events. The complementary sum factors as 360 ( 1 - 1 / 2 ) ( 1 - 1 / 3 ) ( 1 - 1 / 5 ) = 96 . Exponents of the prime factors are already included in 360. Equivalently subtract the union of multiples of two, three and five from 360; all selected prime products divide 360 exactly. Repeating a factor for every exponent would incorrectly exclude the same event several times. Result. 96.

questions.text: Question 12. Onto maps with no extra relabeling Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent numerical application of Cornell Example 4.26 and CMU §2.5 surjections Count functions from a five-element labeled domain onto a three-element labeled codomain. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Start with 3 5 maps. Missing a specified codomain value leaves 2 5 maps; missing a specified pair leaves one map. The count is 3 5 - 3 · 2 5 + 3 · 1 5 = 150 . Missing all three yields zero because the domain is nonempty. The codomain values were labeled throughout. questions.text: Question 13. Exactly two properties Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A universe has 100 objects. questions.title: Question 18. Recover an unknown triple range

Recover an unknown triple range Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Three sets have sizes 12, 11 and 10 in a universe of 25. Inclusive pair sizes are five, four and three. Determine the attainable integer range of the unspecified triple size t . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The pair-only atoms are 5 - t , 4 - t , 3 - t , requiring 0 ≤ t ≤ 3 . The single-only atoms are 3 + t , 3 + t , 3 + t and remain nonnegative. questions.title: Question 19. An attainable minimum outside
questions.text: Question 19. An attainable minimum outside Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem In a universe of 50, three sets have sizes 24, 18 and 12, with exactly three objects in all three. Find the minimum possible number outside the union. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Total memberships are 54. Every triple member creates two duplicate memberships, forcing six duplications in total. The union can contain at most 48 objects, so at least two are outside. Additional pair-only atoms would reduce the union further. The bound is attained with single-only groups of sizes 21, 15 and nine, three triple members, and two outside. Every marginal is correct. The construction is necessary: a lower bound without an arrangement attaining it would not establish the exact minimum. Result. 2.

questions.title: Question 20. Invert four-event aggregate data
questions.text: Question 20. Invert four-event aggregate data Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Four events on 50 objects have intersection sums S1 = 70 , S2 = 40 , S3 = 10 , S4 = 1 . Find the counts N0 through N4 for exactly each membership multiplicity. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Use the triangular system from the largest index: N 4 = 1 , N 3 = 10 - 4 = 6 , and N 2 = 40 - 3 · 6 - 6 = 16 . Then N 1 = 70 - 2 · 16 - 3 · 6 - 4 = 16 and N 0 = 50 - 16 - 16 - 6 - 1 = 11 . The vector is nonnegative and totals fifty. Objects of each multiplicity can be assigned to arbitrary masks of that size, establishing aggregate feasibility. These aggregate counts do not prescribe individual intersection sizes. In particular S2 is a sum of six inclusive pair counts, not the exact-two count. Result. [11, 16, 16, 6, 1].

questions.title: Question 21. A symmetric difference is not a union
questions.text: Question 21. A symmetric difference is not a union Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A and B have sizes 30 and 25, with ten objects in both. Count objects in exactly one of the two sets. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The two disjoint single-only groups have sizes twenty and fifteen. The symmetric difference has | A | + | B | - 2 | A ∩ B | = 30 + 25 - 20 = 35 objects. Subtracting the overlap only once yields the union size 45, which still contains the ten shared objects. The correct coefficient of each shared object is two minus two, so it disappears from the exact-one event. Result. 35.

questions.title: Question 22. Equal margins, different triple overlap
questions.text: Question 22. Equal margins, different triple overlap Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Construct two three-event systems with marginal probabilities one half and pair intersections one quarter, but different triple intersections. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For three mutually independent fair bits, the all-one outcome has probability one eighth. For independent fair bits X and Y , let Z be their exclusive-or. The four equally likely triples are 000, 011, 101 and 110. Each bit is fair and each pair is independent. In the second system 111 is absent, so the triple intersection has probability zero. Pairwise data therefore do not determine the triple. The probability of the union is seven eighths in the first system and three quarters in the second, despite matching singles and pairs. Result. Triple 1/8 versus 0; union 7/8 versus 3/4 .

Impossible fixed-point multiplicity Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Can a permutation of nine labels have exactly eight fixed points? Prove the answer. Read the complete derivation and reasoning If eight positions contain their own distinct labels, the unused label is the label of the remaining position. The final position is forced to contain that label and is therefore fixed too. A permutation cannot have exactly n minus one fixed points. The exact-count formula agrees: ( 9 8 ) D 1 = 9 · 0 = 0 . The obstruction is bijectivity, not a lack of arrangements of eight chosen positions. Result. 0.

Question 31. Impossible fixed-point multiplicity

Can a permutation of nine labels have exactly eight fixed points? Prove the answer.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

questions.title: Question 32. The empty permutation exception
questions.text: Question 32. The empty permutation exception Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Evaluate D0 and determine whether nearest-integer rounding of 0!/e gives it. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There is one empty permutation, and no position violates a fixed-point restriction. Thus D0 = 1 . The nearest integer to one divided by e is zero. The nearest-integer rule therefore does not hold at n equal to zero. For n ≥ 1 the alternating-series error is strictly less than 1 / ( n + 1 ) ≤ 1 / 2 , making the nearest integer unique. This is a boundary-domain exception, not a contradiction of the exact finite alternating sum. Result. D0 = 1 ; rounding gives 0.

questions.title: Question 38. Unlabeled nonempty blocks
questions.text: Question 38. Unlabeled nonempty blocks Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Partition six labeled elements into three nonempty unlabeled blocks. Count partitions. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Map the elements onto three labeled outputs, producing a nonempty fiber partition with named blocks. The onto count is 3 6 - 3 · 2 6 + 3 = 540 . Every unlabeled partition has exactly 3 ! = 6 block labelings. Dividing by six gives ninety partitions. Equal-sized blocks do not change this factor because the blocks contain different labeled elements. The Stirling recurrence independently gives S(6,3) = 90 . Result. 90.

questions.title: Question 40. Image size after a forced equality
questions.text: Question 40. Image size after a forced equality Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Count onto maps from six inputs to three labeled outputs if the first two inputs must have equal images. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Contract the two equal-image inputs into one labeled choice unit. The remaining four inputs form four other units. The equality changes six independent choices to five, while the onto condition still requires all three outputs. The count is O ( 5 , 3 ) = 3 5 - 3 · 2 5 + 3 = 150 . There is no separate factor choosing the common image: that choice is already one of the five map decisions. Enumeration of five-unit maps and expansion of the contracted unit gives a bijection. Result. 150.

questions.title: Question 41. Empty domain and empty output set
questions.text: Question 41. Empty domain and empty output set Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Give the onto counts for size pairs (0,0), (0,3) and (3,0). Explain the zero-power convention. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The empty domain has one function into any set, but that function is onto only when the codomain is empty. A nonempty domain has no function to the empty codomain, because even one input would need an output value. The counts are one, zero and zero respectively. In the finite sum, zero to the zero power is interpreted as one to count the empty function. This is a combinatorial convention for a discrete count, not a limit of a real-valued expression. Result. [1, 0, 0].

questions.title: Question 42. Subset-required outputs versus exact image
questions.text: Question 42. Subset-required outputs versus exact image Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A seven-input map to four outputs must contain output labels one and two. Is its count the same as the count of maps with image exactly {1,2}? Give both counts. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Requiring labels one and two but allowing three and four gives 4 7 - 2 · 3 7 + 2 7 = 12138 . Requiring the image to equal the specified pair removes outputs three and four and requires both remaining labels, giving 2 7 - 2 = 126 . The first predicate allows image size two, three or four; the second fixes both the size and the actual labels. There is no factor choosing the pair in either expression because the pair was specified. Result. 12138 versus 126.

questions.title: Question 43. Bounded occupancy: 3,3,3,3
questions.text: Question 43. Bounded occupancy: 3,3,3,3 Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Count nonnegative integer vectors of sum 8 in 4 labeled coordinates with respective upper caps 3, 3, 3, 3. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The objects are occupancy vectors of identical tokens. The first forbidden coordinate values are [4, 4, 4, 4], one above each allowed cap. For a specified violating subset I , subtract its threshold sum. The residual unrestricted count is H m ( T - ∑ i ∈ I ( c i + 1 ) ) , with zero for a negative residual. Add these residual counts with subset-parity signs. Exact evaluation gives 31; unequal caps are retained separately rather than replaced by an average. The coefficient of the same total in the product of finite coordinate polynomials independently checks every allowed vector. Result. 31.

questions.title: Question 52. Unequal alphabets by position
questions.text: Question 52. Unequal alphabets by position Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A four-position word has alphabets { A , B }, { A , B , C }, { B , C }, { A , C }. Count words containing each of A , B and C . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The universe has two times three times two times two = 24 words. Required symbols define missing-symbol events. Missing A leaves one times two times two times one = four words; missing B leaves one times two times one times two = four; missing C leaves two times two times one times one = four. Every two-symbol missing intersection is empty because at least one position then has no allowed symbol. Therefore the result is 24 − 4 − 4 − 4 = 12 . A single alphabet-size power cannot express these intersections because the position alphabets differ. Result. 12.

questions.title: Question 58. Compatible congruences

Compatible congruences Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Count integers from one through one hundred satisfying x congruent to one modulo four and x congruent to three modulo six. Multiplying moduli to get 24 would miss half the solutions. The intersection consists of one class modulo the least common multiple, not necessarily modulo the product. Result. 8.

questions.title: Question 68. Directed adjacency compatibility 1
questions.text: Question 68. Directed adjacency compatibility 1 Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Permute labels one through 5 in a linear row. Count arrangements containing at least one directed adjacency from [(1, 2), (1, 3)]. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For each specified event subset, check that every symbol has at most one required successor and predecessor and that no directed cycle is forced. A compatible subset of k edges forms directed path blocks and has ( n - k ) ! arrangements. An incompatible subset contributes zero, not the same factorial. Apply the union alternating sum over actual compatible subsets. The result is 48. Direct enumeration of permutations independently confirms it. Two edges sharing a source conflict; a path sharing its middle symbol is valid; a directed two-cycle cannot occur in a linear row. The specific edge topology determines which case applies. Result. 48.

questions.title: Question 72. Cell-disjoint is not component-independent
questions.text: Question 72. Cell-disjoint is not component-independent Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem On a three-by-three forbidden board, take one component {(1,1)} and another {(1,2)}. Is multiplying their rook polynomials valid? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each one-cell component has polynomial 1 + x . Their product would be 1 + 2 x + x 2 . The actual union has two cells in the same row, so both cannot be selected as nonattacking rooks. Its polynomial is one plus two x , with zero x -squared coefficient. Therefore the product is invalid. The components are cell-disjoint but share a row. Independent multiplication requires both row sets and column sets to be disjoint. Result. R(x) = 1 + 2x ; product invalid.

questions.title: Question 73. Certified union interval
questions.text: Question 73. Certified union interval Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A universe has 200 objects with S1 = 150 , S2 = 60 and S3 = 15 ; higher intersections are unknown. Give Bonferroni intervals for the union and its complement. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Order two gives the lower union bound 150 minus 60 = 90 . Order three gives the upper bound 150 minus 60 plus 15 = 105 . Hence the union lies in [90,105]. Subtract the upper and lower bounds from 200 in reverse order to obtain complement interval [95,110]. These are certified inequalities. Without further constraints they must not be advertised as exact attainable ranges. A first-order upper bound of 150 is valid but weaker than the available third-order bound. Result. union [90,105]; complement [95,110].

A closer-truncation counterexample Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem One object belongs to each of ten events. Compare the first- and second-order union truncations to the true union count. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The intersection sums are S 1 = 10 and S 2 = ( 10 2 ) = 45 . The true union count is one. The first truncation is ten with absolute error nine. The second is negative thirty-five with absolute error thirty-six. The second is farther away but is still a valid lower bound. Taking its maximum with zero gives a more useful lower bound. This disproves a blanket statement that every consecutive truncation improves absolute accuracy. Result. T1 = 10 ; T2 = -35.

questions.title: Question 75. Prove the exact-two coefficient
questions.text: Question 75. Prove the exact-two coefficient Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem For arbitrary m events, derive the coefficient of Sj in the count of objects satisfying exactly two events. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The coefficient is ( - 1 ) j - 2 ( j 2 ) for j ≥ 2 . An object with t memberships receives the sum of these coefficients times ( t j ) . Use ( t j ) ( j 2 ) = ( t 2 ) ( t - 2 j - 2 ) . The alternating sum becomes ( t 2 ) ( 1 - 1 ) t - 2 . It is one for t equal to two, zero for larger t , and zero for t below two because there are no terms. This indicator proof applies to arbitrary finite sets, including asymmetric intersection sizes. Result. coefficient (-1)^( j -2) C(j,2) .

Question 75. Prove the exact-two coefficient

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard

Original examination-style problem

For arbitrary m events, derive the coefficient of Sj in the count of objects satisfying exactly two events.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

  1. The coefficient is (-1)j-2(j2) for j≥2. An object with t memberships receives the sum of these coefficients times (tj).

  2. Use

(tj)(j2)=(t2)(t-2j-2)

  1. It is one for t equal to two, zero for larger t, and zero for t below two because there are no terms.

  2. This indicator proof applies to arbitrary finite sets, including asymmetric intersection sizes.

questions.title: Question 77. Recover specified atoms from inclusive counts
questions.text: Question 77. Recover specified atoms from inclusive counts Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem For three events, the complete inclusive table in masks 000 through 111 is [20,10,9,4,8,3,2,1]. The only-A atom is ten minus four minus three plus one = four; only-B is nine minus four minus two plus one = four; only-C is eight minus three minus two plus one = four. questions.title: Question 78. Uniform conditional counting
questions.text: Question 78. Uniform conditional counting Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Roll two fair six-sided dice. Given that their sum is even, find the probability that at least one die shows six. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The conditional universe has eighteen outcomes: both dice even or both odd. All eighteen retain equal conditional weights. The first-die-six event has three outcomes in this universe, and the second-die-six event also has three. Their shared outcome is (6,6). The conditional union therefore has five favorable outcomes and probability five eighteenth. Unconditioned independence cannot be substituted directly after conditioning. Intersect the hit events with the even-sum universe first. Result. 5/18 .

questions.text: Question 79. Nonuniform atomic weights Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A two-event system has atom weights 1/10 outside, 2/10 only A , 3/10 only B and 4/10 in both. Find the union and conditional probability of A given B . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The marginals are P(A) = si x tenths and P(B) = se ven tenths, with shared weight four tenths. questions.title: Question 80. Complete-table feasibility is sufficient
questions.text: Question 80. Complete-table feasibility is sufficient Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Prove that nonnegative integer atoms reconstructed from a complete inclusive intersection table are sufficient for finite-set realization. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For each mask, create a disjoint set containing exactly the reconstructed number of objects. These sets are distinct atoms by construction. Place every object in event i precisely when its mask has bit i set. The intersection at a specified mask is the union of all atom groups at supersets of that mask. The inverse transform guarantees those superset sums equal the supplied inclusive counts, so every requested cardinality is realized. This proof certifies arbitrary finite sets, not a requested geometric representation by circles or a separate probabilistic independence property. Result. Construct disjoint objects per mask.

questions.title: Question 81. Subset-transform invariant and cost
questions.text: Question 81. Subset-transform invariant and cost Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Explain why the bitwise subtraction transform recovers exact atoms from inclusive intersections, and state its complexity. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Before processing a bit, each count includes membership in its mask and already excludes previously processed outside bits. Subtracting the superset with the current bit removes outcomes having that extra membership. Masks containing the bit are not modified at that stage, so their role as the needed superset count is preserved. After all bits, each count enforces every membership and nonmembership. There are m stages and half of the 2^ m masks are updated at each stage: O(m 2^m) integer arithmetic operations and O(2^m) storage. The complexity assumes the complete table is already supplied. It does not account for obtaining each intersection from an implicit event description. Result. O(m 2^m) time; O(2^m) space.

questions.text: Question 82. A mixed-model diagnosis Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A solution counts bounded distributions of ten distinct balls into three boxes using one stars-and-bars count per occupancy vector. Identify the error and give the correct general expression. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Distinct balls distinguish assignments even when their occupancy vectors agree. A vector (x1,x2,x3) represents ten factorial divided by the product of the three occupancy factorials assignments. The correct count is ∑ x 1 + x 2 + x 3 = 10 , 0 ≤ x i ≤ c i 10 ! / ( x 1 ! x 2 ! x 3 ! ) , where the caps must be supplied. A unit weight per vector counts identical-token allocations instead. Inclusion-exclusion on vector counts cannot silently change those unit weights into assignment counts. Without numerical caps, no single numeric answer is determined. An exact multinomial occupancy sum or labeled-map enumeration preserves the specified universe. Result. Use multinomial weights, not unit vector weights.

questions.title: Question 1. A subset containing an odd pair sum
questions.text: Question 1. A subset containing an odd pair sum Authentic examination revisit · checked English adaptation Phd CS 1404 · Q25 · PDF page 7 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. How many four-element subsets A of { 1 , 2 , … , 10 } contain two elements x , y such that x + y is odd? 1. 200 2. 205 3. 208 4. 209 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. There are ( 10 4 ) = 210 four-element subsets. A pair has odd sum exactly when its values have opposite parity. The only failures are all-even and all-odd selections. Each parity class has five elements, so failures number 2 ( 5 4 ) = 10 . The answer is 210 - 10 = 200 , printed option 1. Four selections do not universally force opposite parity: four even values are a counterexample. Six distinct selections would force it because either single parity class has capacity five. This authentic problem counts successful subsets; it does not ask for the universal pigeonhole threshold.

questions.title: Question 2. Worst-case search for an odd three-digit password
questions.text: Question 2. Worst-case search for an odd three-digit password Authentic examination revisit · checked English adaptation MS CS 1405 · Q116 · PDF page 25 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. A combination lock has an unknown odd three-digit password whose digits are chosen from 1 through 9. Each trial takes two minutes. What is the maximum time required, in hours? 1. 12 2. 12.5 3. 13 4. 13.5 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. The first two digits each have nine choices. Oddness restricts only the final digit, which has five choices: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Repetition is permitted because distinctness is not stated. Thus there are 9 · 9 · 5 = 405 candidate passwords. In the worst case the correct password is the last candidate tried, and the successful final trial also takes two minutes. The time is 405 · 2 = 810 minutes, or 810 / 60 = 13.5 hours, printed option 4. This is a finite worst-case search bridge problem, not a direct repeated-class pigeonhole question. The conclusion assumes a systematic search without repeated trials and no additional feedback eliminating candidates.

questions.title: Question 3. What the finite-function theorem actually forces
questions.text: Question 3. What the finite-function theorem actually forces Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Independent reconstruction of Stanford CS103 Winter 2026 Lecture 11 A total function maps seven distinct objects to five labels. Which property is forced for every such function? 1. Noninjective 2. Injective 3. Surjective 4. Not surjective Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. If the function were injective, its seven images would be distinct elements of a five-element set, which is impossible. Surjectivity is not forced: a constant function uses only one label. It is not ruled out either: send the first five objects to distinct labels and repeat two labels afterwards. The forced conclusion is a repeated image, hence noninjectivity. Equal output labels do not make the original objects identical. Conclusion. Noninjective.

questions.title: Question 4. An inclusive calendar model
questions.text: Question 4. An inclusive calendar model Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium Independent reconstruction of Cornell CS2800 §4.5 Assume 366 possible birthday dates. Among 800 people, what is the largest occupancy guaranteed independently of their birthdays? 1. 2 2. 4 3. 800 4. 3 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. The 800 people are objects and the 366 dates are labels. Since 800 = 2 · 366 + 68 , the ceiling of 800 / 366 is 3. A distribution with 68 dates containing three people and 298 containing two has total 800 and maximum three, so four cannot be universally required. The answer is a deterministic bound. No assumption of uniform birthday probabilities is needed. Conclusion. 3.

questions.title: Question 5. ID sums with a fixed first digit
questions.text: Question 5. ID sums with a fixed first digit Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 6.042J §14. 8 / re lated class problems Each of 75 nine-digit ID strings begins with digit 9. Digits may repeat, and each student sums all nine digits. How many sum labels are possible, and what repeated-sum occupancy is guaranteed? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The remaining eight digits range from 0 to 9, so the sum lies between 9 and 9 + 8 · 9 = 81 inclusive. This gives 81 - 9 + 1 = 73 labels. Every integer sum in this range is realizable: distribute the desired increment among eight slots, each holding at most nine. The digits being ordered does not introduce extra sum labels. There are 75 objects and 73 labels, so two sums coincide. Three are not forced because a vector with two doubled labels and 71 single labels has total 75. Counting 81 labels by omitting the minimum, or counting 72 by omitting an endpoint, changes the guarantee. Conclusion. 73 labels; occupancy 2.

questions.title: Question 6. A stronger residue occupancy
questions.text: Question 6. A stronger residue occupancy Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 6.042J §14. 8 / re lated class problems Among 100 integers, how many are guaranteed to have the same remainder modulo 37? 1. 37 2. 3 3. 2 4. 4 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. There are exactly 37 canonical remainder labels. Division gives 100 = 2 · 37 + 26 , so some remainder class contains at least 3 positions. Two members in this class have a difference divisible by 37. Three equal residue labels do not require three equal numerical values. The balanced residue occupancies are 26 classes of size three and eleven of size two. Distinct integers with those residues can be chosen by adding multiples of 37, so the guarantee three is sharp. Conclusion. 3.

questions.title: Question 7. Thirty bounded positive values
questions.text: Question 7. Thirty bounded positive values Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 18.310 Pigeonhole Principle lecture Thirty positive integers are all less than 10 7 . Use an exact image-size comparison to show that disjoint nonempty equal-sum index subsets exist. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The total is at most 30 ( 10 7 - 1 ) = 299999970 . questions.text: Question 8. A symmetric monotone guarantee Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 18.310 Pigeonhole Principle lecture A sequence contains 37 distinct real values. What is the largest universally guaranteed length of an increasing or decreasing subsequence? 1. 6 2. 8 3. 37 4. 7 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. The product-label theorem forces a monotone subsequence of length ⌈ 37 ⌉ = 7 . Equivalently, 37 is one more than 6 2 . To exclude a guarantee of eight, use seven descending blocks with at most seven elements each and keep 37 values. Each increasing subsequence uses at most seven blocks and each decreasing subsequence stays within a block of at most seven. The theorem supplies either direction. A completely decreasing input shows why it cannot force increasing length seven specifically. Conclusion. 7.

questions.title: Question 9. Divisibility among 101 selections
questions.text: Question 9. Divisibility among 101 selections Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Toronto MAT344 Lecture 7 §4 Choose 101 distinct integers from { 1 , … , 200 } . Prove that one divides another, and show that 100 selections need not have this property. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Write each selected integer as a power of two times its odd part. The possible odd parts are the 100 odd integers from 1 through 199. Two distinct selections share an odd part. Their powers of two differ, so the smaller divides the larger. The 100 integers from 101 through 200 form a counterexample: a proper multiple of any of them exceeds 200. Hence the threshold 101 is exact. Grouping by parity alone would only prove matching parity, not divisibility. Conclusion. 101.

questions.text: Question 10. Triangle proximity and a counterexample Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Oxford Discrete Mathematics §6. 5 / Ex ercises 6.7–6.8 What is the minimum number of points in a closed unit equilateral triangle that forces two at distance at most 1 / 2 ? 1. 8 2. 5 3. 4 4. 6 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. Joining the side midpoints partitions the triangle into four equilateral cells of side one-half. Assign any shared boundary point to the first containing cell in a fixed ordering. Five points place two in one cell, whose diameter is one-half. Therefore five suffice. The three vertices and the centroid give four points with smallest pair distance 1 / 3 > 1 / 2 . Thus four do not suffice. A strict distance smaller than one-half is not what the cell-diameter proof establishes. Conclusion. 5.

questions.title: Question 11. Saturated workshop attendance
questions.text: Question 11. Saturated workshop attendance Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Stanford CS103 Winter 2026 Lecture 11 Twenty people attend at most three of four workshops. The four attendance totals are 18,16,14,12. How many people necessarily attend at least one of any two specified workshops? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The total number of attendance incidences is 18 + 16 + 14 + 12 = 60 . The sum of personal capacities is 20 · 3 = 60 . Every person must therefore reach the capacity three: if one attended fewer, no other person could compensate by attending more than three. A person missing both specified workshops could attend at most the other two, contradicting exactly three. Thus all twenty satisfy the conclusion. This does not imply everyone attends both specified workshops; some can miss one of them. Conclusion. 20.

The friends-and-strangers threshold Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Stanford CS103 Winter 2026 Lecture 11 Find the least party size forcing either three mutual acquaintances or three mutual strangers. Every pair has exactly one of the two relationships. 1. 5 2. 7 3. 8 4. 6 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. At a person in a six-person party, the five incident relationships have two labels, so at least three share a label. Suppose these are acquaintance relationships to three people. For five people, let acquaintance edges form a five-cycle. Its complement is another five-cycle; neither contains a triangle. Thus five fail and six suffice. Conclusion. 6.

questions.title: Question 13. Sevens followed by zeros
questions.text: Question 13. Sevens followed by zeros Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 6.042J §14. 8 / re lated class problems Construct a positive multiple of 8 consisting of one or more decimal digits 7 followed by one or more zeros. Explain the residue collision. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The numbers 777 and 7777 both have remainder 1 modulo 8. Their difference is 7777 - 777 = 7000 . The quotient is 7000 / 8 = 875 . Removing a common suffix of three sevens produces one seven followed by three zeros, so the requested form is satisfied. An all-sevens multiple of 8 is impossible because its last digit is odd. The zeros cannot be discarded without checking coprimality with the decimal base. Conclusion. 7000.

questions.title: Question 14. Products as modular labels
questions.text: Question 14. Products as modular labels Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Oxford Discrete Mathematics §6. 5 / Ex ercises 6.7–6.8 A set has ten positive indexed elements. Show that two distinct index subsets have congruent products modulo 512. Must common factors be cancelable? Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are 2 10 = 1024 index subsets, including the empty subset whose product is 1. Product remainders have only 512 labels. A repeated label is unavoidable, irrespective of whether the values are coprime to 512. The subsets are distinct even if some numerical values repeat. Cancellation is a separate issue. If the common product has a factor 2, it is not invertible modulo 512; a congruence c u ≡ c v does not then imply u ≡ v . The proof asserts a pair of subset products, not necessarily a single nonempty subset with product zero modulo 512. Conclusion. Collision guaranteed; cancellation not guaranteed.

  1. The avoidance capacities are (2,4,3), because each cap is the minimum of inventory and one less than its target. Their total is 9.

Conclusion. 10.

questions.text: Question 23. How many bins must be heavy? Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Eight bins each have capacity six. Place 31 objects. A bin is heavy when it contains at least three. Find the minimum possible number of heavy bins. 1. 4 2. 1 3. 3 4. 5 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. If h bins are heavy, the total is at most 6 h + 2 ( 8 - h ) = 16 + 4 h . Hence 31 ≤ 16 + 4 h , giving h ≥ 4 . The vector six, six, six, five, two, two, two, two totals 31 and has exactly four heavy bins. All capacities are respected. A simple ceiling of 31 divided by eight only forces one large bin; it does not determine the number of heavy bins. Conclusion. 4.

questions.title: Question 24. Full capacity implies every bin is heavy
questions.text: Question 24. Full capacity implies every bin is heavy Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Place twenty objects in five bins of capacity four. How many bins contain at least three? 1. 1 2. 3 3. 4 4. 5 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. The total equals the sum of the capacities. Every deficit from four is nonnegative and the deficits sum to zero. All five bins therefore contain exactly four objects, and all are heavy. The general heavy-bin bound also gives ⌈ ( 20 - 5 · 2 ) / ( 4 - 2 ) ⌉ = 5 , consistent with saturation. Conclusion. 5.

Unequal saturation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Three bins have capacities ( 2 , 3 , 5 ) and jointly contain ten objects. Determine their occupancies. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Write the three deficits from capacity. They are nonnegative integers whose sum is two plus three plus five minus ten, namely zero. Every deficit is zero, giving occupancy two, three, five. The conclusion does not require equal capacities or a uniform average. The balanced unrestricted vector would violate the first capacity, so unrestricted balancing is not the relevant construction. Conclusion. 2,3,5.

questions.title: Question 27. Strictness when the mean is an integer
questions.text: Question 27. Strictness when the mean is an integer Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Twenty-one objects occupy seven unrestricted bins. Is a bin with more than three objects forced? 1. Not forced 2. Forced in every distribution 3. Every bin is above the mean 4. Every bin is below the mean Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. The mean is three. The distribution with exactly three in every bin is allowed and has no occupancy strictly above the mean. Therefore the strict claim is false, although the weak claim at least three is true. In any particular distribution, a value above the mean exists if and only if one below it exists. The equal vector has neither. Conclusion. Not forced.

questions.title: Question 28. Nonintegral mean forces both strict directions
questions.text: Question 28. Nonintegral mean forces both strict directions Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Twenty-two objects occupy seven bins. Must some bin be above the mean and another below it? 1. Only the above direction is forced 2. Only the below direction is forced 3. Neither is forced 4. Both are forced Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. The mean is 22 / 7 , which is not an integer. Integer occupancies cannot all equal this value. If no occupancy were above the mean, every occupancy would be at most three and the total at most twenty-one, a contradiction. Thus an above-average occupancy exists. If none were below the mean, every occupancy would be at least four and the total at least twenty-eight. A below-average occupancy also exists. Conclusion. Both are forced.

questions.title: Question 29. Fractional loads cannot be rounded into objects
questions.text: Question 29. Fractional loads cannot be rounded into objects Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Two servers carry total real load 0.8. Does the pigeonhole average prove a server carries at least one unit? 1. Yes, if the loads are equal 2. No server can reach 0.4 3. No; 0.4 is the sharp lower bound 4. Yes, by taking the ceiling Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 3. A server must carry at least the mean 0.4, but the loads need not be integers. The vector 0.4,0.4 meets the total and has no load of one. Thus rounding the mean upward to one is invalid. The ceiling bound applies to discrete counts; real weights retain the unrounded average inequality. Conclusion. No; 0.4 is the sharp lower bound.

questions.title: Question 30. Capacity-weighted utilization
questions.text: Question 30. Capacity-weighted utilization Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Bins have positive capacities ( 2 , 4 , 6 ) and nonnegative loads totaling nine. What maximum-utilization lower bound follows, where utilization is load divided by capacity? 1. 1 2. 3/4 3. 1/2 4. 9/3 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. If every utilization were less than 9 / ( 2 + 4 + 6 ) = 3 / 4 , multiply each inequality by its positive capacity and add. The total load would be less than nine. Thus some utilization is at least three-quarters. Loads one-and-a-half, three, four-and-a-half attain equality if real loads are permitted. An unweighted mean of the three utilizations does not equal nine divided by total capacity unless extra relations are assumed. Conclusion. 3/4 .

There are 2 12 = 4096 possible output words. An injection from 4097 keys into these outputs is impossible. With 4096 keys, a function can assign each a different output. Thus 4097 is the exact universal threshold. This does not claim a particular hash function first collides at that input count; it may collide much earlier. Conclusion. 4097.

questions.title: Question 40. Four equal birthdays
questions.text: Question 40. Four equal birthdays Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Under 366 possible birthday dates, what is the least group size forcing four people with a common birthday? 1. 1098 2. 1464 3. 1100 4. 1099 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. questions.title: Question 41. Strictly shorter binary codes
questions.text: Question 41. Strictly shorter binary codes Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem How many distinct ten-bit messages can at most be assigned injectively to binary strings of length strictly less than ten, when the empty string is permitted? 1. 1024 2. 1022 3. 1023 4. 512 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 3. The available output count is 1 + 2 + … + 2 9 = 2 10 - 1 = 1023 . Injectivity cannot assign more messages than that. This bound is attained for a chosen restricted set of 1023 messages by matching them bijectively to the 1023 short outputs. All 1024 ten-bit messages cannot be shortened at once. Counting only outputs of length nine would miss the shorter permitted outputs; counting length ten would violate strict shortening. Conclusion. 1023.

questions.title: Question 42. Convert a prefix collision into indices
questions.text: Question 42. Convert a prefix collision into indices Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem For modulus five and values ( 3 , 4 , 2 , 7 , 1 ) , scan prefixes from the start and use the first repeated remainder. Give the resulting one-based block and its sum. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Prefix remainders including the empty prefix are zero,three,two,four,one,two. The first collision pairs prefix indices two and five. Subtracting these prefixes retains entries three through five, not entry two. Their sum is two plus seven plus one, namely ten. The endpoints are ordered and different, so the block is nonempty. Ten is divisible by five, providing a verifiable certificate. Conclusion. Positions 3–5; sum 10.

questions.title: Question 43. Difference versus sum
questions.text: Question 43. Difference versus sum Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Eight integers are selected. What is forced modulo seven: a divisible difference or a divisible sum? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The eight positions have only seven remainder labels. Two different positions therefore have equal remainders. Subtracting their values gives remainder zero. Adding their values instead gives twice their common remainder, which need not be zero. For a counterexample to the sum claim, choose eight distinct integers all congruent to one modulo seven. Every two-element sum has remainder two. Conclusion. A divisible difference, not necessarily a divisible sum.

questions.text: Question 44. Equal remainders need not sum to zero Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem The numbers 1 and 6 have the same remainder modulo five. Does their sum or their difference give a zero remainder? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Both remainder labels are one. The difference six minus one is five and is divisible by five. The sum is seven and has remainder two. The equality of labels supports subtraction, not arbitrary combination. For a sum argument one instead groups complementary remainders, taking care with remainder zero and a possible self-complementary class. Conclusion. Difference only.

Their five prefix remainders, including the empty prefix, are zero,one,two,three,four. No remainder repeats. Every nonempty block has length between one and four and, because all entries are one, has the same sum as its length. None is divisible by five. questions.text: Question 46. The first all-ones multiple Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Find the shortest positive decimal all-ones multiple of seven. 1. 1110 2. 111111 3. 11111 4. 1111111 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. questions.title: Question 47. A zero-one multiple without decimal invertibility
questions.text: Question 47. A zero-one multiple without decimal invertibility Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Use a repeated repunit remainder to construct a decimal zero-one multiple of six. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The repunits of lengths one and four have equal remainder one modulo six. Their difference is 1111 minus 1, namely 1110. This difference is 6 · 185 . It has only zero and one digits and is positive. An all-ones multiple cannot exist because every repunit is odd. Multiplication by ten cannot be canceled modulo six; that obstruction is compatible with the zero-one construction. Conclusion. 1110.

questions.title: Question 48. A base obstruction
questions.text: Question 48. A base obstruction Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Can a positive decimal repunit be divisible by ten? 1. Length ten works 2. Length eleven works 3. Every length works 4. Impossible Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. Its final digit is one, so its remainder modulo ten is one, irrespective of length. Therefore no positive length works. The existence theorem for all-ones multiples requires the modulus to be coprime with ten. The broader zero-one theorem remains true: ten itself is a zero-one multiple. The two statements have different hypotheses. Conclusion. Impossible.

questions.title: Question 49. Modular cancellation needs a unit
questions.text: Question 49. Modular cancellation needs a unit Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Modulo six, 2 · 1 ≡ 2 · 4 . May the factor two be canceled? 1. Yes, in any modulus 2. Only if both products are positive 3. No 4. Yes, because two is nonzero Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 3. Both products have remainder two, but one and four have different remainders. Thus cancellation would assert a false congruence. The factor has gcd ( 2 , 6 ) = 2 and has no multiplicative inverse modulo six. Cancellation would only yield equality modulo three here. In a prime modulus every nonzero factor is a unit; in a composite modulus nonzero alone is insufficient. Conclusion. No.

questions.title: Question 50. Overlapping square images
questions.text: Question 50. Overlapping square images Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Oxford Discrete Mathematics §6. 5 / Ex ercises 6.7–6.8 How many residues occur as x 2 modulo eleven, and why does x 2 + y 2 ≡ - 1 ( mod 11 ) have a solution? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The square image is zero,one,three,four,five,nine: six values. Pairing each nonzero x with its negative explains the image size six. The second image minus one minus a square also has six values in an eleven-element universe. Two six-element subsets must intersect. One certificate is x equals one and y equals three: their squares sum to ten, which equals minus one modulo eleven. This is an existence proof plus a checked witness. Conclusion. 6 residues; a solution exists.

A composite counterexample Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Does x 2 + y 2 ≡ - 1 ( mod 8 ) have an integer solution? 1. questions.title: Question 53. Equal sums with an explicit cancellation
questions.text: Question 53. Equal sums with an explicit cancellation Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem For indexed values ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ) , give two disjoint nonempty equal-sum subsets and explain the counting proof. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The sixteen index subsets have sums in the eleven labels zero through ten. A collision follows from 16 > 11 . The subsets containing values one and four, and values two and three, both sum to five and are disjoint. If a counting collision initially shared indices, subtract their common contribution from both sides. Positivity ensures neither residual side is empty when the original subsets are distinct. Conclusion. 1+4=2+3 .

Fixed-cardinality subset sums Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Among four-element subsets of { 1 , … , 8 } , show that at least two have equal sum. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are ( 8 4 ) = 70 objects. Their sums range from ten to twenty-six inclusive, so there are at most seventeen sum labels. Seventy exceeds seventeen; therefore two distinct four-element subsets have the same sum. For example one,two,seven,eight and one,three,six,eight both sum to eighteen. Canceling the common values one and eight yields two plus seven equals three plus six. Equal size survives cancellation, although the residual size need not remain four. Conclusion. Guaranteed.

Question 55. Fixed-cardinality subset sums

Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard

Original examination-style problem

Among four-element subsets of {1,…,8}, show that at least two have equal sum.

Read the complete derivation and reasoning

  1. There are (84)=70 objects. Their sums range from ten to twenty-six inclusive, so there are at most seventeen sum labels.

  2. Seventy exceeds seventeen; therefore two distinct four-element subsets have the same sum. For example one,two,seven,eight and one,three,six,eight both sum to eighteen.

  3. Canceling the common values one and eight yields two plus seven equals three plus six. Equal size survives cancellation, although the residual size need not remain four.

Conclusion. Guaranteed.

questions.title: Question 56. A subset collision is not a zero sum
questions.text: Question 56. A subset collision is not a zero sum Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem For indexed values ( 2 , 2 ) modulo three, two singleton subset sums coincide. Must a nonempty subset have sum zero? 1. Yes, by subtracting labels 2. Yes, the pair works 3. Only a singleton works 4. No Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. The two singleton index subsets are distinct and each has remainder two, so a collision exists. The nonempty sums are two,two,four, whose remainders are two,two,one. None is zero. Subtracting collided sums gives equality between two disjoint subsets, not a positive sum of selected entries. The contiguous-prefix theorem has an additional nesting property that arbitrary subsets lack. Conclusion. No.

questions.title: Question 57. Cancelable product images
questions.text: Question 57. Cancelable product images Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Take indexed values ( 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ) modulo seventeen. Show that two distinct subsets have equal product remainder and state what cancellation preserves. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are thirty-two subsets and seventeen remainder labels, so distinct subsets collide. The empty product is one. Every chosen value is nonzero modulo the prime seventeen and hence invertible. The product of common indices is also invertible and may be canceled. The residual subsets are disjoint and remain distinct. One side can be empty, since positivity of ordinary products does not exclude a nonempty modular product of one. Conclusion. Collision with valid cancellation.

questions.title: Question 58. Why positivity was stated
questions.text: Question 58. Why positivity was stated Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem The indexed list consists only of the value zero. Two subset sums coincide. Does this yield two disjoint nonempty equal-sum subsets? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The empty subset and the singleton both sum to zero. These are the only subsets. Two disjoint nonempty subsets are impossible because there is only one index. The collision therefore cannot meet the strengthened conclusion. Strictly positive entries rule out an empty residual side with sum equal to a nonempty side; nonnegative entries alone do not. Conclusion. No.

questions.title: Question 59. Complementary pairs without a fixed point
questions.text: Question 59. Complementary pairs without a fixed point Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem What is the least number of distinct selections from 1 through 20 that forces a pair summing to 21? 1. 11 2. 10 3. 12 4. 20 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. Partition the twenty values into ten disjoint complement pairs: one with twenty through ten with eleven. Eleven distinct selections force two in one pair. Ten can avoid the target by taking exactly one member per pair, for example one through ten. The bins contain two distinct complementary values; choosing repeated copies of one value would not provide the same proof. Conclusion. 11.

questions.title: Question 60. A self-complementary value changes the count
questions.text: Question 60. A self-complementary value changes the count Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem What is the least number of distinct selections from 1 through 21 forcing two distinct selected values summing to 22? 1. 11 2. 10 3. 21 4. 12 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. There are ten two-element complement pairs and the singleton eleven. The singleton cannot supply a pair of distinct values. An avoiding selection may take one value from each pair and also eleven, giving eleven selected values. Twelve force a completed pair. The values one through eleven give an attaining counterexample at eleven. Treating the singleton as an ordinary two-element pair would create a false answer. Conclusion. 12.

questions.title: Question 61. Construct the actual divisibility witness
questions.text: Question 61. Construct the actual divisibility witness Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Find a divisibility pair in ( 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 10 , 11 , 12 ) by grouping odd parts. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The odd parts are respectively one,five,three,seven,one,five,eleven,three. The first repeated odd part is one at values four and eight. The smaller divides the larger, with quotient two. There are other witnesses: five divides ten, and six divides twelve. Equal parity by itself would not identify these divisibility chains. Conclusion. 4 divides 8.

questions.title: Question 62. The sharp avoiding half interval
questions.text: Question 62. The sharp avoiding half interval Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Why do the twenty values 21 through 40 contain no pair of distinct values where one divides the other? Read the complete derivation and reasoning A proper positive multiple of a selected value is at least twice that value, hence at least forty-two. Every selected value is at most forty, so such a multiple cannot lie in the selection. The full interval one through forty has twenty odd-part chains. This example attains one value from each without a divisibility pair, proving the twenty-one threshold sharp. Conclusion. No proper multiple remains in the interval.

questions.title: Question 63. Consecutive integers with an odd endpoint
questions.text: Question 63. Consecutive integers with an odd endpoint Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Find the smallest number of distinct selections from 1 through 15 forcing two consecutive integers. 1. 9 2. 8 3. 10 4. 15 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. An avoiding set can contain the eight odd values one,three through fifteen. Thus eight are insufficient. Group the interval into seven adjacent pairs and the singleton fifteen. At most one selection from each of these eight groups avoids completing an adjacent pair. Nine force a completed pair. Other consecutive pairs cross group boundaries, but ignoring them cannot invalidate this sufficient bound, and the odd set proves sharpness. Conclusion. 9.

Consecutiveness supplies a coprime witness Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Oxford Discrete Mathematics §6. 5 / Ex ercises 6.7–6.8 Show that eleven distinct selections from 1 through 20 force a coprime pair, and show ten may fail. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The ten adjacent pairs one,two through nineteen,twenty force a completed pair under eleven selections. Consecutive integers have greatest common divisor one, so the pair is a coprime witness. The ten even values have pairwise greatest common divisor at least two. They prove that ten cannot give the universal coprime guarantee. Conclusion. 11.

questions.title: Question 65. Chains by powers of three
questions.text: Question 65. Chains by powers of three Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 6.042J §14. 8 / re lated class problems Choose 201 distinct positive integers less than 300. Show that the quotient of two is a positive integral power of three. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Write each value uniquely as a power of three times a core not divisible by three. Among one through 299, there are 299 minus ninety-nine, namely two hundred possible cores. Two hundred and one selections force equal cores. Distinct values with one core have different exponents. Dividing the larger by the smaller gives three raised to a positive exponent. This establishes sufficiency without claiming the selected number is the unique sharp threshold for every variant. Conclusion. 200.

questions.title: Question 66. A sufficient grid threshold is not an optimum theorem
questions.text: Question 66. A sufficient grid threshold is not an optimum theorem Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Use a square grid to force two points in a closed unit square at distance at most one-quarter. What is the best threshold from this equal-grid method? 1. 17 2. 37 3. 36 4. 33 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. With r divisions along each axis, the cell diameter is 2 / r . To make it at most one-quarter, r must be at least six. The six-by-six grid has thirty-six cells. Thirty-seven points force two in one cell, whose distance meets the requested bound. This is the least threshold among these equal axis-aligned grids. It is not a proof that thirty-seven is the smallest threshold among all geometric arguments or all point configurations. Conclusion. 37.

questions.title: Question 67. A rectangular partition
questions.text: Question 67. A rectangular partition Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A closed rectangle has side lengths six and four. Divide it into three columns and two rows. How many points suffice to force distance at most 2 2 ? 1. 7 2. 6 3. 8 4. 12 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. The partition has six cells, each a square of side two and diameter two times the square root of two. Assign shared-boundary points to a fixed containing cell. Seven points force two in the same cell and hence the stated distance bound. Six points need not collide in a cell, but that observation alone does not prove the global geometric threshold is seven. The claim is sufficient, tied to this partition. Conclusion. 7.

questions.title: Question 68. A numerical approximation certificate
questions.text: Question 68. A numerical approximation certificate Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem For α = 2 and m equals five, exhibit integers q , p with one at most q at most five and | q α - p | < 1 / 5 . Read the complete derivation and reasoning The fractional parts of zero through five multiples of the square root of two share one of five half-open interval labels. In particular the fractional parts at indices zero and five are close. Take q equal to five and p equal to seven. The error is 5 2 - 7 , about 0.071068, which is positive and less than 0.2. Dividing by q gives | 2 - 7 / 5 | < 1 / 25 . The theorem bounds this rational error by 1 / ( m q ) , not by the original unscaled 1 / m . Conclusion. q=5 , p=7 .

questions.title: Question 70. An asymmetric monotone threshold
questions.text: Question 70. An asymmetric monotone threshold Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Toronto MAT344 Lecture 7 §4 Find the least length forcing a strictly increasing subsequence of length five or a strictly decreasing subsequence of length seven, when all entries are distinct. 1. 36 2. 25 3. 24 4. 35 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. Avoidance requires increasing ending length at most four and decreasing ending length at most six. Each distinct entry receives a different ordered pair of these labels. The twenty-four possible pairs permit at most twenty-four entries. Twenty-five force the desired conclusion. Four descending blocks of six values, with every block larger than the preceding block, attain twenty-four without either target. This proves necessity as well as sufficiency. Conclusion. 25.

questions.title: Question 71. A sharp short monotone construction
questions.text: Question 71. A sharp short monotone construction Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem For the sequence ( 2 , 1 , 4 , 3 , 6 , 5 ) , compute the longest increasing and decreasing subsequence lengths. 1. LIS 3; LDS 2 2. LIS 4; LDS 2 3. LIS 3; LDS 3 4. LIS 2; LDS 3 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. An increasing subsequence takes at most one value from each descending two-element block. Taking one,two-block representative values one,three,five attains length three. A decreasing subsequence cannot cross into a later block, because every later value is larger. Inside a block its length is at most two, attained by two,one. Thus LIS is three and LDS is two. Six is the sharp avoiding length for targets increasing four or decreasing three. Conclusion. LIS 3; LDS 2.

questions.title: Question 73. Duplicate values break the strict theorem
questions.text: Question 73. Duplicate values break the strict theorem Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem A sequence has twenty equal values. Does the distinct-entry monotone theorem force a strictly monotone subsequence of length five? 1. Yes, strict length twenty 2. No weak subsequence exists 3. No; strict maximum is one 4. Yes, strict length five Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 3. Every strict increasing or strict decreasing subsequence has length one, because every comparison is equality. Its weakly nondecreasing subsequence has length twenty. The weak conclusion differs from the strict one. With duplicates one can use a mixed nondecreasing/decreasing theorem, or explicitly specify tie handling. The distinctness hypothesis cannot simply be deleted. Conclusion. No; strict maximum is one.

Subsequence does not mean contiguous Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem For ( 1 , 4 , 2 , 5 , 3 , 6 ) , compare the longest increasing subsequence and the longest increasing contiguous block. questions.title: Question 76. Degree labels and their forbidden coexistence
questions.text: Question 76. Degree labels and their forbidden coexistence Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of Stanford CS103 Winter 2026 Lecture 11 Why do nine vertices in a simple undirected graph force repeated degree, while a directed tournament can have all distinct outdegrees? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The undirected degree labels are zero through eight, but zero and eight cannot coexist: a degree-eight vertex would connect to the supposedly isolated one. At most eight labels are usable simultaneously for nine vertices, so a repeated degree follows. Orient a nine-vertex complete graph from the lower ordered vertex to the higher. Its outdegrees are eight,seven through zero, all distinct. The undirected exclusion does not apply to outdegree. Conclusion. Repeated undirected degree; distinct tournament outdegrees possible.

questions.title: Question 77. The five-cycle Ramsey counterexample
questions.text: Question 77. The five-cycle Ramsey counterexample Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem Color a complete graph on five vertices red on a cycle and blue on its complement. How many monochromatic triangles occur? 1. 2 2. 5 3. 0 4. 1 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 3. A five-cycle contains no triangle, so no triple has all three edges red. Its complement is also a five-cycle and likewise has no triangle. Thus no triple has all edges blue. The count is zero. This is an actual lower-bound certificate for the six-vertex Ramsey theorem, not merely a failure of the star argument at five. Conclusion. 0.

questions.title: Question 78. A sharp three-color rectangle threshold
questions.text: Question 78. A sharp three-color rectangle threshold Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 6.042J §14. 8 / re lated class problems A grid has four columns, arbitrary rows, and three colors. Find the least row count forcing a rectangle whose four corners have one color. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Each row has four entries and only three colors, so it contains a same-color pair of columns. Choose one such pair and its color as a certificate. There are six column pairs times three colors, namely eighteen certificates. Nineteen rows repeat one, producing the rectangle. For each of the eighteen certificates, construct a row with its chosen pair in its chosen color and the other two cells in the other two colors. It has exactly that one same-color pair, so different rows never repeat a certificate. Eighteen avoid the rectangle, proving sharpness. Conclusion. 19.

questions.title: Question 79. The smaller rectangle construction
questions.text: Question 79. The smaller rectangle construction Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem With three columns and two colors, find the sharp row threshold forcing a monochromatic rectangle. 1. 7 2. 6 3. 8 4. 9 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. Every row has a same-color pair. Three column pairs times two colors give six possible certificates. Seven rows repeat a certificate. Six avoiding rows can be formed by taking each certificate once and coloring the remaining singleton with the other color. This construction works because columns equal colors plus one. For more columns, a row may realize multiple certificates, so one cannot automatically claim the same sharp construction. Conclusion. 7.

questions.title: Question 80. Binary decision-tree information
questions.text: Question 80. Binary decision-tree information Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Original examination-style problem At least how many arbitrary truthful yes-no answers are required in the worst case to identify one of one thousand possibilities? 1. 9 2. 11 3. 1000 4. 10 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 4. A binary decision tree of worst-case depth q has at most two to the q leaves. Each possibility needs a distinct leaf. Nine answers support at most 512 leaves, whereas ten support 1024. Thus the minimum is ten if arbitrary subset questions are allowed. A balanced identification strategy realizes this minimum. Restrictions on the permitted questions, or lies, can raise the requirement. Conclusion. 10.

questions.title: Question 81. One lie: a necessary packing bound
questions.text: Question 81. One lie: a necessary packing bound Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 18.310 Pigeonhole Principle lecture With twenty adaptive yes-no questions and at most one lie, what possibility-count upper bound follows from transcript packing? 1. 49933 2. 1048576 3. 49932 4. 52428 Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 3. For a fixed hidden possibility, the truthful run and each choice of one lie position yield twenty-one distinct transcripts. Distinctness follows at the first position where the lie schedules differ. Transcripts belonging to different hidden possibilities must be disjoint for unique decoding. Thus the number of possibilities times twenty-one is at most two raised to twenty. The integer upper bound is 49932. This is a necessary condition; no strategy attaining it has been constructed here. Adaptive transcript sets are not automatically ordinary Hamming balls around a fixed truthful word. Conclusion. 49932.

questions.title: Question 82. The card channel and the impossible variant
questions.text: Question 82. The card channel and the impossible variant Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed hard Independent reconstruction of MIT 6.042J §14. 8 / re lated class problems From five cards in a thirteen-rank four-suit deck, one is hidden and four are ordered visibly. Explain the six-way rank code and why hiding one of only four cards cannot always work in a 52-card deck. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Among five cards, two have the same suit. Their distinct ranks have one directed cyclic gap between one and six. Show the first as an anchor and hide the second. The other three visible cards can be placed in six permutations under an agreed total ordering. Their order encodes the gap; the anchor supplies suit and initial rank, permitting exact decoding. For the four-card variant, an ordered visible triple has at most 52 times 51 times 50 states, while hidden hands number the binomial coefficient of 52 choose 4. The latter is larger: 270725 exceeds 132600. Thus no protocol can uniquely decode every hand. For the five-card variant in an arbitrary n -card deck, a necessary state-count condition gives n at most 124. That upper bound alone does not provide a construction for every such deck. Conclusion. Six rank codes; four-card variant impossible.

questions.title: Question 1. A matrix representation for row and column operations
questions.text: Question 1. A matrix representation for row and column operations Authentic examination revisit · checked English adaptation Phd CE 1405 · Q18 · PDF page 5 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. The outer product of two vectors A = ( a 0 , … , a n - 1 ) and B = ( b 0 , … , b n - 1 ) defines C i j = a i b j . Which listed representation is most suitable when C must be stored in correspondence with the vectors at arbitrary dimension n and matrix addition and multiplication should be straightforward? 1. A circular singly linked list with a head node whose heads are also linked in a list. 2. An orthogonal linked list. 3. A circular singly linked list with a head node. 4. A circular singly linked list. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 2. The question asks for a matrix representation supporting matrix operations, not merely evaluating one entry of a rank-one formula. Orthogonal links organize every represented entry in both its row and column, providing the two traversal directions needed to combine corresponding rows and columns. A row-list hierarchy organizes rows but lacks an explicit column chain. The one-chain choices organize only one successor relation. Thus option 2 is the most suitable listed general matrix representation. Factorized storage of A and B can be smaller for the single outer product, but arbitrary addition is not closed within one outer product and factorization is not among the listed choices. This is a suitability judgment under the question’s general-operation requirement, not a claim that no other representation can perform matrix arithmetic. The answer is independently reasoned; no official key was available.

questions.text: Question 2. Recursive reverse-stride copying Authentic examination revisit · checked English adaptation MS CS 1393 · Q167 · PDF page 34 . Independently derived answer; not an official key. Copy every other element of an N -element array a , starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0) . Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure. 1. if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1); 2. if(n<0)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1); 3. if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+1); 4. if(n<0)return; b[i++]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+2); Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 1. At call depth t , source rank must be N - 1 - 2 t and destination rank t . Option 1 maintains both indices and stops once the source becomes negative, giving ⌈ N / 2 ⌉ writes. Option 2 starts at b [1] and leaves b [0] unwritten. Option 3 copies every element rather than every other element. Option 4 advances the destination by an extra two between calls, in addition to its post-increment behavior, leaving gaps. All source options have the same negative-source stopping guard. Missing parameter declarations are not treated as a compilable-C test. The answer is independently derived, not an official key.

Stable insert and erase in one buffer Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem An array of length 17 and capacity 24 receives a stable insertion at rank 6, then a stable deletion at rank 10. The length becomes 18. Deletion then shifts 18 - 10 - 1 = 7 old slots. Thus there are 18 shifts and 19 element writes. Using the original length for deletion gives an off-by-one error; counting a metadata update as an element write changes the specified model.

An array of length 17 and capacity 24 receives a stable insertion at rank 6, then a stable deletion at rank 10. Count old-slot shifts and new-value writes separately. Do not clear unused reference slots.

Insertion shifts 17-6=11 old slots and writes one new value. The length becomes 18. Deletion then shifts 18-10-1=7 old slots. Thus there are 18 shifts and 19 element writes.
