questions.text: Question 5. Expected insertion work with biased positions Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A length-12 array has spare capacity. questions.title: Question 6. Insertion loop counterexample
questions.text: Question 6. Insertion loop counterexample Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Independent reconstruction of Oxford B16 §3.1 shift invariant For [3,5,7,11] , insert 2 at rank 1 by looping j=1,2,3 with A[j+1]=A[j] , then writing A[1]=2 . Give the actual result and the correct result. Read the complete derivation and reasoning The first copy overwrites 7 with 5; later copies read the overwritten 5, so the actual live array is [3,2,5,5,5] . questions.title: Question 8. Overlapping range movement
questions.text: Question 8. Overlapping range movement Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Move A[2..7] to A[4..9] without temporary storage. Which direction is safe, and what invariant proves it? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The destination lies to the right and overlaps the source, so copy indices 7 down to 2. Each unread source lies at or left of the current source and is not overwritten by the larger destination index. Ascending order would overwrite A[4] before it is read. For a destination to the left, ascending order is safe. There are exactly six slot copies.

questions.title: Question 12. Sublinear capacity increment
questions.text: Question 12. Sublinear capacity increment Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Grow a full buffer of capacity C by approximately C slots. Derive the order of total copy work needed to reach length N . Ignore rounding for the asymptotic derivation. Read the complete derivation and reasoning At capacity scale C , one resize pays C copies and supplies about C future append positions. Thus the local cost per new slot is about C . Summing this scale over positions up to N gives Θ ( ∫ 1 N x d x ) = Θ ( N 3 / 2 ) . A scale argument also proves the lower bound: within the last constant fraction of N , each growth adds at most O ( N ) slots and copies Ω ( N ) slots, forcing Ω ( N ) such events.

questions.title: Question 14. Amortized versus worst case
questions.text: Question 14. Amortized versus worst case Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Independent reconstruction of Princeton COS226 resizing distinction Select the correct claim for doubling arrays under append-only workloads and constant slot-copy cost. 1. Every append has constant worst-case time. 2. Constant amortized time requires random inputs. 3. Append is amortized constant but can be linear individually. 4. Amortization removes all stable insertion shifts. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Correct option: 3. A full buffer of length n must copy n slots, so a single append can take linear time. Across any m appends from an empty structure, geometric sums give linear total work, hence constant amortized cost. This uses deterministic accounting, not random inputs. Real-time latency constraints cannot be inferred from amortization alone.

questions.title: Question 15. Quarter-full contraction accounting
questions.text: Question 15. Quarter-full contraction accounting Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A buffer has length 17 and capacity 64. Deleting its last element triggers half-capacity contraction at one quarter full. Charge one deletion plus live-slot copies. Compute actual cost, potential change, and amortized cost. Read the complete derivation and reasoning After deletion n=16 and capacity becomes 32. Actual cost is 1 + 16 = 17 . Before deletion the sparse-branch potential is 32 - 17 = 15 ; afterward it is zero. Thus amortized cost is 17 - 15 = 2 . Clearing a reference slot or allocation work would require an adjusted actual-cost convention.

questions.title: Question 20. Tail pointer and removal
questions.text: Question 20. Tail pointer and removal Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Independent reconstruction of Berkeley CS61B Chapter 5 tail-removal exercise An acyclic singly linked list stores head, tail, and size. For n>1 , what is the worst-case time to remove tail while preserving node identities? Explain why caching the second-last node once is insufficient for repeated removal. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Tail has no back pointer; its predecessor must be found by a head traversal, costing linear time. A cached second-last handle permits one removal, but after it becomes tail the next predecessor is unknown. Maintaining that extra handle through repeated removals again needs traversal unless a richer structure stores predecessor information.

questions.title: Question 23. Node-only deletion counterexample
questions.text: Question 23. Node-only deletion counterexample Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A singly linked list A→B→C stores external handles to all nodes. The value sequence can match deletion of B , but object identity and handle validity do not. At a tail there is no successor to copy. The contract must distinguish deleting a value position from deleting an object.

questions.title: Question 26. Range splicing and cached size
questions.text: Question 26. Range splicing and cached size Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Move a known consecutive range of 70 nodes between circular doubly linked lists. Endpoints and destination neighbors are supplied, but range length is not supplied to the operation. Each list caches size. Is the entire operation constant time? Sentinel traversal termination Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A circular doubly linked list has sentinel S and three real nodes. questions.title: Question 30. Recursion and storage
questions.text: Question 30. Recursion and storage Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Independent reconstruction of Stanford CS106B Handout 21 reverse-print routine A routine recursively calls itself on next, then prints the current value, without modifying links. questions.title: Question 37. Binary search comparisons versus pointer work
questions.text: Question 37. Binary search comparisons versus pointer work Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem An array and a sorted singly linked list each perform O(log n) key comparisons. The list repeatedly obtains midpoint by get(mid) from global head. Must its total time be O(log n) ? Read the complete derivation and reasoning No. For a search above all keys, midpoint ranks approach n , and Theta(log n ) retrievals each traverse Theta( n ) links, giving Theta( n log n ) link work. Stable compaction exact writes Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Keep nonnegative values from [-2,5,0,-1,8,-3,4]. The compaction algorithm tests each element once and assigns every survivor to the write cursor even when it is already in place. Count tests and assignments and give the live prefix. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are seven predicate tests and four surviving values: 5,0,8,4. Thus four payload assignments produce that live prefix. Write never exceeds read, so no unread value is lost. The old suffix is outside logical length; reference cleanup would add assignments if requested.

questions.title: Question 44. A left rotation with cached tail
questions.text: Question 44. A left rotation with cached tail Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem For a length-17 singly linked list with cached size and tail, left-rotate by 40. Find normalized k , cut rank, and links traversed to reach the cut from head. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Normalize k=40 mod17 = 6. New tail is old rank 5; reaching it takes five next traversals. Save its successor as new head, connect old tail to old head, and set newTail.next = null. This performs two next-field writes after searching. If k=0 , no cut or rewiring is needed.

questions.title: Question 45. Intersection is identity, not equality
questions.text: Question 45. Intersection is identity, not equality Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Two acyclic lists have identical numeric suffixes stored in separately allocated nodes. Will the two-switch cursor intersection algorithm report that suffix as an intersection? Read the complete derivation and reasoning No. It compares node identities; equal payloads in distinct nodes are not shared storage. Both cursors eventually reach null if there is no shared node. Value equality can be tested separately, but it answers a different question. The switching argument also assumes no cycles and no concurrent mutation.

questions.title: Question 46. Node alignment model
questions.text: Question 46. Node alignment model Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Payload is 13 bytes, each pointer is eight bytes, and node alignment is eight. Ignore headers. Find singly and doubly linked node sizes and storage for 100 real nodes plus one sentinel. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Singly linked raw size is 21, rounded to 24. Doubly linked raw size is 29, rounded to 32. The 101-node totals are 2424 and 3232 bytes. Treating alignment as a constant extra eight bytes rather than rounding is incorrect. Array element alignment can require its own separate stride assumption.

questions.title: Question 47. Offset block occupancy
questions.text: Question 47. Offset block occupancy Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A scan begins at slot offset 5 in a cache block of 16 slots and reads 100 consecutive slots. How many distinct blocks are touched? Read the complete derivation and reasoning The span ends after 105 slots measured from the beginning of the first block. Hence blocks touched are ceil(105/16)= 7. Ceil( 100/16 ) = 7 happens to agree here, but with 12 slots from offset 5 the correct answer is 2 while ignoring offset gives 1. The question counts distinct blocks, not a hardware miss prediction with reuse.

questions.title: Question 48. Workload with supplied handles
questions.text: Question 48. Workload with supplied handles Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A workload contains n random rank lookups and n deletions at valid supplied node handles. Compare arrays and doubly linked lists; give a condition under which neither simple choice is obviously best. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Arrays perform rank lookups in Theta( n ) total but stable deletions can cost Theta( n 2 ). Doubly linked lists perform known-node deletions in Theta( n ) total but rank lookups can cost Theta( n 2 ). A workload mixing both capabilities may justify an augmented tree or index; the question provides no dominance ratio or ordering that selects one simple representation universally.

questions.title: Question 49. Sparse outer-product support
questions.text: Question 49. Sparse outer-product support Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Over real numbers, vectors of lengths 50 and 80 have 7 and 9 nonzero entries. How many nonzero entries does their outer product have? How many scalar slots does dense factor storage use? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Every nonzero entry of one factor pairs with every nonzero entry of the other, yielding 7· 9=63 nonzeros. Dense factor storage uses 50+80=130 scalar slots; explicit dense matrix storage uses 4000. The product-support statement depends on a field without zero divisors, not an arbitrary ring.

questions.title: Question 50. Rank-one addition counterexample
questions.text: Question 50. Rank-one addition counterexample Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Show why representing every matrix as a single pair of vectors is not closed under arbitrary addition. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Take two 2×2 matrices with single nonzeros at (0,0) and (1,1), both equal to one. Each is rank one. Their sum is the identity matrix, of rank two, and cannot equal one outer product because all columns of a nonzero outer product are scalar multiples of one vector. A general matrix ADT needs a broader representation.

questions.text: Question 51. questions.title: Question 52. Sorted insertion and duplicate semantics
questions.text: Question 52. Sorted insertion and duplicate semantics Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Independent reconstruction and correction of Stanford CS106B Handout 21 duplicate-policy contrast An iterative routine refuses an existing equal key; a recursive routine inserts before the first key greater than or equal to the new key. Are they equivalent? Give a distinguishing input. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Insert key 4 into [2,4,6]. The iterative set-style routine keeps [2,4,6]; the recursive routine produces [2,4,4,6]. Thus duplicate policy is part of the interface. If allocation happens before detecting a duplicate, rejected storage must be released to avoid a leak. Correct sorted order alone does not establish equivalence.

questions.title: Question 53. Deep-copy versus pointer-copy append
questions.text: Question 53. Deep-copy versus pointer-copy append Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem An array stores pointers to variable-length strings. During growth, it copies pointers, not string contents. What controls resize complexity? What changes if it deep-copies each string? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Pointer-copy growth moves n word-sized slots, so cost is Theta( n ). If strings have lengths ell_ i and each must be duplicated, copying costs Theta(sum ell_ i ), plus pointer work. An operation-count theorem must specify the copied unit. Large values referenced by pointers do not automatically enlarge a slot-copy cost.

questions.title: Question 55. Destruction order safety
questions.text: Question 55. Destruction order safety Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Independent reconstruction of Stanford CS106B Handout 21 destruction routine Why must iterative deletion save next before releasing a node? Does reading a deallocated next field become safe if its old bits appear unchanged? Read the complete derivation and reasoning Once storage is released, the program no longer owns a live node at that address; accessing its fields is invalid under the allocation model and may be undefined in a systems language. Save successor while the node is alive, release the node, then advance through the saved handle. Observing unchanged bits does not restore object lifetime.

questions.title: Question 56. Empty and singleton reversal
questions.text: Question 56. Empty and singleton reversal Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Specify the correct postconditions for reversing an empty list and a singleton list with cached tail. Read the complete derivation and reasoning For empty input, head and tail remain null and size stays zero; the loop performs no link writes. For singleton X , X .next becomes null, head and tail both remain X , and size stays one. The general routine may perform one next write even though the value does not change. A cached tail becomes the saved old head for every nonempty input.

questions.title: Question 57. A splice into its own interior
questions.text: Question 57. A splice into its own interior Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A range B through D in a circular list is to be moved after C . Why cannot a generic six-write cross-list splice be applied without a precondition? Read the complete derivation and reasoning C lies inside the moved range, so its adjacency links are among the links being detached and reused. Treating it as an external destination can introduce a cycle disconnected from the sentinel or duplicate placement. Reject the request or define a no-op policy for interior destinations; ordinary same-list splice proofs require the destination outside the range and handle adjacency separately.

questions.title: Question 58. General fast-speed meeting congruence
questions.text: Question 58. General fast-speed meeting congruence Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem For fast speed r>1 and cycle length lambda, derive the period of meeting times once both pointers are on the cycle. Do not infer entry-reset validity. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Equality requires ( r−1 ) t to be divisible by lambda. Dividing by d=gcd(r−1,lambda) , the reduced coefficients are coprime, so t must be a multiple of lambda/d. The first permitted meeting must also be positive and at least mu. This detects collision but does not force t divisible by lambda when d>1 ; standard reset may fail.

questions.title: Question 60. Fused resizing insertion
questions.text: Question 60. Fused resizing insertion Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Resize a full n -slot array while inserting at rank i . Show an implementation using n old-slot copies rather than n+ ( n−i ) copies. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Allocate the new buffer. Copy old positions below i to unchanged ranks; copy positions at or above i directly to rank j+1 ; write x at i . Every old element is copied once, for n copies plus one new write. The original buffer remains read-only until replacement, so overlapping-copy ordering is unnecessary. Nonresizing insertion still has n−i shifts.

questions.title: Question 61. Unrolled-list tradeoff
questions.text: Question 61. Unrolled-list tradeoff Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A sequence stores contiguous blocks of B elements in a linked chain. Locating a rank scans block links; insertion can shift within one block. Derive the balancing scale for cost O(n/B+B) , ignoring splits and rounding. Read the complete derivation and reasoning There are roughly n/B blocks, giving O(n/B) link work; moving within a block costs O(B) . Balancing n/B and B gives B≈sq rt( n ), with O (sqrt( n )) combined work. This is a simplified model, not a full implementation proof: block occupancy, splits, size metadata, and changing n need separate invariants.

questions.title: Question 62. Stable deduplication of a sorted array
questions.text: Question 62. Stable deduplication of a sorted array Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A sorted array of length n is compacted to one representative of each of k distinct values. Derive comparisons and worst retained writes for a one-pass algorithm that keeps the first value. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Compare each later value against the last kept representative, yielding n−1 equality comparisons for n>0 . Each new distinct value may require one write, so there are k retained assignments if the initial value is assigned too, or at most k−1 if it is already kept in place. Adversarial versus random amortization Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem An adversary chooses the times of appends and last-element deletions for a doubling/quarter-shrinking array. Can it invalidate the potential-method bound merely by knowing the current capacity? Read the complete derivation and reasoning No, for operations satisfying the fixed policy and cost model. The potential bound applies to each legal transition and telescopes for every sequence, including adversarial choices. questions.title: Question 67. Circular singly linked tail deletion
questions.text: Question 67. Circular singly linked tail deletion Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A circular singly linked list stores only tail, with head = tail.next. Does circularity make deleting tail constant time? Read the complete derivation and reasoning No. Its predecessor still has only a forward next link. For n>1 , traverse from head until a node points to tail, then reconnect it to head and update tail. This is Theta( n ). Circularity makes head accessible from tail but does not supply predecessor links. The singleton case is constant and sets the list empty.

questions.title: Question 69. Caching the predecessor in a scan
questions.text: Question 69. Caching the predecessor in a scan Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem A singly linked list is scanned once and selected nodes are removed. Explain how retaining the predecessor avoids repeated searches and how the cursor updates after a removal. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Keep predecessor p and current v=p .next, starting with a head sentinel. If v survives, advance p=v . If v is removed, set p .next =v .next and keep p unchanged; the next candidate is its new successor. Each node is examined once. Searching from head for each victim can produce quadratic work. Tail and size must be updated during deletions.

questions.text: Question 75. Batch insertion at a fixed rank 4 Original/course-derived mathematical problem · author-assessed medium–hard Original mathematical examination-style problem Length is 20, ample capacity exists. Insert 6 new values one by one at the same rank 4, preserving order at each step. Count shifts, total writes, and final order of the newly inserted values x1,…,x6. Read the complete derivation and reasoning Before insertion t (zero-based), length is 20+t and shifts are 16+t . Their sum is 6 ( 20 - 4 ) + 6 ( 6 - 1 ) / 2 = 111 . New-slot writes add 6, giving 117. Since every new insertion precedes the previous ones at rank 4, the new block is x6,…,x1, not insertion order. Resizing is excluded by ample capacity.
